en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Six Pāramitās of the Principles of the Dharma, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra by Imperial Decree.
Chapter One: Taking Refuge in the Triple Gem. Chapter One: Taking Refuge in the Triple Gem.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Bhagavān was staying at the Great City of Rājagṛha, in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove Monastery. At that time, he was together with a great multitude of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression, having fully perfected the ten stages and the ten pāramitās;

and also with a great multitude of bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions, having attained their own welfare, with minds well-liberated and wisdom well-liberated.
Furthermore, there were incalculable numbers of sentient beings who had all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, within this assembly, formed this thought:

"Among the various classes of sentient beings in this assembly, there are those who are impoverished, destitute, and without refuge; they wander through birth and death, submerged in the river of craving."
“Desiring to reach the other shore for the sake of hearing the Dharma, I wish to see the World-Honored One and seek all-knowledge,
yet I lack the power and ability. At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, wishing to inquire into the profound meaning and intent— namely,
how all sentient beings may resolve their minds toward Bodhi and seek the certainty of Buddhahood without weariness throughout the three incalculable eons— [spoke thus].

Now, the intention of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is difficult to fathom; it is vast and profoundly deep, with skillful and perfect phrasing that records the distinctions between the causes and effects of sentient beings, as they aspire for the swift attainment of unsurpassed bodhi.

Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gave rise to such a thought; he immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and brought his six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) into perfect harmony, so that his physical, verbal, and mental actions were entirely tranquil. Yet his six faculties—born of a hundred merits, adorned with the wondrous marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and eighty minor signs (*anuvyañjana*), and perfected over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*)—were further embellished by the radiance of a hundred thousand million suns through the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, such that all sentient beings could gaze upon him without weariness as he drew near to the peerless fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi. With such a body, he proceeded to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground at the Buddha’s feet, and then, with hands adorned by immeasurable merit like freshly bloomed lotuses, joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is able to know the minds of all sentient beings—past, future, and present—in a single thought-moment.”

There may be sentient beings who, through the act of inquiry, attain a pure mind; there may be sentient beings who, at the time of receiving a prophecy, attain the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the fruit of an arhat or the fruit of a pratyekabuddha; or they may receive the prophecy of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For this purpose, I respectfully consult the Tathāgata; I pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain it.
The World-Honored One is now the sovereign refuge for sentient beings of the three periods of time. There may be sentient beings who practice the Mahāyāna path and whose minds are gentle and pliant.
I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion and pity, will grant me the Dharma of the Deathless so that I may not enjoy it alone, but share its flavor with others.
How may you cause all sentient beings to enter the secure and correct path of Great Nirvana?
What should these sentient beings do so that they may attain non-retrogression regarding omniscience?
How should they fulfill the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom?
Furthermore, this Prajñāpāramitā serves as the mother of the preceding five pāramitās; how should one practice it so that they may be brought to fulfillment?
Furthermore, how is this great vow manifested?
And how do all sentient beings cultivate the further shore of nirvana?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will provide a detailed explanation for the sake of benefiting, bringing peace and happiness to, and gladdening all sentient beings.
At that time, the Bhagavān praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! Well-born son!”
That you are now able to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings by inquiring into this profound meaning;
that you constantly strive to cultivate wholesome karma for the sake of sentient beings;
and that you now single-mindedly seek the Dharma with great diligence for the sake of sentient beings in order to suddenly sever their fetters—this is truly commendable.
Because you have now, with this mind of great compassion, fulfilled the ocean-like dharmas of the six perfections over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
because you have now drawn near to the seat of enlightenment and the shore of nirvāṇa.
Just as when the morning star has set, the rising sun shines forth, so it is with you now; you shall become a Buddha-sun.
Listen attentively now and reflect upon this well.
I shall now fully analyze for you this profound meaning.
Just as a person of wisdom who is capable of careful reflection observes that within the perilous path of birth and death, nothing surpasses being without a refuge.

It is like a great ocean-going ship that lacks a merchant captain; the sentient beings within it are largely drifting and drowning, as surging waves and eddies wreck and submerge them. Constantly beset by various perils and anxieties, they seek a propitious and unsurpassed master mariner to rely upon for protection.

Furthermore, all sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death are constantly beset by much fear; therefore, they seek out those who possess power and influence to rely upon as protectors, so as not to be harmed by enemies or thieves.

Even if those enemies and bandits possess great and frenzied power, because they have taken refuge with this person who is a king, those enemies will certainly no longer be able to cause further harm;
moreover, once those enemies perceive his power and influence, they will forever abandon their hostile intentions and submit to his righteous transformation.
All sentient beings are likewise; each thinks to themselves:
"Who can act as a place of refuge for me, removing my misfortunes and afflictions so that I may attain peace and happiness?"

Within these three realms and five destinies—among the hosts of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—one searches for anyone who can act as a refuge, but none exists.

Why is this? Those various devas themselves have not yet escaped the fetters of birth and death; bound by afflictions, they wander through the three realms, being devoured by immeasurable and boundless suffering and overwhelmed by all manner of fears. Since they are entangled in the net of craving and desire, how could they possibly serve as a place of refuge for me?

Furthermore, although the various devas are constantly equipped with armor and the implements of battle, they harbor fear toward those asuras, let alone toward humans and other beings in the various realms of existence.

Observing thus the three realms and the six paths of existence, there is no one capable of pulling me out of [suffering] and saving me; therefore, I should take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Apart from the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, there is no other who can protect and save me.

If all sentient beings desire to seek the bliss of nirvana through unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), they should take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
"By these causes and conditions, all sentient beings are led to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What are called the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha?
And what constitutes taking refuge?
The Buddha addressed Maitreya, saying:
"The Jewel of the Buddha is of two kinds:
first, the Buddha-body; second, the Buddha-virtues.

Regarding the Buddha-body, it refers to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Having, throughout immeasurable and boundless asaṃkhyeya kalpas of the past, diligently cultivated the six pāramitās and the myriad practices without sparing body or life until they were perfected, he sat beneath the Bodhi tree upon the diamond throne, subdued the armies of Māra, severed all the thieves of the fetters, attained all-knowledge, and realized equal and perfect enlightenment. Being endowed with such sublime virtues as these, he is designated as the Buddha."

Regarding the virtues of the Buddha: within the Buddha’s body, he is fully endowed with the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*); the three demonstrations (*triprātihārya*); the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); the samādhis that accord with the mind; the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*) and the two wisdoms (*dvijñāna*). He is detached from the objects of cognition, has severed the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and is free from all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Through the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*), he manifests transformations according to suchness (*tathatā*). Whether far or near, his movement and abiding are sovereign and unimpeded; he can contain immeasurable Sumeru mountains within a single mustard seed.
Such merits are immeasurable and boundless; all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, are fully endowed with them.
Furthermore, from one kalpa to immeasurable kalpas, their lifespan is sovereign and cannot be diminished.
Regarding the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhiviṣaya*), he comes and goes and manifests transformations without obstruction, acting with sovereign ease as he pleases.

To whatever cities or villages the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, travel, they first emit a subtle, golden light that illuminates those places; any sentient beings who encounter this light find their physical and mental ailments completely healed.
Once the fire of the mind was extinguished, his body attained coolness.
Those who were hunched straightened themselves; those who were lame were able to walk; the blind regained their sight; the deaf were able to hear; and the mute were able to speak.
Those whose minds were distracted regained their original state; those possessed by demons, malevolent spirits, or madness were all completely healed.

The naked obtained clothing; those with arrogant minds became humble; the sorrowful found peace of mind; those who had lost their way found the correct path; the hungry and thirsty obtained food and drink; those in bondage attained liberation; and those in fear attained fearlessness.

Hills, mounds, ravines, gullies, mountain torrents, and ridges were all made level and smooth as if pressed by the palm of a hand; low and narrow gateways naturally became tall and grand; cramped streets and alleys all became wide and spacious; markets and residential quarters naturally opened up and cleared; filth and impurities were instantly rendered fragrant and pure; and thorns, brambles, tiles, rubble, sand, and stones entirely disappeared.

The sunlight shone brilliantly yet was devoid of scorching heat; the fragrant breeze blew harmoniously and pleasantly, free from all dust and grime. White cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāris, kalaviṅkas, kokilas, kuṇālas, and jīvañjīvakas—these birds produced sounds of exquisite beauty and refined, elegant melodies.
Elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, water buffaloes, yak, gayals, and rhinoceroses each uttered their natural cries, their sounds being subtle and exquisite.
Lutes, harps, flutes, pipes, zithers, lyres, drums, and wind instruments—such musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
Furthermore, he manifested all manner of various clever, marvelous, and extraordinary supernatural feats.
Such diverse and wondrous events varied day by day, becoming increasingly sublime; all were due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
If there are sentient beings who doubt whether the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the Buddha’s merits are identical or distinct, one should speak to them thus:
"The Buddha and his merits are neither identical nor distinct."
It is like lighting a lamp: the oil, the wick, and the light are neither identical nor different; apart from the oil and the wick, there is no separate lamp-light.
If one were to say that the lamp-light exists apart from the oil and the wick, then wherever that light reaches, everything should be consumed by fire.
The merits of the Buddha’s body are likewise so.
This subtle and wondrous body is the Buddha’s merit-based, untainted *dharmakāya*, serving as the equal basis for the enjoyment of both oneself and others.
However, this Buddha-body is also not a substantial entity; apart from such an entity, there is no separate Dharma-body.
If it were a substantial entity, it would possess the characteristics of the four great elements like external objects.
Therefore, one knows that it is neither with marks nor without marks.
If it were without marks, it would be identical to great empty space; being identical to great emptiness, its nature would be eternal, which entails the fault of lacking expedient means.

It is naturally pure, unstained, and unattached; profoundly deep, immeasurable, and immutable; difficult to understand and difficult to know, subtle and tranquil; endowed with boundless, true, and eternal virtues, transcending all conceptual proliferation.
Only the Buddha realizes this; it is beyond the reach of others and cannot be measured by means of analogy.

Maitreya, you should know that such a body as this is the characteristic of the *dharmakāya* of all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The Buddha’s reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) refers to the boundless, true merits produced by all Tathāgatas through their cultivation and accumulation of immeasurable provisions of merit and wisdom over three incalculable eons. It is eternally abiding and immutable, characterized by the primary and secondary marks; its light of wisdom pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*. Because it arises from supramundane, untainted roots of goodness, it is inconceivable and transcends worldly cognition. To bring sentient beings to full maturity, this form is manifested, expounding inexhaustible teachings to extensively benefit the infinite.
Maitreya! You should know that this is the perfection of the Tathāgata’s *saṃbhogakāya*.
As for the *nirmāṇakāya*, in order to transform those sentient beings according to what is appropriate for each, he manifests immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* bodies of transformation Buddhas.

As for his emanated bodies, he may manifest his form within the hells to deliver those sentient beings, causing them to leave behind all sufferings; by guiding them with the True Dharma, he inspires in them a superior resolve, whereby they are reborn among humans or devas to experience sublime happiness. Within the Buddha-dharma, they develop deep faith and joy, attaining a portion of the Buddha’s teachings and realizing the fruits of the Noble Path.

Or they may be born in the realm of hungry ghosts to transform those sentient beings, causing them to leave behind the various oppressions of hunger and thirst; by transforming them with the True Dharma, they cause them to give rise to a superior resolve, whereby they are reborn among humans or devas to experience all manner of happiness, and deeply enter the Buddha-dharma to attain the fruits of the Noble Path.

Alternatively, he may manifest as an animal within that realm, or take the form of a *garuḍa*, or a nāga, or the body of a lion, elephant, horse, bear, brown bear, tiger, leopard, jackal, wolf, wild dog, fox, rabbit, viper, snake, scorpion, fish, turtle, tortoise, crocodile, white crane, peacock, phoenix, mandarin duck, parrot, śāli bird, or various other forms. He causes all sentient beings to cease their mutual harm and to face one another with a heart of loving-kindness; he enables them to escape various fears and terrors, and reveals the True Dharma so that they may develop deep faith and joy, taking refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. Thus they attain birth among humans or devas to experience all manner of happiness, and gain a portion of the Buddha-dharma to realize the fruits of the Noble Path.

Or they may transform sentient beings in other lands, or in various places where the Buddha-dharma does not exist—such as those not illuminated by the sun or moon—establishing the True Dharma there. They cause sentient beings to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; they shave off their hair and beards to receive the Buddhist precepts, becoming bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, or becoming upāsakas and upāsikās. They establish monasteries to protect and uphold the True Dharma, establishing immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings and placing them on the further shore of human, celestial, and nirvanic fruition, thereby attaining the realization of the fruits.

Or they may be born in the celestial realms to transform those sentient beings, causing them to abandon the five desires so that their minds are free from attachment; they lead them by means of the True Dharma to resolve upon Bodhicitta, take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and enter deeply into the True Dharma, establishing them in the realization of the fruit of Nirvana and liberation.

Or, taking birth in the human realm, manifesting within a royal palace in the Śākya clan, he employs skillful means to transform sentient beings, severing the afflictions, anxieties, and sufferings of the three realms—namely birth, aging, sickness, and death. Thus, he manifests birth, the departure from the city, the grasping of auspicious grass beneath the Bodhi tree, sitting upon the Vajra Seat at the site of enlightenment, subduing the demonic armies, and attaining Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. To transform sentient beings, he turns the Wheel of the True Dharma, emitting great radiance that pervades all things and illuminates the world. With both self-benefit and the benefit of others fully perfected, he may further manifest a state of quiescence and enter Great Parinirvāṇa; this is what is called the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body) of the Buddha.
Such various skillful means are immeasurable and boundless; they are all the sovereign spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
This is precisely the three bodies (trikāya), whose essence is without any difference in characteristics.
At that time, the Bhagavat addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son,
what do you think?"
If there are sons or daughters of good family who take refuge in the Buddha, they should take refuge in the pure *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas.
If they wish to seek the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*, they should make this great vow:
“May I and all sentient beings attain such a *dharmakāya* of merit.”
Why, then, should one make such a vow?

Because the Buddha’s response-body (nirmāṇakāya) undergoes momentary transformation, and the emanation-body (upapattikāya) quickly enters parinirvāṇa, whereas the merit-dharma body (guṇadharmakāya) is profoundly and eternally abiding; it is for this reason that one takes refuge in the pure dharma body.
To take refuge in the Dharma-body is to take refuge in all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
If I were to abandon sentient beings to attain nirvana for myself, I would be subject to the same various sufferings as those in hell.
If one attains liberation together with all sentient beings, then even while dwelling in hell, there is no difference from nirvana.

By these causes and conditions, one leads all sentient beings to take refuge in the Buddha’s Dharmakāya and realize the bliss of nirvana; ultimately, the essence of suchness neither increases nor decreases.
Such a Dharma-body is true peace and bliss; therefore, one should only cause others to take refuge in the Buddha’s Dharma-body.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!
What is called the pure Dharma-jewel?"
The Dharma Jewel also has three kinds. What are these three? The first Dharma Jewel is so-called *nirvāṇa*, the ambrosia of liberation;
it takes as its essential nature permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and is able to bring an end to all birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction.
What is the suffering of birth?

It refers to when, based on the union of the parents, the impure seed enters the mother’s womb; sustained by the winds of karma for nine months, one dwells in pitch darkness without light, amidst the filth between the stomach and the intestines, mixed with eighty thousand types of worms. Following the mother’s exhalations and inhalations, one cannot speak with the mouth nor see with the eyes, while various sufferings such as hunger, thirst, cold, and heat oppress both body and mind.
Such sufferings are immeasurable and boundless, depriving all sentient beings of their autonomy; therefore, they are called the suffering of birth.
Although one undergoes this suffering, there is a single virtue that no enemy can perceive, nor can they speak of its faults, errors, or evils.
In the peerless, blissful Dharma of Nirvana, such suffering does not exist. What is the suffering of old age?

It refers to the passage of time from youth to old age, wherein all that was full and robust is entirely diminished: physical strength decays and movements become unsteady; the hair turns white and the face becomes wrinkled; the eyes and ears grow dim; the teeth fall out and become sparse; the countenance becomes ugly and the body hunches, becoming loathed and despised by others; and one forgets whatever teachings were spoken as they are uttered—bearing this very body as a heavy burden.
It is like lighting a lamp: once the oil and the wick are exhausted, it will soon go out.
Old age is likewise; once the vigor of youth is spent, death will soon follow.
It is also like a *sumokṣa* cap covering a person’s face and head, causing all sentient beings who see it to mock them.
The old Su-mo-cha was likewise; traveling from one city to another, all sentient beings who saw him wearing the cap of old age would mock him.
For these reasons, old age is a great suffering; except for death, there is no medicine that can cure it.
Yet, despite undergoing the suffering of old age, people do not weary of it, but instead pray to the deities, constantly wishing for long life.
Within the incomparable Dharma of the peace and bliss of Nirvana, this suffering of old age does not exist.
What is the suffering of illness?

It refers to the mutual conflict and injury among the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, whereby various kinds of suffering gather within one's body; all sentient beings, regardless of whether they are young or old, share this in common.
He completely abandons the supreme and exquisite five desires that bring peace and comfort to the body, as well as gold, silver, rare treasures, family, and retinue.
All instructions and admonitions are disregarded by his sons, daughters, and relatives; all enemies approach him with feigned intimacy.
Such sufferings of illness are not to be desired; by this one should know that illness is a great suffering.
Within the incomparable dharma of peaceful nirvana, there is pure stillness and no such suffering of illness.
"Furthermore, Maitreya! What is the suffering of death?

It refers to the cessation of breath and the extinction of consciousness in sentient beings, such that there is no longer any perception or cognition; among all forms of suffering, none exceeds the suffering of death."
The sufferings of birth, old age, and illness exist with varying degrees of certainty within the five destinies; however, this suffering of death is common to all.

Just as the suffering of poverty can dispel splendor and glory, and the suffering of enmity and hatred can dispel affection, so too when the suffering of death arrives, it spares neither the young nor the old, neither the foolish nor the wise, neither the noble nor the lowly—it sweeps away everyone without exception.
Once this body has been cast off and one enters the realm of profound darkness, clothing, bedding, and all wealth and treasures can no longer be used.
One wanders naked and alone without a companion; though possessed of goods and riches, one cannot avoid [suffering], and there is no place to turn for a plea.

Alas! Impermanence can inflict such harm; it is utterly base and evil, making no distinction between enemy and kin. No sentient being within the three realms can escape it; all are struck down by death—how can one possibly save them?
Even if one were to capture a universal monarch (cakravartin) endowed with the strength of Nārāyaṇa, one should know that the suffering of death is immeasurable and boundless.
Observing it in this way, one realizes that death is a great suffering.
Within the peerless Dharma of liberation and nirvana, there is tranquil peace and bliss, free from this suffering of death.
It is like a person swept away and drowning in a torrential river who, by climbing a high mountain, escapes all fear.

Sentient beings are likewise; they are constantly swept away and drowned by the torrential river of all birth and death. By ascending the mountain of nirvāṇa, they leave behind the fear of birth and death.

It is also like rain from heaven, which can eliminate obstacles such as poisonous heat and filth; the people find peace and happiness, their bodies and minds become cool and refreshing, and the hundred plants flourish and bear fruit.

The Dharma rain of the Tathāgata is likewise: it can eliminate the poisonous heat of all afflictions, bringing sentient beings peace, happiness, liberation, and coolness; it nurtures all seeds of pure, white virtue, bringing them to fruition so that they may attain nirvāṇa.
"For this reason, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, relinquish their impermanent bodies and realize the bliss of nirvana.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The wondrous body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body; Pure liberation is identical with ultimate truth."
Just as the sun and its light are inseparable, the Tathāgata’s virtues are themselves nirvāṇa; the true self and the Buddha are without distinction, the ultimate refuge for all sentient beings.
Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are equal and non-dual; their nature is indestructible and without fabrication.
Defilement and purity are suchness, their nature no different; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, alone can fully realize this.
All sentient beings possess the Tathāgatagarbha, and thus the Triple Gem manifests in the world.
All sentient beings enter the Buddha’s wisdom, for their nature is pure and without distinction.
The nature of the Buddha and that of sentient beings are not different; ordinary people perceive difference, while the sages see no discrepancy.
All sentient beings are fundamentally pure; thus the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have taught in unison.
Its nature is neither defiled nor pure from the very beginning; sentient beings and Buddhas are without distinction.
Emptiness pervades the ten directions without discrimination, and the equality of the mind-nature is likewise so.

Just as the realms of all sentient beings pervade empty space and undergo birth and extinction, so too do the sense faculties undergo birth and extinction; their abiding within the unconditioned realm is likewise thus.
Just as fire does not burn empty space, Birth-and-death cannot destroy the nature of the unconditioned;
The wheels of earth, water, and wind revolve in mutual dependence, Yet empty space has no characteristic of being supported.
The same applies to the aggregates, bases, and elements; they constantly abide within the nature of karmic seeds and afflictions.
Where do those karmas and afflictions abide?
They dwell perpetually in the source of delusive conceptualization and ignorance.
Where does the mind of false conceptualization dwell?
It constantly abides in the nature of the unconditioned, pure mind.
The three—aggregates, bases, and elements—are merely provisional designations; the nature of all phenomena is fundamentally non-abiding.
Karma and afflictions support one another like earth and water; deluded thoughts and movements are like the wind.
The nature of the mind is fundamentally pure like space; deluded thoughts depend on space and possess nothing in themselves.
Afflictions, karma, and suffering arise from delusion; Karma and suffering, in turn, become the causes of affliction.
Delusion, karma, and suffering circulate without fixed abode; They have no cause, no condition, and no point of convergence.
Without arising or ceasing, its nature is empty and quiescent; its fundamental substance is luminous and its wisdom is pure.
Its self-nature is neither born nor subject to change, yet it is shrouded by the defilements of afflictions and ignorance.
Just as one with cataracts sees two moons, so too do sentient beings hold dualistic attachments;
afflictions are like a swarm of bees, and their honey is a metaphor for the Tathāgatagarbha.
This honey is surrounded on all sides by a swarm of bees; the wise person, protecting themselves, is able to take the honey.
Using the signless six perfections as skillful means, they are able to realize that Dharma-realm body.
Just as the five grains, while their husks remain unremoved, are unfit to provide a fine meal for others;
so too, as long as a bodhisattva has not cast off the chaff of afflictions, they cannot bestow the nectar-food upon others.
If a traveler drops a treasure in a defiled place, even after ten thousand years it remains unsullied;
one with the divine eye sees the treasure and knows its location, so they retrieve it, wash and wipe it clean, and use it as they please.
The Buddha perceives that the nature of sentient beings is non-dual; Desiring to cleanse away the filth of afflictions, he uses the ambrosia of the Mahāyāna as water.

When the dust of worldly toil is entirely washed away, the Buddha-nature manifests, Like newly sprouted shoots of the five grains. At this stage, it is not yet determined whether the rice exists or not.
The Buddha-nature is not apart from existence and non-existence; Only the Buddhas, through their own realization, fully comprehend it.
The intrinsic nature of the Dharma-treasure is eternally pure; Thus have the World-Honored Buddhas spoken.
Enshrouded by adventitious afflictions, like clouds obscuring the radiance of the sun;
yet the stainless jewel of the Dharma is replete with all virtues, its permanence, bliss, self, and purity fully perfected.
How is the purity of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) to be sought?
It is realized through non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna).
Just as the water in a pond is pure and stainless, with lotuses therein that are wondrous and untainted;
Just as the moon regains its brilliance after an eclipse, And like the bright sun emerging from the clouds,
Adorned everywhere with stainless merit, The light of wisdom appears, having washed away all afflictions.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
“You should know that the foremost Jewel of the Dharma is the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, the Dharma-body of liberation.
Furthermore, Maitreya!”

One should know that the second Jewel of the Dharma refers to the sublime qualities of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), namely the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*):

the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*), the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*), the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*), the five powers (*pañca balāni*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*), and the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārgaḥ*).
These thirty-seven factors serve as the skillful means for the aforementioned pure Dharma-treasure.
What are these skillful means?
By practicing these factors, one is able to realize that pure Dharma-body.
"You should know that this is the second Jewel of the Dharma. Furthermore, Maitreya,
what is called the third Jewel of the Dharma?"

The sublime Dharma taught by the immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past—this very same Dharma I shall now likewise proclaim. That is to say, the eighty-four thousand aggregates of sublime Dharma, which tame and bring to maturity sentient beings with whom I have a karmic connection, such that Ānanda and the other great disciples, upon hearing them but once, shall all remember and uphold them.
These are condensed into five divisions: first, the Sūtras; second, the Vinaya; third, the Abhidharma; fourth, the Prajñāpāramitā; and fifth, the Gateways of Dhāraṇī.
These five collections of the treasury teach and transform sentient beings, speaking according to those who are to be delivered.

If there are sentient beings who delight in dwelling among mountains and forests, constantly abiding in seclusion to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), for them he teaches the Sūtra-piṭaka.
If those sentient beings delight in practicing dignified conduct and in upholding the True Dharma, so that it may endure for a long time through harmonious unity, he teaches them the Vinaya Piṭaka.

If those sentient beings delight in expounding the true Dharma, analyzing its nature and characteristics, and investigate them exhaustively until reaching the ultimate profundity, for their sake he teaches the Abhidharma Piṭaka.

If those sentient beings delight in practicing the true wisdom of the Mahāyāna and are free from the conceptual clinging to a self and to phenomena, he teaches them the treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā.

If those sentient beings are unable to uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, the Abhidharma, or the Prajñāpāramitā; or if there are sentient beings who have committed various evil deeds—such as the four grave offenses, the eight grave offenses, the five crimes of immediate retribution, slandering the Vaipulya sūtras, or being icchantikas and other such heavy transgressions—and you wish to cause them to be extinguished and swiftly attain liberation and sudden awakening to nirvāṇa, you should preach for them the treasury of dhāraṇīs.

These five treasuries of Dharma are like milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, and the exquisite *sarpis* (cream of ghee). The *Sūtras* are like milk; the *Vinaya* is like curd; the teachings of the *Abhidharma* are like fresh butter; the Mahāyāna *Prajñāpāramitā* is like clarified butter; and the gateways of *Dhāraṇī* are like *sarpis*. Just as the flavor of *sarpis* is the most subtle and supreme among milk, curd, and butter, capable of removing all ailments and bringing peace and happiness to the body and mind of all sentient beings, so too are these five treasuries of Dharma.

The gateway of dhāraṇī is the foremost among the sūtras and other scriptures; it can eliminate grave offenses and enable all sentient beings to be liberated from birth and death, swiftly realizing the blissful dharma-body of nirvāṇa.

"Furthermore, Maitreya! After my parinirvāṇa, let Ānanda uphold the Sūtra Piṭaka that I have taught; let Upāli uphold the Vinaya Piṭaka that I have taught; let Kātyāyana uphold the Abhidharma Piṭaka that I have taught; let the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī uphold the Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā that I have taught; and let the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi uphold the profound and subtle gateways of dhāraṇī that I have taught."
This teaching is able to dispel the long night of darkness of the afflictions of birth and death for sentient beings, enabling them to swiftly transcend and realize the fruit of liberation.

Just as a bright lamp can remove the gloom of darkness so that one may see the path, so too is the Buddha; he kindles the torch of wisdom to illuminate the darkness of the ten unwholesome paths of sentient beings, enabling them to see the path of virtue.
If those sentient beings are stingy with wealth and treasures, upon hearing this Dharma they will immediately practice generosity toward all who are poor;
if there are sentient beings with evil karma, upon hearing this Dharma they will abandon evil and cultivate goodness;
and if there are those who harbor anger, they will be able to practice patience.
Upon hearing this, sentient beings who are indolent become diligent;
those who are distracted become tranquil;
and foolish sentient beings, having heard this Dharma, give rise to wisdom. Having attained wisdom, they are all able to turn their minds toward the cultivation of various kinds of goodness.

Furthermore, when sentient beings hear this Dharma, they close the gates to the evil realms and open the path to Nirvana; it is like nectar that brings about the realization of the fruit of liberation.
You should know that this is the third Jewel of the Dharma.
Regarding these Three Jewels, all sentient beings should take refuge in the unconditioned Jewel of Dharma; among all phenomena, nothing is more honored or supreme than the unconditioned.

Why is this? Because it can serve as a boat or raft amidst the great ocean of the suffering of birth and death; it can act as the excellent medicine of nectar for sentient beings; and it is the fruit realized by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, through the six perfections and myriad practices over three incalculable eons.
Thus, the merits of this sublime Dharma are perfected; by means of this, one takes refuge in the unconditioned Jewel of the Dharma.
If there are sentient beings who receive and uphold this sutra, they should make this vow:
"May I take refuge in such a Jewel of the Dharma."
Having taken refuge in this Dharma, I vow that all sentient beings of the five realms shall likewise give rise to this aspiration:
"I now take refuge.
May they also cause sentient beings to dwell securely within these meritorious dharmas and lead them to the true jewel-treasury of Nirvāṇa.
"Maitreya! You should know that this is called the third Jewel of the Dharma.
Furthermore, Maitreya!"
What is called the true Sangha Jewel?
Regarding the Sangha Jewel, there are also three kinds:
the first is the Sangha of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-saṃgha).
That which is called the noble Saṅgha of the Buddhas abides in accordance with the Dharma:
it cannot be seen, cannot be grasped, cannot be destroyed, cannot be burned or harmed, and is the inconceivable field of merit and blessing for all sentient beings.

Although they serve as fields of merit, they accept nothing and grasp at nothing; all their meritorious qualities are eternally unchanging. This is called the Sangha of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-saṃgha*).

"The second, the Noble Sangha (*ārya-saṃgha*), refers to those on the path to and those who have attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*; those on the path to and those who have attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*; those on the path to and those who have attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*; those on the path to and those who have attained the fruit of *arhat*; those on the path to and those who have attained the fruit of *pratyekabuddha*; and the eight types of noble awareness, the three levels of worthies, and the ten stages of sages."
This is called the second Jewel of the Saṅgha.
"The third, the Saṅgha of the Field of Merit, consists of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others who uphold the prohibitive precepts and possess great learning and wisdom;
they are like the celestial *kalpavṛkṣa* tree, capable of providing shade for all sentient beings."

Furthermore, it is like a person parched with thirst in a vast wilderness or a desert who encounters a celestial rain falling in copious torrents, thereby being fully satisfied according to their need.
It is also like the great ocean, from which all manner of precious jewels emerge.
The Sangha Jewel as a field of merit is likewise able to bestow peace and happiness upon sentient beings.

Furthermore, this Sangha Jewel is pure and unstained; it can extinguish the darkness of greed, hatred, and delusion within sentient beings, just like the light of the full moon on the fifteenth night, which all sentient beings gaze upon with reverence.
It is also like a mani jewel, capable of fulfilling all the virtuous aspirations of sentient beings.
This is called the third Jewel of the Saṅgha.
Regarding these three Jewels of the Saṅgha, how do all sentient beings take refuge?
It should be stated as follows:
"One should cause them to take refuge in the Sangha Jewel of the unconditioned ultimate truth. Why is this?

Because this is the Sangha that is unconditioned and eternally abiding; and because this Sangha Jewel is the dharma of self-realization—untainted, unconditioned, immutable, and non-differentiated. By taking refuge in such an untainted Sangha Jewel, one is able to extinguish all the sufferings of sentient beings."
Furthermore, I vow that sentient beings shall likewise attain such untainted merit; having attained this Dharma, may they expound the Three Vehicles to deliver all sentient beings.

I take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha not out of fear of the sufferings of the three evil realms, nor with the desire for rebirth among humans or devas, but with the solemn oath to rescue sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death.
"This is what is called taking refuge in the Sangha Jewel.
"Furthermore, Maitreya! If there are sentient beings who take refuge in the Three Jewels, they should give rise to this thought:"

"Now that this body of mine has been born into the human realm and has attained freedom from the eight difficulties—having achieved what is difficult to achieve—I shall, through skillful means, practice all the most excellent and sublime dharmas."
If I were to violate such a supreme vow and fail to seek the wholesome Dharma, I would be deceiving myself.
It would be like someone who boards a ship and enters the ocean, yet returns empty-handed after reaching the place of treasures.
"Since taking refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha is the expedient means for liberation from suffering, what can be done if one regrets it after failing to take refuge?
Having understood this, you must exert yourself and practice with diligence, swiftly aspiring for its accomplishment."
Once the wholesome dharmas have been accomplished, one should repent of past transgressions so that they may be eliminated.
Furthermore, one should say:

"From beginningless birth and death until now, the various offenses committed by my body, speech, and mind are immeasurable and boundless; all arise from a mind of false and inverted views. Regarding the offenses committed toward my parents, preceptors, teachers, elders, and the revered objects of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha Jewels—I now repent of them all."
Furthermore, for two reasons one commits various offenses and extremely grave evil karma as vast as Mount Sumeru.
What are these two? First, affectionate attachment; second, resentment and aversion.

If, amidst the urgent perils of saṃsāra, those two classes of sentient beings—both enemies and kin—are unable to benefit my person, I should examine this thoroughly: since both they and my own body will ultimately return to total extinction, why should I commit such a transgression?

Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions who perform various wholesome deeds, as well as those in training and those beyond training, the pratyekabuddhas, the śrāvakas, the Buddhas, and their disciples—all noble ones and sages—I rejoice in them all.

Furthermore, throughout the beginningless cycle of birth and death, as I have received bodies within the five destinies, there has never been even a hair’s breadth of benefit obtained from my immeasurable enemies and kin; such benefit shall likewise not be found in the present or the future. For all the sins I have committed toward those enemies and kin since beginningless time, I vow to undergo them myself, swearing never to disturb any other sentient being.

When I am afflicted by a grave illness and seek out those who are dear and beloved to care for me with compassion, to attend to my body, to massage and wash me, to provide food and drink, and to assist me in various ways with medicines for my sickness and emaciation—even though they do all this, there is none among them who can take upon themselves the suffering of my illness; how much less could anyone save me from the great suffering of birth and death in the future?
In this present life, this body of mine is without refuge or protector; how much more so will it be in the future?
Since it is thus with my own body, so it is with all sentient beings; as both myself and others lack any reliance, I therefore take refuge in the true Triple Gem.
Why is this? Because it is eternally abiding.
It is like a wise person who, amidst peril and hardship, seeks out one of great strength for protection.
Sentient beings are likewise; in the perilous difficulties of birth and death, they must take refuge in the Triple Gem as their lord before they can cross over the great river of saṃsāra.
Once I have attained [enlightenment], I too shall act as their lord, providing protection for all sentient beings who suffer.

One who is able to make such a great vow attains great faith; then, before the Buddha, kneeling with palms joined and the right shoulder bared, they take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

For example, in the world, when all sentient beings see a person who is poor and lowly, they treat them with contempt, subjecting them to forced labor and service, and insulting and humiliating their person in various ways.
Once they have been treated with contempt and disdain, they seek out a person of noble status and great power to serve as their master, whereby they are able to escape various forms of humiliation.

Sentient beings are likewise: whether born in the evil realms or among humans, they are constantly oppressed in their bodies by manifold sufferings; by seeking refuge in the Triple Gem to escape these conditions, they attain liberation from all such sufferings.
Having taken refuge in the Triple Gem, one further makes this vow:
"May I rescue and protect all sentient beings, ferrying them across the ocean of birth and death to the shore of nirvana, like a great caravan leader guiding his merchants."

Just as one who crosses a vast wilderness of shifting sands and perilous paths reaches a place of fearlessness, so too is the Guide of the Three Jewels: he leads sentient beings across the desolate expanse of the long night of saṃsāra, reaching great nirvāṇa and attaining fearlessness.
"Maitreya! You should know that those who have resolved their minds to practice the Mahāyāna path should take refuge in the Three Jewels in this manner.
*Mahāyānanayaṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*, Fascicle One.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Six Pāramitās According to the Principles of the Dharma, Scroll Second.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Two: The Dhāraṇī for Protecting and Sustaining the Realm. Chapter Two: The Dhāraṇī for Protecting and Sustaining the Realm.

At that time, when the Blessed One desired to proclaim the profound principle of the definitive meaning—the six pāramitās of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas—a great radiance appeared in the eastern direction, a golden brilliance that illuminated the Great City of Rājagṛha, the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery, and even the entire trichiliocosm, turning them all the color of gold.

Furthermore, all the lights of every deity in this world—the Four World-Protecting Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, up to the King of the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations and the Great Brahmā King—as well as the light of the sun, moon, stars, mani-jewels, lamps, and candles, could not compare [to it]. With the exception of the two kinds of light belonging to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and those Bodhisattvas who have received the consecration and office, all other lights were completely eclipsed and no longer appeared.

Furthermore, in this trichiliocosm, there are places not reached by the majestic light of the sun and moon; though these suns and moons possess great majesty and great radiance, they cannot illuminate those sentient beings dwelling in such dark obscurity.
By means of the Buddha’s radiance, those sentient beings are each enabled to see one another.
Furthermore, all the palaces, dwellings, walls, mountains, forests, grasses, trees, and various other objects within these worlds cannot obstruct such light.

All the mountains—the Fragrant Mountain, the Jewel Mountain, the Black Mountains, the Snowy Mountains, and Mount Sumeru; the Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, Mount Mucilinda, and Mount Mahāmucilinda—encountering this light, their shadows passed through both inside and outside without any obstruction.
Reaching downward as far as the Avīci Hell and upward as far as the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, all were likewise bathed in light, with none left unilluminated.
Thus, all the lights existing within this trichiliocosm merged into a single light, devoid of dual characteristics.
Among them, those sentient beings who encountered this light had all their karmic defilements and afflictions eliminated; with bodies and minds at peace and happiness, each thought to themselves:
"We have received this light and attained such peace and happiness."

At that time, suddenly sixty koṭis of seven-jeweled lotus flowers, as large as chariot wheels, welled up from the earth within the assembly. Their fragrance was exquisite, their colors were beautiful, and their various hues were such that they delighted the sight of all who beheld them.
Each and every flower, moreover, possesses immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of petals.

In the midst of the assembly, within the void of space, there spontaneously appear subtle and wondrous jeweled canopies and nets of pearls interlaced together, covering the entire great assembly; they are as soft and exquisite as kācalindika cloth, bringing delight to the touch.

The fragrance emanating from within those lotuses pervaded the trichiliocosm; such that all the celestial perfumes, the perfumes of nāgas and devas, and the various scents of grasses and trees existing throughout those worlds were rendered scentless in comparison to this fragrance.

Furthermore, throughout this trichiliocosm, various sentient beings, having been perfumed by the incense, were overcome with such joy that they all resolved their minds toward enlightenment; all their afflictions, karmic offenses, and defilements were entirely extinguished.

At that time, Ānanda, seeing this light and its rare phenomenon—extraordinary, sublime, and unprecedented—immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
By what causes and conditions has this extraordinary sign of radiance appeared?
This light, along with these precious flowers and incense, have never before been heard of or seen; from where have they come to manifest such an auspicious omen?
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain this, so that this entire assembly may all hear and know it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:

“You should now know that to the east of here there is a world named Akṣobhya. Therein dwells a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Akṣayakośa, who, surrounded and venerated by a great assembly of sixty koṭis of bodhisattvas, has resolved to come; for this reason, he has manifested these auspicious signs.”

When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, this great earth shook in six ways; that Bodhisattva Akṣayagarbha emitted great radiance and manifested great supernormal transformations, his majestic power and sovereignty raining down exquisite fragrant flowers, while immeasurable devas welcomed the Bodhisattva with various kinds of music as an offering.

The Bodhisattva Akṣayakośa, together with an assembly of sixty koṭis of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, came to this Karanda Bamboo Grove Monastery. They remained suspended in mid-air at a height of seven *tāla* trees, all joining their palms in reverent salutation toward the Buddha. With voices of one accord, their sound pervading the trichiliocosm, they praised the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata and spoke these verses in sublime tones:

"O Great One! Great Awakening, free from attachment, Unobstructed wondrous wisdom, eye of purity, Who has severed the three poisons and the habits of ignorance— I pay homage to the Peerless Honored One of Great Compassion!"
Far removed from fear and the web of all doubts, possessing the ten powers and eloquence without dread, all followers of heterodox paths tremble before him; he is sovereign like the lion king.
The Tathāgata’s sun of wisdom emits great radiance, Universally illuminating the ten directions without obstruction.

The darkness of ignorance and the veil of delusion are exhausted; Like the sun spreading its light upon the world, For those who have no support or reliance amidst suffering and calamity, Who have long drifted through birth, old age, sickness, and death—
The Great Compassionate Honored One of True Reality, Who can pull one from the hardships of the ocean of saṃsāra;
Ignorance and inversion are the source of birth and death, With various delusive thoughts as its waves.
Having eliminated the two obscurations, his wisdom is sovereign, Wandering unsoiled like a lotus flower.
All phenomena are selfless, fundamentally empty and quiescent; Like echoes in a valley, their nature is entirely void.
Without creator and without recipient, they are like illusions and transformations— Thus does the Great Compassionate Savior ever proclaim.
The Buddha perceives all phenomena as like floating clouds, And like a torrential waterfall swiftly flowing on;
Worldly dharmas are not solid, being gathered by the ignorant, But noble wisdom can observe them and forever eliminate them.
The Buddha’s eye is like a blue lotus flower, surpassing the sun and moon a hundred thousandfold;
praised together by the world of gods and humans throughout the three periods of time, I pay homage to the inconceivable Tamer of Men.
The Buddha is endowed with such boundless virtues, Broadly delivering all classes of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
With the wondrous adornment of untainted merit, I now prostrate myself before him with my head to the ground.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, together with an assembly of sixty koṭis of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having praised the Tathāgata with these sublime verses, descended from the sky. Prostrating with their heads at his feet and circumambulating him seven times to the right, they followed the Buddha’s holy command and each sat cross-legged upon a lotus flower.
At that time, Ānanda, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From where has this Bodhisattva Akṣayagarbha come?"
What is the name of the Buddha in that world?
How far is it from here?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this in detail.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda: "Ask him yourself;
the Bodhisattva Akṣayagarbha shall explain it for you."
Then Ānanda asked the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayagarbha,
"Noble son! From where have you come?"
What is the name of the Buddha in that world?
How far is it from here?
I only pray that you will explain this for me.
Then the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said,
"Do you still possess the marks of coming and going that have not yet been eliminated? Ānanda replied:
"I have long known this meaning.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayagarbha said:
"If you already know it, why do you ask again?"
Thereupon, two kinds of discriminative thoughts arise:
if one says "coming," it has the meaning of dependent origination; if one says "going," it has the meaning of the cessation of conditions.
Where, then, is there no such characteristic of arising and ceasing?
However, my land has no characteristics of coming or going, arising or ceasing; if there is no coming or going, it is the sphere traversed by noble wisdom;
if there were coming or going, it would be the characteristic of worldly arising and ceasing.
If there are sounds or written characters, these too are phenomena of the world that arise and perish, emerge and cease.
However, in my land, there are fundamentally no written characters, nor are there any phenomena of speech arising or ceasing.
"If there is neither arising nor ceasing, this is the sphere of activity of the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
To be free from the marks of words is liberation.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, saying:

“Noble One! I did not dare to ask the Great Being of Eloquence about such profound and subtle meanings; I have merely asked about matters I have never heard before—namely, the distance from here to the world where you dwell and the name of that Buddha.”

For example, it is like a person collecting taxes at a frontier pass; as long as there is traffic passing through, they inquire of everyone without discriminating between the quantity or presence of wealth and treasures.
Now, my śrāvakas are also like this: hearing the sound of the True Dharma from others, they cultivate with resolute understanding and seek nirvāṇa for themselves; thus they are called śrāvakas.
Now that I behold the Noble One, it is according to the Dharma that I should question him.
Having heard his response, I wish to practice it for the sake of attaining peace and happiness, and because I desire to increase the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) teachings.
Furthermore, because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas emerge from the Mahāyāna, I asked:
"Noble one, from where have you come?"
"How far is it from here?
What is the name of that Buddha?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayagarbha replied to Ānanda:
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is not far away; why do you not ask him?
The Buddha will provide you with a prophetic declaration regarding this matter, so that everyone in this assembly may be free from doubt.”
Then Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes so that his right shoulder was bared, knelt down with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha:
"I pray only that the Great Sage, the World-Honored One, will explain this for me; I pray only that the Sugata will explain this for me."
"In this assembly, immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, having heard this Dharma, all desire to don the armor of diligence and cultivate the bodhisattva practices.
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Listen now attentively and reflect upon it well."
I shall now analyze and explain for you the matters concerning the distance to that Buddha-world, as well as the names of the Buddhas and their adornments of merit.
That Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who possesses unimpeded and unattached omniscience—this you, the great assembly, should all believe and accept, and harbor no fear or doubt.
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Great Sage, World-Honored One!
I now wish most earnestly to hear [this].”
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed Ānanda:
"To the east of here, passing through worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Gaṅgā rivers, there is a world named Animiṣā."

In that world dwells a Bhagavān named Samantabhadra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
At present, he is preaching the Mahāyāna Dharma there; the Bodhisattva Akṣayagarbha has come from that world to this place.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, has only great Bodhisattvas as his assembly; even the names of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not exist there, let alone their actual presence.

That bodhisattva has long accumulated pure karma; through generosity and self-mastery, he has well disciplined the six sense faculties. He constantly practices patience without obstruction, remains firm in his resolve for bodhi, and diligently exerts himself in vigor. He has perfected skillful meditative concentration, liberation, *samādhi*, and *samāpatti*. He sports with supernatural powers and the radiance of great wisdom, possessing mastery and unimpeded eloquence in the art of language. His kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity are like space; he is able to utterly subdue the heterodox views and false arguments of others, and with courageous and indomitable vigor, he overcomes Māra and all enmities, achieving the Buddha’s wisdom—subtle, wondrous, and profoundly deep.

The Tathāgata possesses the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses; his eloquence is uninterrupted and his wisdom is unimpeded. He has deeply penetrated dependent origination and is able to transcend existence and non-existence, practicing the Middle Way while remaining free from the notions of self and what belongs to self, as well as sentient beings, life-force, nourisher, spirit, person, mind-born, and youth.

It is free from the notions of an agent, a recipient, a knower, or a seer, as well as the views of annihilationism and eternalism; it distances itself from all false attachments and views, attains the *dhāraṇī-sūtra-king*, and is sealed with the seal of the Tathāgata.

Universally observing all sentient beings with steadfastness and without forsaking them, regarding them as equal to an only child without dualistic thought, he proclaims the nectar-like Dharma like the roar of a lion.

All sentient beings—whether of superior, middling, or inferior classes—who hear this Dharma, shall without exception obtain benefit; they will swiftly abide upon the true path to Nirvana, become endowed with the three types of knowledge, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, succeed to the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it remains unbroken, and receive the consecration of office to serve as Dharma Kings.

Able to discern those sentient beings who have crossed over and those who have not yet crossed over, he proceeds to the Bodhi tree and sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Seated upon the lion throne, he is sovereign and fearless, subduing the hosts of Māra. He is able to manifest the physical body of a Buddha, complete with all the marks and signs of excellence, and is able to turn the unsurpassed, pure wheel of Dharma. Surrounded by a retinue consisting solely of a great assembly of bodhisattvas, he preaches the Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings.

At that time, all the sentient beings in the assembly, having heard the Buddha’s exposition of the meritorious qualities of those great bodhisattvas, were so filled with joy and exultation that they could not contain themselves. There are no women, nor are there jealousy, stinginess, indolence, anger, distraction, or delusion. There are no hindrances or veils, nor any residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). There are no names for various categories such as superior, middling, or inferior; nor are there designations for the distinctions of the Three Vehicles. That world is vast, magnificent, and pure; it comprises sixty trillion *koṭi* of Buddha-fields as a single buddha-land. It has neither sun nor moon, being illuminated solely by the light of the power of the bodhisattvas' vows.

The ground was as level as the palm of a hand, purely adorned with a variegated array of various precious jewels such as *indranīla*, *vaiḍūrya*, and *maṇi* gems; it was further strewn upon with lotus flowers made of many jewels—flowers of supreme brilliance and softness, like the celestial *kācalindikā* cloth of exquisite touch. Furthermore, there are no pebbles, gravel, pits, hollows, hills, mounds, mountains of earth and stone, black mountains, thorns, or poisonous spines; there are only immeasurable sublime jewel-mountains.

There is also no excrement, urine, filth, or impurity; they always take the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna as their sustenance.

What is this samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha?

It is that which does not arise from the characteristics of form, nor does it arise from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it does not arise from the wisdom of the past, future, or limits, nor does it arise from what is presently seen or heard.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This buddhānusmṛti-samādhi is inconceivable; it functions without engaging in any phenomena, yet contemplates the true mark of all phenomena as they are—beyond speech and demonstration, without marks and without names."

*phaṭ* (two-syllable) one hundred and one. At that time, after Vaiśravaṇa, King of the Heavenly Kings, and the various devas had each recited this dhāraṇī, they addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“Great Sage, World-Honored One!

If we see such a Dharma-preacher who upholds, recites, or even masters a single verse or a single phrase, we shall always provide protection for them, cleansing away all calamities, hardships, and afflictions, as well as all poisonous vapors, verbal abuse, and physical beatings. All manner of illnesses, malevolent spirits, goblins, and inauspicious events shall be entirely extinguished.”
The Buddha addressed the great beings and the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa:

"You should skillfully protect such Dharma-preachers who uphold this sutra. The very name of this sutra is difficult to hear, let alone being able to receive, uphold, read, and recite it in its entirety, or to honor, serve, respect, and praise it with various kinds of ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, robes, exquisite jeweled canopies, silken banners, flags, fragrant oils, and ghee lamps. When making offerings of these hundreds of thousands of millions of varieties to the Dharma-preacher, you should first make this vow:
'Having heard this sutra, we shall practice according to what is taught.'"

"I now entrust this Dharma master who upholds the sutra to you all; you should protect him, and even his kinsmen should guard him, ensuring he is free from decline and affliction and attains peace and happiness."

Chapter Three: Arousing the Bodhicitta The Mahāyāna-sūtra on the Six Pāramitās of the Essential Principles, Chapter Three: Arousing the Bodhicitta. At that time, after the Bhagavān had let out a lion’s roar and clearly revealed the gateway to the secret dhāraṇī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in single-minded devotion, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
O Great Sage, World-Honored One!
You are able, through great compassion, to praise and proclaim this supreme secret nectar *dhāraṇī* for the protection of Dharma-preachers.

We pray only that the World-Honored One will take pity on sentient beings and proclaim the Dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, so that all living beings who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment may know how to generate that resolve.
"How should those who have already resolved their minds practice?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does the mind in the Mahāyāna become non-regressive?
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:

“If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to cultivate the Mahāyāna practice for the sake of sentient beings, and who wish to deliver sentient beings by establishing them in Great Nirvāṇa, they should first give rise to five kinds of superior resolve.”
What are the five? First, universally generating a mind of impartial great compassion toward all sentient beings;
second, never regressing from the mind of omniscience.
Third, one should conceive of all sentient beings as friends and vow to rescue and protect them from peril and hardship;
fourth, one should constantly regard sentient beings as those to whom one owes a debt;
fifth, one should always harbor a sense of shame and remorse, wondering when this debt will ever be repaid.
One who is able to give rise to these five kinds of mind will swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva!
How does one practice with a single-minded focus within the Mahāyāna so as to attain non-retrogression?

Long ago, there was a merchant who was wise, discerning, and always practiced benevolence and filial piety. He constantly saw his parents and kinsmen suffering in poverty and distress, and he was perpetually tormented by anxiety and grief that pressed upon his body and mind. He wondered: "By what means can I provide for and relieve them?"
He reflected thus: "There is no way other than entering the ocean to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) and provide for them, so that they may be freed from the suffering of poverty.

For this reason, he gave rise to a courageous mind and, disregarding his own life, departed from his home. Through various skillful means, he sought out provisions, as well as virtuous companions, a ship, and a navigator.
On the way, he encountered a stranger returning from the sea and asked him, "Why are you in such a great hurry? Where do you intend to go?
The merchant answered in full detail regarding the circumstances as described above.
"To rescue those who are impoverished, I now wish to enter the sea to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) so that we may provide for one another.
That stranger said, "In the past, when I left my home, it was also for this purpose: to relieve the suffering of poverty among my kinsmen."

Having set out from home, he traveled through a vast wilderness, crossing a great desert where water and grass were utterly absent. There were many wild elephants, tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, venomous snakes, and lions; he encountered bandits, great mountains, and mighty rivers, as well as various perils such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, alarm, fear, and dread. Only with the help of that mariner did he finally reach the great ocean.

Furthermore, they encountered fierce winds, great fish, and malevolent dragons, as well as thunder, lightning, hail, rain, surging waves, and eddies; there were many such obstacles that cannot be described in detail.

Although they endured these various sufferings, they still could not obtain the wish-fulfilling jewel; they merely obtained enough coarse provisions to sustain themselves, yet were still unable to relieve their impoverished relatives.
I now exhort you, O virtuous one, not to force yourself into hardship and weary yourself in vain.
I wish to manage affairs separately from you. Why is this so?
However, that great ocean is fraught with various perils—black winds, black mountains, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and makara sea-monsters; its many dangers are not just one.
I have merely heard the name of the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi), yet among those who have gone forth in the past by the millions, not even one or two have obtained it.
For this reason, I urge you, O virtuous one, that you should quickly turn back.
At that time, having heard these words, the merchant leader redoubled his resolve and, giving rise to three superior thoughts, entered the sea without turning back.
What are these three? First:
"My parents, brothers, and kinsmen are suffering such poverty and misery; how could I return empty-handed without providing them with relief?"

"Secondly, my kinsmen were formerly wealthy; they provided me with food and clothing and showed me compassion. Now that they are impoverished and can barely sustain their own lives, how could I abandon them and wish to return?"

Third, when I lived at home, I managed the household affairs and employed and commanded my male and female servants, reprimanding them in various ways; how could I now fail to provide relief for their poverty and suffering, so as to make them joyful and desire to return?

For these reasons, mindful of repaying their kindness and virtue, he rouses great courage and determination to press forward; he must enter the sea to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel, and having obtained it, return home to relieve his kin, allowing them to use it as they please so that they may forever be free from hardship and poverty.

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also like this in their arousal of the bodhicitta: they contemplate the six destinies and four modes of birth throughout the ten directions, seeing that all were their own parents in past lives; out of pity for them, those beings committed various evil karmas and fell into the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.”
For this reason, he reflected to himself:
"By what skillful means may I deliver these beings from such suffering?

Having formed this thought, he realized that only by entering the great ocean of the Dharma of the six pāramitās and seeking the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes could he rescue sentient beings from the sufferings of birth and death.

Having reflected thus, he gave rise to a mind of great courage and non-retrogression, seeking with diligent effort and without weariness through various skillful means the provisions, the Dharma of virtuous companions for awakening, and the Dharma masters.

As he traveled along the road, he encountered a māra king leading his retinue; some manifested as celestial bodies, some appeared as human bodies or brahmin bodies, some took the form of merchant leaders, bhikṣus, or bhikṣuṇīs, and others assumed various other kinds of diverse forms.
Then that Māra, the King, asked the Bodhisattva:
"Where are you now hurrying to?
The Bodhisattva replied:

"For the sake of all sentient beings afflicted by suffering, I now wish to enter the great ocean of the six perfections to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel of the Buddha’s omniscience, in order to rescue all sentient beings who are impoverished."
The Māra King spoke again:

"When I first resolved my mind, it was also like this: for the sake of delivering all sentient beings from suffering and affliction, I left the home of birth and death and crossed the great flow of saṃsāra. I underwent many hardships—hunger and thirst across vast wildernesses and sandy deserts, and various perils such as the fear of bandits—only then reaching the great ocean of the Dharma of the Six Pāramitās."

Sometimes they encounter those begging for their heads; sometimes they meet those begging for their eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, hands, feet, limbs, joints, heart, lungs, intestines, stomach, liver, gallbladder, spleen, kidneys, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, slaves, servants, or attendants.
Thus, giving in various ways according to whatever was requested, they did not give rise to stinginess but diligently sought the treasure of wisdom.

For immeasurable kalpas, they transmigrated through birth and death within the ocean of suffering; although they underwent all manner of hardships and difficulties, they were still unable to attain unsurpassed bodhi, but instead turned their efforts toward seeking the fruit of arhatship—the nirvana of extinction that transcends the triple world.
I now exhort you not to exhaust yourself in vain toil, but rather to cultivate and maintain your practice; I wish to ascend to this fruit together with you.

Why is this? I recall that in the three miserable realms we constantly suffer from hunger; my mind longs to devour [food] as I gaze upward toward the sky, wondering who will come into my mouth to satisfy me with a single full meal.

Various kinds of suffering and hardship press upon body and mind; human life is impermanent, passing away faster than water over mountains; a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) is difficult to encounter and meet—if you do not believe and accept this now, what can you do to remedy it later?
Wandering indeterminately within the ocean of birth and death, how can the mind—like the moon reflected in water—possess any reality?

Those who are evil associates are easy to see and easy to encounter; they constantly delight in exhorting others to practice the Bodhisattva path, encouraging them to relinquish wealth and even their lives in the hope of attaining Bodhi.
Moreover, when the Buddhas appear in the world, they manifest but once; though those who seek them may number in the millions, not one or two in a thousand succeeds.
For this reason, I urge you, O virtuous one, that you need not undergo such toil and hardship; you should instead seek liberation and attain nirvāṇa for yourself.
Furthermore, it requires undergoing various hardships and sufferings throughout three incalculable eons before one can finally attain the enlightenment of Buddhahood.
One may realize Arhatship in this very life or after three births; as a member of the single class of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), what need is there for such suffering?

Those of ignorant and foolish minds who aspire to the fruit of Buddhahood undergo hardships and endure them for immeasurable kalpas, yet they have not even heard of or realized the fruit of Arhatship, let alone be able to attain unsurpassed Bodhi.
It is like a person who, having caught a small bird, upon seeing a garuḍa king, immediately releases the bird he was holding and goes forward to seize the garuḍa king.
The large ones fly away, while the small ones are lost.
It is just the same for the fool who seeks the fruit of Buddhahood: by abandoning this [present life] to seek other fruits, both are lost.
Having understood this, I pray that you will quickly turn your minds; within this very life, you shall surely realize Arhatship.
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva further increased his vigor and gave rise to three kinds of thoughts.
What are the three? First:

"All sentient beings, from the beginningless past of birth and death until now, have all been my kin or my friends; they are currently undergoing suffering and affliction and have not yet attained liberation. How could I turn back and retreat?"

Second, all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, provided me with food and clothing and have shown me profound compassion; yet now they undergo the various sufferings and hardships of saṃsāra. How can I fail to repay them and instead give rise to a mind of retreat?
