Third, all sentient beings from beginningless time have all been my own kin; yet I have instead exploited, driven, and commanded them, even rebuking one another, never having repaid even a fraction of their kindness.
For these reasons, you should not be discouraged; rather, increase your vigor and seek to realize Bodhi.
Once you have realized the jewel of omniscience (sarvajñāna), use it to rescue sentient beings from the hardships and sufferings of birth and death.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing with a single-minded focus within the Mahāyāna,
thereby attaining non-retrogression. "Furthermore, Maitreya,
you should know that this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivating the practices of the Mahāyāna by giving rise to five kinds of mind."
Among these five mental states: first, one gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings;
second, one seeks omniscience for the sake of all sentient beings with a mind that never regresses—these two mental states constitute the diligent practice of the Mahāyāna Dharma;
third, one regards all sentient beings as one's own kinsmen and friends.
Fourth, all sentient beings have been kind to me, yet I have not repaid even a hair’s breadth of their kindness;

fifth, all sentient beings are my own kin, and I have previously committed unwholesome acts against them—insulting them in various ways and punishing them unjustly—and with a heart of deep shame, when will this debt ever be fully discharged? These three thoughts cause Bodhisattvas to be courageous and non-retrogressive, until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-ṣaṭpāramitā-naya-sūtra, Fascicle Two;
The Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-ṣaṭpāramitā-naya-sūtra, Fascicle Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kasmīra by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Four: On Non-Retrogression At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya prostrated himself with his head at the ground to pay homage to the feet of the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Great Sage, World-Honored One, you have already spoken of the five kinds of generating the mind of a bodhisattva through which one practices the Mahāyāna and attains non-retrogression.”
However, how is the mind of great compassion aroused?

How is it practiced? We only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings and for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all living beings, will explain this extensively.
At that time, the Bhagavat addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
Ask quickly about this meaning.
Listen attentively now!
Reflect upon it well.
I shall analyze and explain this for you to sever the net of your doubts.
Regarding what are called the five kinds of mind, the first is the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

You should maintain this mind with firm resolve and never abandon it; you should keep in mind those sentient beings in the evil destinies and hells, reflecting upon their suffering as described in the sūtras.
You should know this: I now speak it again for you within this sutra.
Observe that all sentient beings were, in past lives, your own parents, kinsmen, or objects of respect;
yet they now dwell in hell, manifestly undergoing manifold sufferings, being encircled by thirteen fires—two of which are [as follows]:
Flames enter through his feet and emerge from the crown of his head; again, two flames enter through the crown of his head and pass out through his feet;
again, two flames enter through his back and emerge from his chest; again, two flames enter through his chest and emerge from his back;
again, two flames enter through his left flank and pierce through his right flank.
Emerging [from one side], two further flames enter through the right flank and pierce through the left flank; another flame descends from the head,
winding down to the feet— yet the bodies of these sentient beings in this hell are as soft and supple as refined butter,
being scorched and consumed by those interlacing fires.
The fires of that hell consume the fires of the human world, just as cotton flowers are incinerated until not even a trace of ash remains.
There are sentient beings who, scorched by the flames, run hither and thither seeking protection, yet they do not know what to do;
there are other sentient beings who, finding no place to hide their bodies, return once more to rush into the fire.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are suddenly cast into deep pits of excrement and filth; within these pits dwell insects with sharp, piercing beaks made entirely of copper and iron, sixteen finger-widths long, which peck and devour the skin, bones, marrow, and brains of the beings.
Again, there are sentient beings dwelling amidst hot ashes, being scorched and boiled;
or there are sentient beings in salt water, being tossed about and drowned.

At that time, the hell-wardens use a great iron net to scoop them out from within, as if catching fish, and place those sentient beings upon a floor of glowing red-hot iron, where they lie prostrate to be scorched and roasted.
Next, they use iron tongs to pluck out their tongues and pour molten copper into their mouths; they faint and die, only reviving after a long time.
They then wish to run away, seeking escape, but in the end, they cannot be liberated.
Furthermore, iron dogs immediately pursue them, while iron crows with iron beaks fly along and peck at them, tearing their flesh and bones apart to devour them.
Seeing a grove of trees in the distance, they wish to climb up to escape, but on every tree in that grove grow iron thorns; each individual thorn is sixteen finger-widths long and is burning hot.
When sentient beings desire to climb upward, thorn-tips hang down; they enter through the chest and exit through the back, undergoing immeasurable suffering with no means of escape.
Crows and vultures fly in to peck out their two eyes, and further split open their skulls to extract and devour the marrow.

As they attempt to descend from this point, the points of the spikes turn upward; their eyes, ears, noses, tongues, bodies, hands, feet, and all ten finger-joints are completely torn apart, hanging from the trees so that there is no way to escape or free themselves.
The hell-wardens seize them and place them inside iron bags, repeatedly beating them with red-hot iron clubs.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose hands, feet, heads, and hair—these five parts—are torn apart and sawn asunder.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings placed inside iron mortars, where they are pounded from head to foot with iron pestles.

Again, there are sentient beings in cauldrons of boiling water; turned over with iron forks, they are boiled until they are a mass of rotting flesh, with only their bones remaining, yet their lives still persist.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings dwelling in hell who take cinnabar as their dwellings; they set fire to them so that the flames blaze forth intensely, and the molten cinnabar flows and drips like scorching arrows.

Furthermore, there are hells with iron mountains on all four sides; sentient beings dwell within them as two mountains press against one another, sometimes from north to south and sometimes from east to west. When the two mountains close together, pus and blood flow out from the sentient beings therein.

Furthermore, there is a hell where iron snakes coil around the bodies of sentient beings; from their feet to their heads, the snakes bite their heads, binding them with all their might so that the marrow and blood gather at the crown of the head, which they then suck and devour until only skin and bone remain.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings in the hells whose bodies are impaled by the hell-wardens with three-pronged iron forks; entering through the two feet and emerging from the crown of the head and the shoulders—these three points—the fierce flames of the fire erupt simultaneously with the thrusting of the fork, and likewise, fire issues forth from their eyes, ears, nose, and mouth.

Furthermore, there is a hell where sentient beings lie upon hot iron ground, either supine, prone, or on their sides; then black iron cords are stretched along their bodies, and they are further hacked and chopped with axes and hatchets, just as a master craftsman works wet wood.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are stripped of their skin by various hell-wardens from their feet to their heads; having been flayed, the skin is made into ropes used as bridles and reins, and they are forced to mount high mountain peaks. These mountains are made of glowing iron, and they are driven up them at bay, being whipped and beaten in myriad ways with unspeakable suffering.

These sentient beings have been my own parents and close relatives, both internal and external, since beginningless time. Now they wander in the hells, passing through immeasurable kalpas, constantly experiencing suffering and affliction as if it were their own home. Only when their evil karma is exhausted are they briefly born among humans or devas; yet having committed offenses here once more, they fall back into the hells.
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva observes these sentient beings undergoing such various sufferings, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Next, observing the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), he again gives rise to a compassionate mind.

He sees that for sentient beings dwelling among the hungry ghosts, one day and night is equivalent to one month for humans; calculating by days, twelve months constitute a year. Within the realm of hungry ghosts, their lifespan is five hundred years, which corresponds to fifteen thousand years in the human world. They constantly endure hunger and thirst, never even hearing the names of liquids or water with their ears, let alone seeing them with their eyes.

Yet those hungry ghosts have bodies as large as great mountains and heads like felt tents; their throats are as thin as needles, and their matted hair hangs down, covering both shoulders. It is as if sharp blades were cutting and slicing their limbs, transforming them into fierce flames that burn and rot their bodies; like fire consuming kindling, the suffering is unbearable. The hair on their two armpits covers their waists and bellies, while the hair of their private parts hangs down to their knees and ankles; it is likewise as if cut by knives and burned by fire, and they endure such suffering for immeasurable years.

Or, seeing water from afar, they rush toward it to seek it; yet upon reaching its edge, they fall prostrate, for by the power of their evil karma, the water transforms into pus, blood, excrement, and filth, or becomes hot sand.

On both banks of that water, there are further hell-wardens who brandish bows, arrows, swords, clubs, battle-axes, spears, and lances, striking and piercing with various forms of flogging and beating. Tormented by the fire of hunger and bewildered by parching thirst, they flee in haste; yet, as fierce fires burn and scorch them, they know not where to go.
The hell-wardens pursue them, beating, striking, hacking, and severing them until their hands, feet, and all their limbs and joints are completely shattered.

Furthermore, there are hungry ghosts who give birth to five children in the morning and eat them as soon as they are born; at night they give birth to another five children and eat them as soon as they are born, remaining perpetually hungry and never for a moment satiated.

Should they encounter rain from the heavens, they catch it with their upturned mouths; yet by the power of their karma, not even a single drop enters their mouths, for as soon as it flows into their bellies, it turns into a fierce fire that passes straight through and out.

Or, when hot winds arise during the summer months, they blow the hungry ghosts down into sandy deserts; below, they are scorched by hot sand while above they are roasted by the sun. Driven by hunger, thirst, and heat, they see a forest from afar and run toward it seeking shade and coolness; yet as the hungry ghosts arrive, the shade shifts away from them.

Why is this? Formerly, when he was among humans, there were times when, though the sky was pure and free from clouds, a radiant light would strike him; the scorching heat burned his body no differently than being roasted by the midsummer sun.

Furthermore, there are hungry ghosts who, during the height of winter, encounter great winds arising; by the power of their karma, these winds blow the hungry ghosts along like flying dust, casting them onto mountains of ice where they endure various sufferings of cold.

Having suffered such pain for immeasurable time, they die there and fall back into hell; thus they come and go for countless years until their evil karma is exhausted. Only then do they rarely obtain a human body, but are born into a poor and lowly family, being stingy and refusing to give, sustaining themselves by begging while their greed and attachment increase all the more.
Because of their poverty, they commit the ten unwholesome deeds and various other sins; when their lives end here, they fall again into hell and undergo manifold sufferings.
Once those sufferings are exhausted, they are born among the hungry ghosts; thus they wander back and forth for incalculable eons, undergoing such misery.

These sentient beings, throughout immeasurable and boundless kalpas of birth and death in the past, have constantly been my parents and close relatives; for my sake, they frequently committed unwholesome karmas, and now they undergo this retribution of suffering as hungry ghosts.
Having contemplated this suffering, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to a mind of great compassion.
"Furthermore, Maitreya! Just as it is with the realm of hungry ghosts, one should next contemplate the animal realm in the same way."

There were various beasts such as deer, wild asses, jackals, foxes, rabbits, tigers, leopards, dholes, and wolves; as well as various flying birds such as wild cocks, geese, ducks, widgeons, wild geese, and mandarin ducks—beings of these kinds, whether walking or staying still, perching or soaring, were constantly afraid of humans and powerful birds and beasts. Whether drinking or eating, they never found even a moment’s peace, always harboring fear throughout the day and night.

Furthermore, there are various species of animals—tortoises, crocodiles, turtles, soft-shelled turtles, fish, oysters, shrimp, frogs, and aquatic creatures such as the *śiṃśumāra*—who are constantly caught in nets, born and dying within the waters.
Furthermore, there are animals such as snakes, vipers, lizards, chameleons, centipedes, and weasels; these types of animals are born in darkness and die in darkness.
There are also animals such as nits, lice, and fleas, which are born depending upon the human body and likewise die depending upon the human body.

Furthermore, there are animals that either depend on corpses, or depend on damp excrement, or depend on grass and wood; they are born in those very places and die in those very places, or are born through transformation and die through transformation—namely, such species as maggots, moths, locusts, grubs, cicadas, and butterflies.

Furthermore, there are animals that constantly feed on pus, blood, and various impurities as their preferred flavors—namely, such creatures as pigs, dogs, dung beetles, flies, and gadflies—who, from afar, perceive the stench as fragrant and delicious, flying and running toward it in haste for fear they might not get to eat.
Furthermore, there are animals that do not eat fine grass but eat only thorns, and do not drink clear streams but drink only turbid water.

There are also animals that do not live by depending on grass yet constantly consume it—namely, the species of domestic animals such as elephants, horses, oxen, donkeys, camels, and mules. Some have their brains probed and gouged with iron hooks to subdue them so they may be ridden; others have their noses pierced or are harnessed with bridles and headstalls to bind their heads, forced to carry heavy loads while being constantly whipped and subjected to various scoldings and insults. They must proceed whether slow or fast; some are so emaciated that they fall over again after rising, beaten beyond measure and unable to move forward—all because of past causes they now undergo this suffering.
Or, having consumed the offerings of the faithful without further diligent effort, they encounter such hardships as the repayment of past debts.

Thus driven into service and subjected to various lashings, they have yet to repay their full debt; some are even taken and killed. Suffering in myriad ways, they have no one to whom they can appeal for relief.
In life they lack water and grass; in sickness they have no medicine; after death, their bodies are flayed and torn apart for people to devour.
Having died in this manner, they fall into hell. Why is this?

Due to mental delusion, they do not distinguish between good and evil; they do not reflect upon the arduous toil of their parents in giving them birth; they do not recognize cause and effect nor have they heard the True Dharma; furthermore, they possess no roots of goodness such as generosity or observance of precepts, but think only of water and grass, knowing nothing else.
These animals are those kept as domestic livestock by humans;

apart from those so kept, there are other classes of animals, namely lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, and wolves, as well as the aforementioned aquatic and terrestrial animals. These beings mutually harm and devour one another; due to such karma, they are born in the hells, where they undergo various intense sufferings for immeasurable kalpas. Once their hellish retribution is exhausted, they again enter the realm of animals, thus wandering back and forth for immeasurable kalpas.

These animals, too, throughout immeasurable and boundless kalpas of birth and death in the past, have constantly been my parents and kinsmen; for my sake, they constantly committed unwholesome karma, and now they undergo this retribution of suffering as animals.
Having contemplated this suffering, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Just as it is with those in the animal realm, he next contemplates the human realm.

There are sentient beings who, though born into the human path, suffer much poverty; for long periods they endure hunger and go about naked and exposed. They travel through mud, sleep in the rain, harvest in the frost, and toil in the heat; day and night they are driven on until their hands and feet crack and split. Their hair is disheveled as they stumble forward, begging from door to door without ever being satisfied. By evening they lie down to sleep hungry, dependent on others with no one to provide for them.

Though they speak, people do not believe or follow them; though they possess a handsome appearance, they instead encounter contempt and disdain. Constantly practicing patience and benefiting others, they are yet reviled and accused of being timid and fearful.
Some artists and scholars do not record them, while others, visiting their kinsmen, are met with suspicion and treated as mere seekers of food.
Some who place their faith in the Triple Gem are slandered as being after fame, and those who praise others are immediately labeled as sycophants.

Or they may be born into lowly and base circumstances, never finding peace for themselves; bound to others, their every advance and retreat depends solely on the commands of another. They constantly endure cold and heat without knowing warmth or coolness, fetching water and gathering firewood without shrinking from toil or exhaustion.
The master’s mind is entirely devoid of compassion; even for the slightest delay, one is immediately subjected to flogging.
What one reaps is what one has sown oneself—it is not bestowed by Heaven nor granted by others. It is summoned by one's own meager merit, and the suffering exceeds that of death itself.
"Just as a withered tree, devoid of branches and leaves, provides no place for any flying bird to alight and dwell, so too is it with a person of meager merit.
At that time, the Bhagavat spoke again in verse: "To remain silent is called the darkness of folly;
To speak is said to be madness. [But] one who speaks of the Dharma without attachment Is called a sage by the world."
Associating with those who are resentful and sycophantic, distancing oneself out of fear,
speaking of patience as cowardice, and professing faith for the sake of reputation—
living in poverty and lowliness among men is truly worse than the suffering of death.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!
You should know that poverty is an extreme suffering.

Although one may constantly associate with and praise others, because of a lack of merit, calamities arise in its wake. Because of this poverty, one is perpetually subjected to humiliation; consequently, one further creates evil karma and falls into the hells."

Furthermore, there are those of noble and wealthy lineage who possess many servants, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; surrounded before and behind by kinsmen and relatives, they enjoy supreme and wondrous pleasures like the devas. Yet, deluded and distracted by the five desires, their greed and anger increase all the more, and they constantly give rise to pride and arrogance, treating others with contempt.
At that time, the Bhagavān spoke these verses:
“Failing to restrain the five faculties and being greatly negligent, Craving wealth harms oneself as if by an enemy;
Addicted to the five desires like a drunken man, Both noble and base alike invite the suffering of birth and death.”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya:

"All sentient beings do not realize that their own past actions in the present and future follow them like a shadow follows a form. Greed is the root cause of all suffering; they fail to cultivate the bridges of wholesome dharmas, and having burned away their prior causes, their pure qualities (śukladharma) are utterly exhausted. Having perished from this state, they fall once again into the three miserable realms."

Why is this so? Because, due to their greed, they constantly take life; relying on their own power, they plunder the wealth of others; using various means, they violate the wives and concubines of others; they indulge in perverse sexual conduct without distinguishing between kin and strangers; they constantly harbor desires and engage in false speech; they deceive the virtuous with flowery rhetoric; they revile sentient beings with harsh and evil words; they spread rumors to create discord among others, preventing relatives and kinsmen from living in harmony; they always harbor greed and jealousy, showing contempt for others while exalting themselves; burned by the fire of anger, their roots of goodness are utterly exhausted; they praise non-Buddhist paths and slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, performing sacrifices to celestial deities in search of blessings and protection.

They do not recognize the profound kindness of the Triple Gem in their past lives—how, throughout immeasurable kalpas, it has diligently and painfully cultivated supreme practices and the provisions for enlightenment; how it is called "Buddha" because it possesses all-knowledge; and how, within the dark night of birth and death, it acts as a lamp, a refuge, a savior, a boat, and a raft to rescue living beings and establish them on the shore of the Great Nirvana of humans and devas.
Sentient beings, with their false views, pride, and arrogance, are like those intoxicated; bound by the five desires, they do not cultivate wholesome dharmas.

When their lives end here, they fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, or among humans they are born lowly and impoverished, undergoing various sufferings as if their bodies and minds were pierced by poisoned arrows.
Failing to cultivate wholesome dharmas leads to the experience of such bitter retribution.
Having contemplated this suffering, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to great compassion.
Next, he contemplates the realm of the devas.
Observe those devas, whose lifespans are long and who are free from all suffering and affliction; yet when their lives are about to end, the five signs of decline appear:

first, the flower garlands upon their heads wither and fade; second, their celestial robes become stained with dust and grime; third, sweat spontaneously breaks out from beneath their arms; fourth, their two eyes blink repeatedly; and fifth, they no longer take pleasure in their own abodes.

When this sign appears, the newly born celestial maidens all distance themselves and abandon them as if they were blades of grass; however, the long-serving celestial maidens, their love and attachment deep, surround and gaze upon them, sobbing with choked voices as if they were about to lose their lives, each approaching before them to wail and offer words of inquiry.
Then the deva replied:
"That new celestial maiden—I too have compassion for her and harbor no dualistic thoughts toward her; why now do you abandon me as if I were mere grass?

You all are now grieving and cherishing me—for this reason, you feel love for the old and anger toward the new. With the five signs appearing before you, you must know that death has arrived. Will you leave this celestial palace, with its exquisite sounds, the colors, fragrances, and delightful pleasures of heaven, losing your mindfulness in confusion and departing from this abode?"
"We cannot remain long within this assembly of devas; has my life now come to its end?
Such suffering pierces me like an arrow in the heart. We are without refuge or protection, without kin or lord, without a resort or savior."
He lost his voice and lamented in sorrow:
"Have the devas, in their happiness, abandoned me?
He then reflected further:

"The Palace City of Sudarśana is now about to be abandoned; there will be no further way for us to pay court at the precious throne of Śakra. Within the Hall of Exquisite Victory, we shall forever lose the sight of it; on what day shall we again ride together upon the precious elephant of the Lord of Śakra?"

In the Grove of Various Flowers, they can no longer be seen; in the Grove of Coarse and Wickedness, their armor is parted from forever; in the Grove of Mixed Forests, there will be no more days of banquets; and in the Garden of the Joyful Grove, there will be no time for further wandering or dwelling.

The Pārijāta and Kalpavṛkṣa trees, the white jade and soft stone seats—these can no longer be enjoyed; the assemblies for deliberation in the Sudharmā Hall are now far removed; there is no means to bathe in the sublime waters of the Mandākinī pool; the four kinds of nectar are likewise difficult to obtain; and the five kinds of exquisite music have suddenly ceased to be heard.
"Alas! What great suffering! Impermanence is so swift that it causes this body of mine alone to be afflicted by such misery; how can it be that birth and death occur in a single kṣaṇa?

The lifespans of the devas are like illusions and dreams; to strip off one's clothes and cast them upon the ground is a pain that cuts through both body and mind, a most extreme agony like being bitten by a venomous snake."
He gazed up at the other devas and said:
"I pray that you will show me compassion and grant me a respite for my life; would it not be a joy to extend it by even a few more days?
Could you remove from my body the five signs of decay, so that I do not fall to that place on Mount Horse-Head within the Voca Sea?"
Although these words were spoken, none of the gods who heard them were able to save him.
Seeing this, the god thought to himself:
"Since those other gods cannot save me or prolong my life, I know for certain that my death will come before long."
At the time of his death, that deva sees for himself the place where he is to be reborn—falling into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.

Having seen this sight, he chokes with sobs and wails in grief, faints and falls to the ground; with eyes rolling upward, he gazes about and immediately passes away, being born according to his karma to fall into the three evil destinies.
By this one should know that among the gods there is great suffering, which flows on without interruption and has no end.
Having contemplated this suffering, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to a heart of great compassion.

“Maitreya! You should know that it is like this: suppose there were a person who used the tip of a horn-bow to scoop up water from the great ocean. Between the water obtained by the bow and the water of the great ocean, which is more?”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The water at the tip of that bowstring is extremely minute; how can it be compared to the great ocean?"
"Since this great ocean is so exceedingly deep and vast, how can it be compared to the water at the tip of a bow?
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
"O son of good family!"
Falling from the realms of humans and devas into the three evil destinies is like the water of the great ocean;
being reborn again as humans or devas is like the water on the tip of a bowstring.

Those who fall into the three miserable realms undergo immeasurable suffering that cannot be described or conceived. Of the sufferings of the three evil destinies briefly explained above, it is like obtaining a single grain of sand from the Ganges River; what remains unsaid is like the sands of the Ganges.

The lifespan is likewise: as one hundred years in the human realm constitutes a single day and night for Śakra, the Lord of the Devas; thirty such days and nights make a month, and twelve such months make a year. His lifespan is one thousand such years, which, when calculated by human reckoning, totals three koṭis and sixty billion years.

This lifespan constitutes one day and night in the Black Rope (Kālasūtra) Great Hell; thirty such days and nights constitute a month, twelve such months constitute a year, and a full one thousand such years constitutes their lifespan.

One thousand such years constitute a single day and night in the Saṃghāta Great Hell; thirty such days and nights make a month, and twelve such months make a year. A lifespan of two thousand such years is the measure of life there, up to a full intermediate kalpa for the lifespan in the Avīci Great Hell.
By this one should know that the lifespan of sentient beings in the hells is exceedingly long.

When the gods approach their end, they observe with their divine eyes and are able to perceive that [the hell-beings] are filled with extreme distress; all their sensual pleasures are lost at once. Since suffering and pleasure are each divided into sixteen parts, the arising of even one part of suffering can extinguish sixteen parts of the pleasure within the heavens.
This is how a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, observing the gods as they undergo such suffering at the time of their death, gives rise to great compassion.
Maitreya, you should know that this is the first of the great compassionate minds of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"In our poverty and destitution, by what skillful means can we escape this hardship?
Having thought thus, he found no other way; there was only the option of entering the sea to retrieve the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi).
Having obtained it, he returned home to provide for and attend to his parents.

Having formed this thought, he entered the sea to seek it; having found the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), he placed it atop a high banner-pole. It was able to rain down all manner of rare treasures, clothing, food and drink, fragrant flowers, and music, so that his parents and kinsmen were fully satisfied with whatever they required according to their wishes.
It is likewise with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who, having resolved upon bodhicitta, seeks all-knowledge (sarvajñatā). He reflects thus:

"All sentient beings have been my parents and kinsmen in past lives; as they wander through birth and death, they currently undergo various sufferings. By what skillful means can they be liberated from these?"

Having reflected thus, he realized there was no other way; there remained only to enter the ocean of the Dharma of the six pāramitās and seek the wish-fulfilling jewel of omniscience to rescue them from this suffering.

Having formed this thought, he enters the ocean of Dharma to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) and place it atop the banner of Dharma. He spreads great clouds of loving-kindness, raining down everywhere the *dhāraṇī* gates of all supernatural powers and merits; he provides the clothing of shame and remorse, constructs dwellings as his abode, uses the fragrance of pure precepts, the flower garlands of patience, the food of diligence, and takes meditative concentration as his couch. With the nectar of wisdom as his sustenance and the emptiness and quiescence of all phenomena as his seat, he takes Great Nirvāṇa as his precious citadel and the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as his spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), showering down such wondrous jewels, garments, fragrant flowers, and music.

The wish-fulfilling jewel of omniscience—save for the Unsurpassed Great Teacher, the Tamer of Men—none is able to deliver others from all suffering and hardship, so that they may forever attain the peace and bliss of ultimate nirvāṇa.
Having reflected thus, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva gains the certain knowledge that he has attained the stage of non-retrogression and further makes this vow:

"May I be born in places of suffering and hardship, and there, on behalf of all sentient beings, undergo all manner of pain and affliction; may I not seek to personally realize liberation or nirvāṇa, nor abandon those sentient beings to seek my own peace and happiness."

Why is this? Because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, having sought their own liberation and entered nirvāṇa—though they are immeasurable, boundless, and beyond counting—are unable to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, nor can they extol the merits of the Buddha’s body.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, even while situated within the three miserable realms, can cause sentient beings to abandon unwholesome karma, cultivate wholesome dharmas, and escape all suffering to attain liberation, how much more so when among human beings?
By these causes and conditions, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
For this reason, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Mahābrahmā, Maheśvara, and the various seers and non-Buddhists all respectfully make offerings to him, and he accepts them all.
This bodhisattva attains the non-retrogressive mind, which is praised by all Buddhas of the three periods of time and for which they bestow a prediction of enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who cultivates the Mahāyāna is sovereign and fearless like a lion king; though all sentient beings follow after him, he is forever without fear until he reaches Bodhi.
The Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats, upon hearing the teachings of the Bodhisattvas, enter deep mountain caves and cover their heads with robes to pursue nirvāṇa.
How can they be compared to those of the Mahāyāna who cultivate the bodhisattva path, benefiting both themselves and others so that none fail to receive its grace?
For this reason, I redouble my diligence; rather than seeking my own benefit by entering nirvana, I would endure immeasurable suffering within the three miserable realms.

May all the evil karma committed by sentient beings of the past, present, and future—karma that would cause them to fall into the evil destinies and undergo various sufferings—be gathered into my own body so that I may undergo it in their stead.

May all the meritorious dharmas and all the sublime practices I have cultivated throughout the past and present worlds be dedicated for the sake of all sentient beings, so that they may swiftly realize nirvana.

I vow to relinquish all my precious wealth; should I be beaten, reviled, or insulted, I shall never retaliate but endure it all, wishing that those sentient beings may be entirely free from karmic transgressions.

Throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I vow to practice all difficult austerities; for the sake of sentient beings, I swear to seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, diligently cultivating meditative concentration and liberation until I attain the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, just as in the past immeasurable and boundless bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently cultivated the wisdom of all-knowledge, I too shall practice in this same way.
Why is this? It is to deliver all sentient beings wandering in saṃsāra and establish them in the unsurpassed liberation of nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, I vow that for all classes of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or formless; whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception—I shall cause them all to enter into Great Parinirvāṇa.

May all sentient beings be brought to fulfillment in the six pāramitās, fully accomplishing the unsurpassed Buddha-body adorned with a hundred merits, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and a halo behind the neck and back surpassing a hundred thousand suns, such that sentient beings delight in beholding and gazing upon them without weariness.
Furthermore, I vow that all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions shall be adorned with merit and virtue exactly as the Buddha is.
Again, I make this vow:

"May I sacrifice this body to endure being beaten, reviled, or scolded for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm; may I sometimes be bound, subjected to harsh treatment and humiliation, or even have my life-force severed; may I perform all manner of service and obedience without resistance, and may those sentient beings be entirely free from the burden of sin."
Having made this vow, he further reflected:

"May I swiftly fulfill this aspiration; furthermore, may this body remain within the five realms of existence to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, acting as a refuge for those without refuge, even while wandering through foreign lands."
They act as guides for those traveling; they provide boats and rafts for those entering the sea; they construct bridges for those crossing ravines and streams;
they provide springs and wells for those dwelling in the wilderness; they provide firewood for those suffering from cold and frost;
they provide coolness for those oppressed by the intense heat of midsummer; and they provide lamps and light for those dwelling in darkness.
For those who are weary, he provides soft bedding; for those who are hungry, he prepares sweet delicacies;
for those who are parched with thirst, he manifests sweet syrups; for those who are naked, he provides clothing;
during droughts and famines, he causes the five grains to rain down; and for those suffering from illness, he acts as a skilled physician to eliminate their maladies and prolong their lives.
For the long-term, he acts as an attendant to the orphaned, the widowed, and the solitary; for those who are impoverished, he serves as a hidden treasure.
He follows them whether they walk or stay, never abandoning them; if they travel afar, he becomes their companion, providing them with carriages and horses so that they may reach their destination.
If there are those with wrong views, I shall preach the True Dharma to them so that they may abide in right view.
As for those suffering in the hells, I vow to enter therein and rescue them, causing them to emerge from the midst of hell.
For those who have fallen among the hungry ghosts, he provides cool and sweet food and drink to eliminate their feverish hunger and thirst.
For those who have fallen among the animal realm—such as tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, bears, brown bears, and lions—he transforms himself into a mountain of flesh to satisfy their devouring.
He further made this vow:
"May all those who eat my flesh be fully satisfied and never devour one another.
For elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, deer, and other such beasts, may I become lush, fatty, and soft grass."
If there are sentient beings who eat meat, grass, or the five grains for food and drink, I shall cause them all to be fully satisfied according to their needs.
For those dwelling in the human realm, I shall provide whatever they desire and delight in, ensuring that none lack anything.
Furthermore, he made this vow:

"May I fully accomplish all dhāraṇī-bodies; wherever sentient beings may be, may I provide them with protection and refuge, acting as a wish-fulfilling tree and a precious vase, producing inexhaustible wealth to bestow upon all, providing for them in complete abundance."

Sometimes he acts as a King of Physicians to eliminate their illnesses; with the hand of great compassion, he grasps the key to the Dharma, opening the city of Nirvana to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Through difficult and ascetic practices over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he rescues all sentient beings and establishes them in the true liberation of Nirvana.
In whatever place they are born, they always apply themselves with diligent vigor and without indolence, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
To rescue living beings, they dwell in the hells, experiencing immeasurable suffering as if it were the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, he made this vow:
"If any sentient beings have not yet attained liberation, I vow to remain forever in the hells and not realize bodhi. Maitreya!
You should know that this is the second diligence of the bodhisattva mahāsattva: the diligent pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Furthermore, Maitreya, having practiced this conduct, one should further give rise to three superior states of mind to seek non-retrogression, practicing with diligence for up to three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeyakalpa*) without allowing even a single moment to be interrupted.

There may be various Māras who take the form of śramaṇas, or the form of brahmins, or practitioners of asceticism, appearing in all manner of strange guises. Within the Mahāyāna, they seek out faults and exhort practitioners to regress, speaking thus:

"The path of the Buddha is remote; it requires hundreds of thousands of kalpas of difficult practices and austerities to abandon what is hard to abandon—kingdoms, cities, wives, children, elephants, horses, the seven treasures, slaves, servants, and even one's own flesh, hands, and feet—without any stinginess. Only after practicing such giving for thousands of millions of kalpas will one realize bodhi."
Innumerable sentient beings have practiced in this manner, yet none have attained Buddhahood; they have all regressed and sought their own nirvana.
Even if they were to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, they would still enter nirvana; since it is one and the same nirvana, why must one undergo such arduous effort?

In seeking your own benefit, you should cultivate two kinds of practices: first, to seek the constant experience of happiness in this present life, performing at will the various kinds of sublime and excellent five sensory desires of humans and devas; as for minor sufferings, you need not fear them.
Why is this? It is like a farmer; would he fear insects or deer and thus refrain from tending his seeds?
The happiness of humans and devas is likewise: although there may be minor sufferings, their joy is inexhaustible. Therefore, simply cultivate your own practice; what need is there for worry or fear?

Second, one seeks nirvana for oneself, thinking: "In this life or within three lives, I shall attain arhatship and be naturally liberated; what need is there to undergo such diligent hardship to seek the fruit of Buddhahood?

Alternatively, if one is unable to proceed toward the two vehicles, one may for the time being enjoy the various pleasures of humans and devas, and later, having become weary and detached, swiftly enter nirvana.
For example, there may be a person who, though expending little effort, gains great profit; yet another person may expend immense labor and effort, only to fail in accomplishing anything at all.
Even if you undergo various hardships in practicing giving, if nothing is achieved, you are merely deceiving yourself.
"You now walk and dwell together with me; we share the same station regarding supramundane nirvāṇa. Maitreya!
You should know that when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the Mahāyāna hears these words, they do not believe or follow them at all, but instead reflect as follows:
"This is an evil Māra who has disturbed my ears, creating obstacles and seeking to seduce and deceive me so that I might retreat from Bodhi.
Having realized this, he further resolved:
"I must not now violate my original vow by accepting such words; I shall resolutely advance in my quest for the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood."
"Furthermore, one vows not to regress from the Mahāyāna and gives rise to three kinds of resolve.
What are these three?

First, all sentient beings have been my parents, relatives, and friends in past lives; since beginningless time, they have wandered through the cycle of birth and death, undergoing great hardships and suffering within the eight cold and eight hot hells. They have likewise experienced such suffering among the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, as well as among humans and devas."

How much less, then, should I feel grief or attachment for my parents and relatives of both internal and external kin from past lives? Therefore, I now vow to attain bodhi and shall not retreat or yield.
Maitreya! You should know that this is the first mind among the stages of non-retrogression for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.

Second, all sentient beings have been one's own parents since beginningless time; in every single birthplace, while dwelling within the mother’s womb, they could not find peace even in sleeping or eating. Through the toil of giving birth and raising them, the blood of great compassion was transformed into milk. For a long time, without weariness, they swallowed what was bitter and spat out what was sweet, daily cultivating merit with the wish: "May you grow up."

Since my own meager merit led to an untimely end, my parents wailed in grief, tearing out their hair, beating their breasts, and shedding tears; though they ate delicacies, they found no pleasure in them.

Throughout a single lifetime, such suffering is constant: the volume of tears shed from the eyes exceeds the four great oceans, and the milk drunk from the mother’s breast exceeds the four great rivers.

Furthermore, from beginningless time until now, all sentient beings have been my parents due to the bonds of affection; for various reasons, they have sacrificed their lives for me, and because of this, the cycle of rebirth continues to flow without ceasing until the present day.
If these sentient beings diligently and painfully cultivate unsurpassed enlightenment, then all these sentient beings will together become Buddhas; because of me, saṃsāra would thus be endless.

Furthermore, since beginningless time, all sentient beings have committed unwholesome karma out of a lack of compassion for me, their minds never feeling regret or remorse; if the form of this evil karma were to take shape, its accumulated measure would exceed Mount Sumeru.
Since their accumulated karma is thus, they fall into the three evil realms without ceasing even to this day.
For this reason, how can you turn your back on such kindness, seeking liberation for yourselves alone by entering nirvana?
For example, suppose a multitude of people have collectively violated the king’s law and are bound in prison, with no way to escape their punishment.
Among them, one person sees a small hole in the wall; by employing various skillful means, he frees himself and departs. By this cause and condition, he is liberated from suffering and hardship.

The followers of the Two Vehicles are likewise so: in the past, they were together with all sentient beings bound within the prison of birth and death in the triple world by ignorance and craving, having no means of escape. Among them, one person beheld the gateway of the Four Noble Truths; knowing suffering, severing its accumulation, realizing its cessation, and practicing the path, he attained the state of an Arhat and personally realized Nirvana.

Those who practice the Mahāyāna are not like this; they vow to attain liberation together with all sentient beings. Taking precepts and meditative concentration as their two hands, wisdom as their axe and halberd, and great compassion as their hook and key, they shatter the thieves of affliction, destroy the armies of birth and death, open the city of Nirvāṇa, and ascend to the palace of wisdom.
Maitreya! You should know that this is the second irreversible mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the Mahāyāna.
Thirdly, a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects as follows:

"From the beginningless past until the present, as sentient beings have flowed through the cycle of existence, each has been mutually bound to the others; they have afflicted others with the karma of body, speech, and mind; they have disturbed their minds and incited their anger; they have plundered wealth and treasures out of various cravings; they have severed the life-roots of others and consumed their flesh and blood—thus committing such killings in measureless and boundless numbers."
Even if they have not yet died, they constantly contemplate by day and night what means they might employ to sever their life-faculty, so as to take their flesh and blood for their own consumption.

Furthermore, harboring arrogance and relying on themselves to despise others, they declare others to be wrong while claiming "I am right. Upon hearing of another's excellence, jealousy arises in their hearts; unable to endure others, they seek to poison them to death. Seeing those in suffering and distress, they feel no compassion, but instead rejoice beyond measure, thinking, "When will they pass away soon?"

Seeing those who are wealthy and noble, one does not desire them; instead, one wishes to violate laws and regulations to be degraded and reduced to poverty and lowliness. One wishes for others to suffer while one enjoys glory and splendor oneself.
One wishes that the wealth and treasures of others perish day and night, while one’s own resources increase daily.

May they suffer grief and pain while I am ever at peace; may they receive hatred and disdain while I receive love and respect; may others treat them as enemies while I treat them as kinsmen and friends; and while they constantly fall into decline, may I attain transcendence and elevation.
"May others be poor while I alone am wealthy; may they be ignorant while I attain wisdom.

Thinking thus day and night throughout beginningless birth and death, one seeks peace and happiness for oneself alone, while directing benefit toward oneself and consigning suffering to others. Not a single sentient being remains unharmed by such conduct. One does not wish for others to possess fame or virtuous deeds; though the mouth promises otherwise, the heart acts in opposition, constantly behaving in this way. Through various forms of coercion and intimidation, one causes others to be ill at ease—immeasurable and boundless, beyond full description.

Furthermore, by instructing and guiding others with evil teachings, they fall into perilous paths in the present and future; they feign knowledge and insight to refute others, causing them to lose their precious wealth and official rank; using divisive speech, they incite strife between kin and strangers; through manifold deceptions, they cause hearts to harbor mutual resentment, leading them to fall into hell from which there is no time of escape.

With coarse and wicked speech, they revile and insult others, as if piercing their bodies and minds with burning arrows; until the end of their lives, they shall never forget this for even a moment. Under false names, they disparage others in manifold ways, using various harmful and distressing words.

Or, acting as heretical sages of wrong views, their hearts are consumed by the fire of anger as they preach evil and wicked doctrines; their hatred blazing fiercely, they cause sentient beings to fall into ruin. Through sorcery, incantations, demonic charms, and talismanic scripts, they cause all sentient beings to practice these together, resulting in mutual injury and the widespread prevalence of disease.

The strong are made frail and decrepit, the young are transformed into the aged; those with clear vision are made blind, and those with keen hearing are rendered deaf; the handsome are made to appear ugly, and the arrogant are afflicted with leprosy; those who cultivate goodness are led to commit evil, and those possessed of wisdom are driven to madness; those with long lives are brought to an untimely end, and the wealthy and noble are reduced to poverty and low status—a phenomenon that continues to prevail even unto this day without ceasing.
He further reflected:

"In the past, I was a teacher of non-Buddhist paths; with wrong views, I taught people, speaking of what is not the Dharma as the Dharma and the Dharma as what is not the Dharma. I caused immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to retreat from the bodhicitta and fall into wrong views and what is not the Dharma, so that after their lives ended here, they fell into the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts."

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, in past lives, received my false teachings and threw themselves down from steep, precipitous mountains, entering the Yamunā River and thereby ending their lives, claiming they had attained rebirth in heaven; this practice continues unabated to this day.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable sentient beings who went to the space between the two rivers—the south bank of the Gaṅgā and the north bank of the Yamunā—where there was a great divine tree named Nyagrodha. This tree was upright and beautiful, its lush, verdant leaves spreading out in dense foliage that cast deep shade. The ground there was level, vast, and expansive, serving as a place for giving; beneath the tree, many three-pronged iron spears had been set up.

Those sentient beings who seek rebirth in heaven first practice giving within that arena; next, they shave their beards and hair and enter the river to bathe, hoping thereby to remove the defilement of their sins. Thereafter, they ascend a tree and cast themselves down upon iron spears, seeking their own death. Having died from this, they claim to have attained rebirth in heaven; this practice has been current from time immemorial until now, without ceasing.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who receive my false teachings; they are constantly stingy and do not practice giving. When they see someone giving, they give rise to great anger, and when they see the recipient of the gift, they further produce resentment and wrath.
Why is this? Because I perceived both the giver and the recipient of the gift, by reason of this karmic condition, we both fell into hell.
Due to this perception, I have suffered the torments of a hungry ghost for immeasurable kalpas, and even now I have not yet been liberated from them.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who receive my false teachings, killing many oxen and sheep to offer their blood as sacrifice to the heavens.

Why is this? They believe that such oxen and sheep were bestowed upon them by heaven; they eat their flesh and ought to sacrifice their blood to the heavens. Having practiced these teachings from time immemorial until now, those who have already passed away fall into the evil realms, while those still living remain in a state of unrest, harming one another and devouring each other. Because of their ignorance, they do not attain Nirvana.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who receive my false teachings and constantly engage in slandering the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

Moreover, there are sentient beings who receive my false teachings and do not believe in the causes and effects of good and evil throughout the three periods of time; they say there is no giving and no making offerings, nor is there any fruit thereof, nor is there any Dharma for protecting oneself. They claim there is no virtuous conduct, no evil conduct, and no karmic results; there is no this world and no other world, no hells, no hungry ghosts, no animals, no devas, and no humans; and that there is neither father nor mother. They say that all sentient beings are like those intoxicated by wine: just as the one who makes wine uses yeast and rice, which, when tempered with warmth and coolness, acquires the name "wine" and intoxicates the drinker—does this intoxication arise from the parents?
Sentient beings are likewise: their birth as "I" originally arises from the union of parents through defiled craving; once my life has ended, there shall be no further birth.
It is like a tree that is cut down, burned, and reduced to ash; from these ashes, how could a tree ever grow again?
My own body is likewise; once dead, there is no rebirth. For this reason, I know that cause and effect certainly do not exist.

Because of this, I have no respect for my parents, teachers, or elders, but constantly revile them. Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, I have taught this false dharma, causing sentient beings to fall into hell.
Some non-Buddhists burn their bodies with fire;
some throw themselves into water to drown;
others end their lives by rolling upon sharp spears.
Some practice the conduct of dogs, seeking rebirth in heaven by eating excrement with their mouths;

some observe the "cow-vow," imitating the behavior of oxen—drinking water, grazing on grass, and wandering about naked—failing to distinguish between their six kin while engaging in sexual promiscuity;
and there are non-Buddhists who starve themselves and abstain from food, standing all day long and only eating after nightfall.
Some non-Buddhists scorch their bodies with the five heats while turning with the sun;
some non-Buddhists constantly stand on one leg;

some non-Buddhists constantly serve the moon, eating one mouthful on the first day of the waxing moon, two mouthfuls on the second day, and so on until they eat fifteen mouthfuls on the full moon; then, on the first day of the waning moon, they reduce their food by one mouthful, two mouthfuls on the second day, continuing until the end of the waning moon when they eat only one mouthful, or perhaps do not eat at all.

There are some non-Buddhists who constantly observe the "chicken precepts": they scatter food on the ground and pick it up with their feet, gathering it with their mouths to eat, and they crow at the proper times;

there are some non-Buddhists who wander about naked without shame, singe off their hair and body hair, stand in the midday sun turning with the movement of the sun, and during the height of winter, they stand in the shade while facing the wind;
there are some non-Buddhists who, having taken the lives of human beings, take their skulls to hold their food and drink.
There are some non-Buddhists who go naked without shame, smearing their bodies with ash;

there are some non-Buddhists who smear their bodies with charcoal and ink, using human skulls, limbs, and various bones as ornaments for necklaces, flower garlands, rings, and bracelets to adorn their bodies and heads;
and there are some non-Buddhists who weave the tails and manes of horses into garments to wear.
Some non-Buddhists use tree bark as clothing;
some non-Buddhists make clothing from vulture feathers;
and some non-Buddhists use chicken feathers for clothing.
By teaching such heterodox and false dharmas to sentient beings through the karma of speech, countless beings remain deluded and ignorant to this day, failing to attain liberation.

Furthermore, from beginningless time until the present, through bodily unwholesome karma, they have afflicted sentient beings with suffering and distress. They take the form of hell-wardens, grasping iron tongs in their hands to tear out the tongues of sentient beings and pour molten copper upon them; they also smash their bones with iron hammers, dismember various sentient beings with iron saws, and drive them up sword-trees to pull out their entrails and five viscera for consumption. Moreover, they bind sentient beings with iron chains and hurl them into rivers of ashes to undergo various sufferings, then immediately drag them out and place them upon hot iron.
Like fish on a griddle, they writhe in agony.
Furthermore, being forced to rise and sit, they are made to drink molten copper poured from a heated iron ladle into their mouths.
Moreover, their tongues are pulled out with iron tongs and stretched long and wide to be plowed by iron plows.
Regarding the sufferings of the hells described above, since beginningless kalpas, I have engaged in these deeds, inflicting various physical karmic torments upon sentient beings.

Furthermore, I have manifested as beasts such as lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, bears, and brown bears, harming and killing sentient beings while drinking their blood and devouring their flesh.
Furthermore, while occupying positions of authority as kings, officials, commoners, elders, or lay practitioners, they unjustly impose laws and taxes and inflict unreasonable beatings;
they fail to administer the royal law and thereby cause harm to sentient beings.

Reflecting thus from the beginningless past until now, there is not one among the sentient beings of the five destinies who has not been afflicted and harmed—having their heads cut off, their eyes gouged out, their ears sliced, their noses snubbed, their tongues severed, their flesh devoured, their bones broken to extract the marrow, or their hands and feet hacked off, even unto the taking of their lives.

Furthermore, among human beings, they do not perform other occupations but act as executioners; they hunt, fish, and trap with nets, snares, and arrows, seizing the lives of various creatures—namely the bodies of oxen, sheep, deer, wild boar, foxes, rabbits, chickens, pigs, fish, turtles, and so forth. They cut these into pieces and joints, piling them into great heaps for sale. Thus they commit immeasurable and boundless slaughter, and throughout immeasurable *koṭi* eons, they sustain their own lives by such trade.
"Furthermore, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva!
Those who practice the Mahāyāna should give rise to this mind and reflect in this way:

'Because of greed, hatred, and delusion, I have performed such actions of body, speech, and mind, deceiving and harming all sentient beings, and am now falling into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm to undergo various sufferings.'"
I am now filled with deep shame and remorse, reproaching myself for what I have done.

As I contemplate by what means I might repay this kindness, I find no other way to atone for this transgression than to resolve to seek Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; there is nothing else that can discharge this debt.

Once I have attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, I shall extensively deliver sentient beings from this wilderness of saṃsāra and establish them in the city of nirvāṇa, a place of peace and bliss; with the wish-fulfilling jewel of the knowledge of all modes, I shall repay all my profound transgressions from time immemorial.
"Maitreya! You should know that this is the third non-retrogressive mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
As with the aforementioned three minds, one should initiate practice with diligence and without indolence."
Regarding these three minds within the Mahāyāna,
by practicing with even one mind, one attains non-retrogression.
"Furthermore, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva!
By means of these five ways of generating the bodhicitta and practicing the Mahāyāna, one will swiftly be able to accomplish the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñājñāna*).
*Mahāyānapathakramaṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*, Scroll Three; *Mahāyānapathakramaṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Five: The Perfection of Giving (Dānapāramitā).
At that time, the Buddha, the Bhagavān, amidst the great assembly, let out a lion’s roar and extensively expounded upon the five ways of generating the bodhicitta.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, together with an immeasurable, incalculable assembly of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of great Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas—headed by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī—all of whom had already accomplished the six pāramitās.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable great arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, and purified their holy life;

as well as countless hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, trillions of devas, nāgas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat amidst the great assembly; he adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his palms joined, and with single-minded reverence addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, you have already spoken of the non-retrogressive mind of a Mahāyāna bodhisattva. By practicing how many dharmas does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva receive the name ‘bodhisattva-mahāsattva’?”
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain this.
At that time, the Bhagavat addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:

“If there are good sons or good daughters who, with a pure mind, take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, and give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they attain non-retrogression and are thus called Bodhisattvas; born within my Dharma, they are called Mahāsattvas.”

He became a son of the Dharma to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and served as a parent to those sentient beings; with the radiance of his great merit, he illuminated them more brilliantly than a hundred thousand suns, adorning his body.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How do these bodhisattva mahāsattvas remain far removed [from such faults]?”
How does one draw near?
With what kind of person should one take as a companion?
What should be done first?
How should one dwell?
How should one practice?
How should one subdue the mind?
"How is it sustained?
By whose power is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi swiftly realized?
At that time, the Buddha, the Bhagavān, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:

"If good sons and good daughters should guide sentient beings of the five destinies and establish them in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; should keep them far removed from the false teachings of external paths and from evil associates; and should draw near to and practice the fulfillment of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and should take as their companions those who practice the Mahāyāna."

One should, regarding oneself, listen to the true Dharma and diligently recite and uphold it; one should constantly abide in these six perfections and practice with diligence, subduing the mind and guarding the six sense faculties. By the power of this, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; such a person is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
What are called the six kinds of pāramitās? They are namely:
giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; these are the six kinds of pāramitās.
"Why is the *dānapāramitā* explained first?
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"I shall now explain this to you in detail."
Among the six perfections, this giving is the easiest to practice; therefore, it is explained first.
Just as in the world, whatever task is easy to perform should be done first, so too is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) explained first.

There are no sentient beings who are incapable of practicing generosity—whether they be yakṣas, rākṣasas, lions, tigers, wolves, or various hell-wardens, butchers, and executioners. Even these beings, who among all sentient beings are the most violent and cruel, are still able to abandon stinginess and practice generosity.
What is giving? It refers to nurturing sons and daughters with compassionate thoughts, feeding them at the breast.

Although these sentient beings may not understand the nature of merit and benefit, because of one's pity and love, causing them to obtain physical beauty, strength, longevity, and peace and happiness, and to be free from the suffering of hunger and thirst, is also called giving.
For this reason, among the six pāramitās, the dānapāramitā is taught first.
Furthermore, just as all impoverished sentient beings—starving, cold, and naked, with body and mind in a state of unrest—are unable to undertake various kinds of activities; so it is here.
If one provides them with food and clothing so that they may attain peace and happiness, only then can they engage in various kinds of activities.

It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: seeing that sentient beings are oppressed by poverty and are thus unable to give rise to unsurpassed faith to practice the various activities of the Mahāyāna, [the bodhisattva first provides for their needs].

First, one provides all clothing, food and drink, housing and bedding, and medical treatment for the sick and frail, thereby bringing peace and happiness to their minds; subsequently, one causes them to resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and to practice the various activities of the Mahāyāna.
For this reason, among the six perfections, generosity is the gateway, and the practice of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) is its primary aspect.
Just as all things in the world depend upon the great earth for their growth, for this reason the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is taught first.

The yakṣas and other such beings mentioned above, though unaware of what constitutes a field of merit or a non-field of merit, give milk out of affection; they shall be reborn as human beings, possessing abundant wealth and lacking nothing for their needs.

Due to this habitual practice, in whatever place one is born, one will always be free from stinginess and greed; one will provide for all and be able to eliminate the poverty and suffering of sentient beings. Why is this so?
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, first practice the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

To any who come as supplicants, they give everything; they do not frown, nor do they look askance with anger or resentment while practicing giving. They bestow according to what they possess, never hesitating or giving rise to stinginess.

Regarding cherished objects—clothing, bedding, food, drink, medicine, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, slaves, servants, elephants, horses, and the seven treasures—he does not give rise to stinginess but bestows them upon whoever asks, and he does not harbor even a single thought of regret.
If doubt arises, you should know that this is Māra. Why is this?
The Māra King Pāpīyān transforms himself into wealth and treasures to incite stinginess; by these means, he deludes and confuses my mind, creating an obstacle to Great Bodhi.
"For this reason, one should not be stingy.
Reflecting in this way, one should abandon all attachment to precious wealth.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all cherished wealth and treasures should be given in charity without giving rise to stinginess, then when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva becomes a Wheel-Turning King, surrounded by all seven treasures and a thousand sons, how should he act?”
For example, when fine grasses and trees in a mountain stream encounter a torrential rain from heaven, the waters swell and overflow, sweeping everything away until nothing remains.

In the same way, when a Wheel-Turning King indulges in the five sensory pleasures with sovereign power and is accompanied by a thousand sons, his bodhicitta is washed away and swept entirely away; how then can he practice the perfection of giving?
"For this reason, it is difficult to relinquish.
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
"O son of good family!"
In whatever place a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is born, they shall always obtain wealth, nobility, and abundant treasures; such is the natural law.
If he becomes a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), he should engage in these two kinds of reflection:
first, reflecting upon the difficult practices performed by the Buddhas of the past, as well as all the teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
These fivefold sensual pleasures of the wheel-turning king all arise from false conceptualization and discrimination, like a phantom or a dream.
Since the noble wheel-turning king does not give rise to discrimination regarding the objects of the five desires nor produce attachment to them, how could they ever obstruct his bodhicitta?

Second, one contemplates all sentient beings, thinking: "I have already led them into the ground of peace and happiness of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Just as the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, were able to relinquish what is difficult to relinquish, I too vow to practice such relinquishment. Desiring to wash away the stain of avarice, I give rise to this thought:

'From this present body until the attainment of Buddhahood, I vow to give this very body to all sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu*. Whatever meritorious deeds I cultivate, whether many or few, I vow to share them with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.'"
Viewing it in this light, I have already sacrificed all my bodies and lives in the past, as numerous as Mount Sumeru.
When I regard this present body as being like a mustard seed, I am willing to relinquish even this life; how much more so, then, precious wealth?

If bodhisattvas accumulate vast wealth but do not practice generosity, they are like white elephants who, after bathing thoroughly in the Ganges River, take up dung, filth, and dust with their trunks and smear it all over their bodies.
“I shall bathe his body with the pure water of merit so that it is upright, dignified, and clean; one should not be stingy or begrudge wealth and treasures by smearing and defiling his body.
Thus spoke Maitreya!
It should be known that a bodhisattva should reflect in this way:
"If someone comes to beg for the skin of my body, I shall immediately flay it without giving rise to anger or resentment, and joyfully bestow it upon them."
"If they beg for my body, head, blood, flesh, marrow, or bones, I am able to give them all.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in order to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, does not abandon saṃsāra to take up nirvāṇa.

Again, he reflects: "This body of mine did not come from a prior limit, nor will it go to a subsequent limit. It exists through the impure seed of the union of father and mother; dwelling amidst impurity between the stomach and the intestines, it is like a tree whose branches and leaves are lush and which bears flowers and fruit. My body is likewise: suffering is its branches, grief and lamentation its leaves, deception its flowers, and delusion its root. The rākṣasa of anger dwells within this tree, and it is surrounded by the beasts of evil karma—tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, lions, and the like."
I shall now rest for a short while beneath this tree; why should I begrudge it?

This tree-body is devoid of self or what belongs to a self; even if such things were present, I would relinquish them. I vow to offer it to sentient beings according to their needs, never being stingy or regretful.
Why is this? Because I have already relinquished [all things], I do not seek karmic retribution nor do I seek gratitude; for I am free from all attachment. Why is that so?
This poisonous body is entwined by three unwholesome dharmas.
What are these three?
First, impurity; second, extreme suffering; and third, ingratitude.

If there should be another person who rescues my body from amidst this crowd of rākṣasas, venomous beasts, and evil predators, you should know that such a person has bestowed great kindness upon me and has brought about great benefit for my life.
I have always harbored feelings of gratitude toward this person; how could I begrudge my own body for his sake?

Furthermore, all the gardens, groves, trees, grasses, and medicinal herbs upon this great earth—whether roots, sprouts, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits that are fit for consumption or wearing—if one were to use a sharp axe to cut these plants and distribute their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits to others, it would be able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
Furthermore, this great earth does not think, "Sentient beings consume my body, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits to cure their illnesses.

Even such insentient things do not engage in discrimination, yet they are able to benefit all sentient beings; how much more so should I, whose very body is capable of performing acts of benefiting others through giving, instead give rise to pride toward beggars and treat them with contempt and derision?
He further observed his own body both internally and externally.
First he observed the internal body: "Is the eye the self? Is it mine?"
If it were not the self, why would one be so stingy and attached? The same applies to the ears, nose, tongue, and body; one should examine them thoroughly to find no self or what belongs to a self.
Next, one contemplates the external body: Is form the self?
"Is this 'mine'? Sound, fragrance, taste, and touch are likewise so.
When one observes these internally and externally in their entirety, there is no self to be found anywhere. Since there is no self, why be stingy and not practice giving?"
One should resolve to reflect in this way:
"I vow to offer this body swiftly to all. Why is this?"
"This body is impermanent, subject to change and instability; it arises and perishes in every moment, for it possesses no inherent existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If others compel one to abandon body, life, or wealth, It is constrained and not free, and brings no benefit."
Having known this, one should contemplate it with discernment; opening the mind to give of oneself is supreme.
If the deluded person awakens to the dream-like and illusion-like nature of phenomena, they will relinquish both the internal and external without attachment.
Such giving is equal to space; being without self and without recipient is supreme.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!
