When a bodhisattva dwells thus amidst the great assembly, they constantly examine their own faults and do not disparage others, remaining far removed from fame and reputation.
If there are those who praise them, they reflect upon themselves:

"I have no share in such renown; I now measure myself and find many transgressions. Among the qualities of merit, I possess not even a small fraction, yet sentient beings, through false perceptions, claim that I have them."
"The Bodhisattva takes great compassion as his reliance and the perfection of pure ethical discipline as his companion.
Furthermore, Maitreya!"

There is pure ethical discipline that is not a pāramitā: when one observes the precepts while grasping at signs and is not embraced by the most supreme [wisdom], it is merely called pure ethical discipline and not a pāramitā.
Why is this? Because they obtain only the tainted (*sāsrava*) retributions of the triple world, which cease when their lifespan ends.

If, however, one universally upholds the prohibitive precepts for the sake of all sentient beings, contemplating the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) that is devoid of the marks of self or person, and thus upholds the prohibitive precepts for the sake of sentient beings, this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), which can cause sentient beings to swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Furthermore, this perfection of pure ethical discipline acts as a guide for all sentient beings; it generates pure faith in those sentient beings who lack faith; it serves as a hidden treasure for sentient beings; it serves as a priceless jewel necklace for the adornment of the bodies of all sentient beings; it serves as a supreme and exquisite unguent for all sentient beings; and it serves as great renown for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, this perfection of pure ethical discipline can bestow equal dignity and majesty upon all sentient beings, whether lay or ordained, and whether old or young.

Without giving rise to pride or arrogance, free from all faults and afflictions, with pure deportment and devoid of all fear, one is able to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi as the most supreme Dharma King.
How is it that one can know that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is supreme?

If there are sentient beings who are able to maintain pure ethical discipline, although they may dwell in a lowly or humble station and lack noble lineage, wealth, or majesty, and though they lack the power to benefit others through their own strength, by means of this perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), they cause all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and non-humans—kings, ministers, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and householders—to all pay them homage, prostrate, make offerings, revere, and praise them.

If even those of the lowest station who uphold the Buddha’s precepts receive such reverence and respect, how much more so for other noble persons who protect and maintain the prohibitive precepts, thereby perfecting the pāramitā of pure ethical discipline.

It should be known that wherever one who guards the pure precepts walks, stands, sits, lies down, or practices walking meditation, that ground is auspicious; all humans and devas should take its soil and honor it by bearing it upon their heads.
By this one should know that those who uphold pure ethical discipline are the foremost, the highest, and the most supreme among all assemblies.
This is what is called the ultimate fulfillment of the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
The Sutra of the Six Pāramitās of the Mahāyāna Principles and Sequence, Scroll Five;
The Sutra of the Six Pāramitās of the Mahāyāna Principles and Sequence, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Seven: The Perfection of Forbearance (Kṣānti-pāramitā).
At that time, the Buddha, the Bhagavān, having thus clearly expounded the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), [proceeded as follows].
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), how does he strive for its fulfillment? Furthermore, how many types of this patience are there, and what is the practitioner’s mode of application? We pray that you will reveal this, for we delight in hearing it.
At that time, the Buddha, the Bhagavān, praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Desiring to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, you are now able to inquire about such a profound meaning."
Listen attentively now and reflect upon it well; I shall now analyze and explain it for you.
Son of good family!
You should know that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are entirely equal; because there is no discrimination, this is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Furthermore, if there are foolish, base, or deranged sentient beings who come to revile and insult one, one should endure them with composure.
It is like a drunken elephant that is difficult to restrain; it must be tamed by means of an iron hook.
The elephant intoxicated by anger is likewise subdued by the hook of patience; to bring it under control is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).

Furthermore, if sentient beings are harmed by thirty-six koṭis of devas, māras, spirits, yakṣas, and rākṣasas who come to assail the Bodhisattva, only the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) can destroy those armies; even when one wishes to subdue the eighty-four thousand enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are likewise eliminated through patience.
Not only the great armies of Māra and the hostile thieves of the afflictions, but even the most lowly and minute of enemies, one subdues through patience.
This is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

Furthermore, it is like a prince who has well-mastered the royal laws; once his father the king has passed away, he succeeds to the throne and shall proclaim the True Dharma to the four quarters, so that throughout the entire realm all shall practice the five kinds of True Dharma.
What are the five? First, not taking life;
second, not committing theft; third, refraining from sexual misconduct; fourth, not engaging in false speech; and fifth, not paying excessive taxes or extraneous levies on property.
If there is one who commits murder within the king’s realm, the king incurs a sixth part of that sin; the same applies to theft, sexual misconduct, and false speech.
Why is this? Whether it be lawful or unlawful, the king is the root; regarding both transgressions and merits, one-sixth of each belongs to the king.

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the mind is the kingdom and great compassion is the king. By means of the five dharmas of patience, he proclaims his decree within the realm—namely, beating, reviling, anger, resentment, and mockery—and these five things are all to be endured with patience. Should anyone violate them, they shall incur a grave and heavy offense.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

It is like a farmer who, wishing to plant crops, first prepares the irrigation channels to lead water; while in the midst of his labor, he encounters mountain rocks, and since there is no way to dig through them, he stops there.

The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is not like this; within the vast wilderness of the cycle of birth and death, he wishes to dig a channel of wisdom to draw forth the water of ambrosia. As he practices in succession, he encounters the rock of anger; having no other means to remove it, he relies solely on patient endurance (*kṣānti*), examining it with precise scrutiny until he pierces and breaks it through.

Furthermore, while all kings, ministers, elders, and householders constantly adorn themselves with necklaces and ornaments, the Dharma-kings of the Buddhas and the great bodhisattvas always adorn their own bodies with the necklace of patience (*kṣānti*).
If one encounters sentient beings who unjustly oppress or deceive them, they shall protect and rescue them through great compassion and patient endurance.
Furthermore, this patient endurance serves as a model for the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.

Taking faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom as its forest, and pure ethical discipline as its branches and leaves, if a fire of anger should suddenly arise within this grove, it would burn the branches and leaves of discipline beyond the possibility of extinguishing them; yet, by means of the rain of patience, they are extinguished, so that all sufferings and hardships of the present and future are forever free from anxiety and distress.

For one who lacks the patience of equanimity, there is no peace or happiness in the present life—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—and how could there be any happiness in future lives?

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva takes the power of patience as his armor. When a person who has committed an offense acts as a *caṇḍāla*, grasping the bow of delusion with the hand of anger and discharging the arrow of harsh speech to strike at the armor of patience, that bow and arrow naturally break apart; the armor of patience remains entirely undamaged, and the shattered bow and arrow are transformed into lotus flowers.
One should know that when a bodhisattva practices in this manner, it is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is like the world’s *agada* medicine, which is able to eliminate all poisonous diseases of both oneself and others.

The Bodhisattva is likewise; through the medicinal herb of patience (*kṣānti-gaṭha*), they are able to cure the toxic diseases of all afflictions of anger in both themselves and others—this is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

For example, it is like a world-renowned moon-pearl jewel that a merchant carries while traveling through a vast wilderness of sand and gravel where water is utterly absent. At night, he holds the jewel toward the moon and catches the water in a vessel; the water immediately flows forth, and by drinking it, the merchant is able to cross the wilderness.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: holding this moon-bright jewel of patience (*kṣānti-maṇiratna*), they cross the vast wilderness of birth and death—a place utterly devoid of the water of wisdom and filled with the afflictions (*kleśa*). Holding the jewel of forbearance amidst the moon of Buddha-wisdom, the Bodhisattva receives the water of the Buddha-dharma; drinking of it, they emerge from birth and death and reach the shore of Nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!
It is like the great earth: all grasses and trees depend upon it to grow, and all sentient beings depend upon it to dwell."
Patience is likewise; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the six perfections throughout the ten stages, relying upon them for growth and development, and abiding therein by means of them.
Furthermore, it is like a staircase that is exceedingly high and large, upon which sentient beings ascend directly to the Brahma Heaven.
The staircase of patience is likewise high and large; the Bodhisattva ascends it to reach the God among Gods.
Furthermore, just as a skilled painter creates various images that are perfected through the application of colors and ornaments, so too is the painter of patience;
he adorns and brings to perfect completion all meritorious qualities.

Furthermore, it is like this: suppose great dense clouds arise in space, pouring down torrential rain until the waters swell into a flood that sweeps away all grasses, trees, flowers, and fruits, entering the Ganges River and flowing on toward the great ocean.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: with a mind like space, they are able to give rise to the dense clouds of all-pervasive great compassion, which let fall the great rain of Dharma and the torrential flow of patient endurance. This washes away all the grasses and trees of anger and the flowers and fruits of ignorance, flowing into the river of wisdom and proceeding onward to the pure great ocean of nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, although a bodhisattva perceives the various sufferings of the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), through the power of patient endurance (*kṣānti*), they undergo these sufferings on behalf of others; for immeasurable eons (*kalpa*), they do not shrink from weariness, nor do they abandon them to enter *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, by the power of patience, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to relinquish everything—head, eyes, marrow, brain, body flesh, hands, feet, and even life itself—without any sense of stinginess or regret in their mind.
Ordinary people, lacking wisdom, are struck with terror upon hearing this, their hair standing on end; how could they ever renounce it?

By the power of such patience, the Bodhisattva is born with a handsome countenance wherever he may be, a sight that all sentient beings delight to behold, and he is constantly praised by all Buddhas within great assemblies.
"Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells securely in the power of patience, firm and immovable,
like Mount Sumeru, which cannot be shaken by the fierce winds of the whirlwind."
Patience is likewise like Mount Sumeru; it cannot be moved by the fierce winds of anger.

Furthermore, all those of external paths, due to evil associates, give rise to minds of false views and practice various asceticisms—such as going naked, self-starvation, scorching the body with the five fires, leaping from cliffs, or rushing into fire—claiming thereby to attain rebirth in heaven while having no faith in the True Dharma.

Having seen this, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion and manifests ascetic practices that exceed theirs even twofold. Consequently, these non-Buddhists revere the Bodhisattva as their teacher and model; he then guides them, revealing the True Dharma, so that those followers of heterodox paths may abide in right view.
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who say:
"In this body there is a self residing within the heart; it is the size of a large thumb, yet it is without obstruction and without form, and can only be seen by those with the divine eye."
This faculty of the eye serves as my attendant; once it has been acquired, it immediately informs me. It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

For this reason, if there are sentient beings who revile or abuse me, a person who kills them will be reborn in the heavens, whereas one who endures such abuse will die and fall into the three miserable realms.
"For example, it is as if many people serve under a single commander; if someone slanders that commander, the multitude will all kill him, and if they do not kill him, the multitude shall be guilty.
With the power of patience, the Bodhisattva takes pity on those with such wrong views and endures them all, employing various skillful means to eliminate their wrong views.
"Just as seasonal rain moistens and causes the growth of grasses and trees, enabling them to bear fruit,
so too is the patience of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bhagavān spoke these verses:
"As when it rains from heaven, ants emerge from their holes, gathering soil into mounds to dwell within;
so too this body is formed from the accumulation of the impurities of parents, and deluded consciousness clings to it within as 'self'."
Relying on the continuity of physical strength and pride in one's power, the wise observe it as being like a phantom or a mirage;
in a single moment it becomes fine dust, just as a seal of clay is utterly crushed under the tread of an elephant.
In the blink of an eye, things arise and perish in an instant; walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—all are suffering.
If one realizes that this physical body is suffering and impermanent, why would a wise person harbor any craving or attachment toward it?
The gods, the Brahmā-dwellers, and the ascetics cannot be harmed by the gaze or touch of venomous snakes;
should they be wounded, mantras and medicines can heal them. But when the venom of impermanence stings, who can provide salvation?
Having utterly abandoned the wholesome dharmas that are easy to cultivate, they crave and greedily pursue sensual pleasures that ruin their character;
when the wise observe this, they see it achieves nothing at all, like saffron dyeing a soiled garment.
“A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should teach the Dharma of non-self to the followers of external paths, saying: ‘The self that you grasp—
is it within, or is it without?’”
Does it come from the past?
Does it go to the future?
If you say that it exists, then at the time of your death, it should be unable to save you; since it cannot save you, it is clear that there is no self.

For example, just as a loyal minister serves his sovereign with single-minded devotion such that the sovereign will surely rescue him when he is in peril, if [the self] cannot do so now, one certainly knows there is no self.
If there were a self, it should possess mastery; why then is it destroyed by impermanence?

Yet all sentient beings are oppressed by the specter of impermanence and the multitude of sufferings; their limbs and joints separate and they pass away in an instant. If there were a self, it should be able to escape this; since it cannot escape such separation, we know that there is no self.
For this reason, you followers of external paths have served me since beginningless time, yet you have created various evil karmas and endured endless suffering.

You should know that I owe you not the slightest debt of gratitude; though you long served others, they abandoned you and departed, leaving your bodies to be devoured by evil beasts such as jackals, wolves, tigers, and leopards. Yet I cast you aside to seek other bodies for you; since beginningless time, the number of times I have discarded you is immeasurable and boundless, and it shall be the same in the present and the future.

Furthermore, if you claim that the mind is the self (ātman) and the body is its servant, you should know that this body is "mine"; since beginningless time, one has received immeasurable bodies, the number of which cannot be known.
Regarding these various bodies, are they a single self or many selves?
If there were many selves, they would be impermanent; because they are impermanent, the principle of a "self" is not established.

If the self were a single entity, it would necessarily be permanent; it would eternally abide within one body and should not migrate elsewhere. Since it does not so abide, even the notion of a "single" self is untenable.
For this reason, you should reflect and examine that both the doctrines of a "multiple self" and a "single self" are equally unestablished.
By this you should know that the mind is not the self.
Furthermore, you should observe that the body is neither "mine" nor a servant.

If the body were to belong to me, then its walking, standing, sitting, lying down, birth, aging, sickness, and death would await my commands; yet these occur one after another even before I have given instructions, clearly showing it does not belong to me.

If it were mine, then birth would always lead to birth and there would be no aging or death; likewise with walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. Since these are subject to change and impermanence, they are not mine.
By this, one knows with certainty that there is no self (ātman) nor anything belonging to a self (ātmīya).
Furthermore, it should be understood that the "self" you grasp at is your greatest enemy. Why is this?

In your previous lives, you accumulated roots of goodness; the karmic retribution of the five desires has now been exhausted in this life. Yet, having committed various evil deeds in the present, by the power of those karmas, you have been handed over to the wardens of hell.
"If there were a self, why would you not rescue one another?

By the power of patience, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva rescues sentient beings from among the evil spirits of "self" and "mine," establishing them in the state of right view; free from "self" and "mine," they perceive that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent. This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
"Furthermore, Maitreya!
It is just as when someone, for the sake of protecting their child, performs incantations so that malevolent spirits cannot cause them harm.
So too is the Bodhisattva: using the incantation of patience (kṣānti), they protect all sentient beings so that enemies such as anger can do no injury."

"Furthermore, Maitreya, it is like a person whose foot has been pierced by a thorn, who wishes to cover the entire great earth with various hides so that he may walk upon them and be free from suffering and distress."
The wise man asked,
"What do you intend to do with the hide you seek?
The man reported the circumstances in detail, as described above.
The wise man rebuked him, saying:
"Alas, you foolish man!
You should not act in this way."
"One need only use a small amount of hide to provide leather for sandals, which is sufficient to protect one's travels from injury; why then use so much hide as to cover the entire earth?
Ordinary beings are just like this: they create enmity and harm everywhere, wielding swords with the intent to kill the enemies of the great earth.

When the Bodhisattva sees this, he gives rise to profound compassion; he takes patience alone as his sandals to protect your body and mind. How could there be any room for various enemies wielding knives to inflict harm everywhere? This is precisely what is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
For example, if someone were to revile and abuse him with various poisonous words, a bodhisattva, upon hearing them, should not suddenly give rise to a mind of anger;
rather, he should investigate: "Who is it that is thus reviling me?"
Furthermore, who is it that receives this abuse?

Both of these bodies consist of twelve bases (*āyatana*): the eye-base sees forms, the ear-base hears sounds, the nose-base smells odors, the tongue-base tastes flavors, the body-base feels tangibles, and the mind-base cognizes phenomena. Now, this eye-base is truly not the self; if it is not the self, then between the eye-bases of oneself and another, who is at fault?
"If there were faults, they ought to be punished.
Thus, upon investigation, he finds no fault in either case; since there is no fault, who is being reviled by whom, such that one would become angry?
Observing in this manner, it is likewise for even the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Beyond the twelve spheres, there is not a single thing; both the one who reviles and the one who receives the revilement are empty.
By reflecting in this way, the mind of anger is immediately stilled.
If one hears harsh words, one should carefully observe:
"Of such speech, what exactly constitutes harshness?"

The two syllables of "harsh speech" do not arise simultaneously; when it is harsh, it is not yet speech, and when it is speech, it is no longer harsh. Arising and ceasing in each moment, they do not depend upon one another.
If this is the case for even two syllables, how much more so for many words of abuse and revilement?
By observing in this way throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one realizes that even such coarse words do not constitute an insult.
Furthermore, one observes both the person who reviles and the object of the revilement; since both are impermanent and do not abide for even a single moment, how could there be any anger?

By this you should know that the past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present does not abide. Since the phenomena of verbal abuse are empty, my own body is likewise so; both are identical to that which is impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, and non-abiding. Because they do not abide, all things are empty.
When one practices this contemplation, immeasurable enemies and thieves are simultaneously extinguished.
If one departs from this contemplation to grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination, it is merely called "patience" (kṣānti), but cannot be termed a "perfection" (pāramitā).

The five aggregates are selfless, and so forth, up to the eighteen elements, all of which are likewise selfless, like illusions and like transformations; even so, praise and blame are equal, for their fundamental nature is empty and quiescent.
"Furthermore, Maitreya! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva encounters one who reviles them, they should give rise to compassion, thinking:
'This person, possessed by the demon of anger and shrouded by afflictions, has committed such reviling.'"

Now, desiring to dispel this Māra, I should skillfully practice and study the *kṣānti-dhāraṇī* so as not to give rise to anger or resentment, ensuring that neither hatred nor other afflictions cause harm to sentient beings.
"If I were to become angry, malevolent spirits would possess my body.
For this reason, one gives rise to great compassion and pity for those who revile them and practices patient endurance toward them.
Although such practice may be called "endurance," it is only designated as a *pāramitā* when one is free from such conceptual discrimination.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices patience, if they see someone wielding a sharp blade who cuts off their hands and feet, they should give rise to a mind of comfort and regard that person as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), just as if someone were bestowing joy upon themselves, thinking: 'I am now obtaining a great reward of merit; I shall always cherish the kindness of that recipient. When bystanders see this, they all give rise to sympathetic joy."
The Bodhisattva is likewise; upon seeing one who cuts or dismembers him, he gives rise to great joy and consolation, thinking:

"He removes my sinful karma and bestows upon me the wealth of the Dharma. It is because of me that he has suffered ill repute, lost the bliss of humans, devas, and liberation, and endured the sufferings of the three miserable realms."
For these reasons, they have been my virtuous friends and noble companions, bringing me to fulfillment in the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
I ought to feel deep respect for such people and never forget their kindness until I reach enlightenment; how much less should I harbor anger toward them?
"If one gives rise to anger, this is to repay kindness with ingratitude.
For this reason, one should generate a twofold heart of reverence and regard [the teacher] as a virtuous master.

Although one may thus endure what is difficult to endure, because one has not yet eliminated the discrimination between self and other, it is merely called "patience" (kṣānti) and cannot be termed a "perfection" (pāramitā).
"Furthermore, while a bodhisattva dwells in a secluded and quiet place, someone may come and slander the bodhisattva, saying:
'You have committed theft, engaged in sexual misconduct, and have struck, reviled, or punished others.'"
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva endures this with patience, reflecting thus:

"This is not another's fault; it is because in my past lives I once slandered others, beat them, reviled them, or punished them, that I have incurred this reprimand and punishment due to the remaining karmic residue of those deeds."
"Because he has harmed me, he shall fall into the evil realms; therefore, I should conceive great compassion for this person.
He further reflected: "My current mind is extremely deceitful;

fearing that I myself might fall into hell, I have given rise to a mind of patient endurance. Furthermore, desiring to personally fulfill the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), I wish instead to cause the one who cuts and mangles me to fall into the three miserable states."

Reflecting in this way, he feels profound shame. At that time, having recognized his own fault, the bodhisattva conceives a sense of remorse and aversion toward the one who cut him, yet regards that person as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and develops deep respect. This is merely termed "patience" (kṣānti), but it is not yet a "perfection" (pāramitā).
Why is this? Because it arises from the discrimination between self and other.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva understands that the dharma of anger is the cause of all suffering, and knows that the practice of patience is the root of all myriad practices.
For these reasons, one practices patience; however, this is merely called "patience" and is not a *pāramitā*.
Why? Because it involves making discriminations between good and evil.

"Furthermore, the bodhisattva contemplates the body of the five aggregates as having five kinds of faults: it is a collection of manifold sufferings, momentary and impermanent, consisting of five kinds of impurities and thirty-six substances; it is devoid of self or what belongs to a self, and is entirely empty."

The heterodox teachers, holding false views, cling to the body as being peaceful and blissful, eternally abiding and unchanging, and as a pure dharma; they maintain the existence of a self and what belongs to a self.
The Bodhisattva contemplates these five kinds of dharmas with discernment and sees that all sentient beings are likewise thus.
Having understood this, one does not become angry when reviled nor feel joy when praised; this is merely called "patience" (kṣānti), but it is not a "perfection" (pāramitā).
Furthermore, Maitreya!
Briefly stated, there are thirty-two kinds of bodhisattva patience (*kṣānti*).
Namely: non-attachment is patience; non-harming is patience; freedom from feverish affliction is patience;
freedom from anger is patience; freedom from resentment is patience; freedom from indignation is patience; freedom from... [the text continues].
To be patient amidst contention is patience; to remain unstained by the objects of desire is patience; to be able to protect oneself and others is patience;
to accord with the bodhicitta is patience; to possess a non-conceptual mind is patience;
to be unattached to birth and death is patience; to accord with the ripening of karma is patience; and for the body to be pure is patience.
Purity of speech and mind is patience; being firm and non-retrogressive is patience; mastery of expression is patience;
the absence of conceptual construction is patience; the noble wisdom of self-realization is patience; protecting the minds of others is patience;
practicing the four Brahma-vihāras without being reborn according to the stages of dhyāna is patience; regarding...
Attaining mastery over the pleasures of humans and devas is patience; the perfection of the marks and signs is patience;
the profound and wondrous Brahma-voice is patience; the eradication of all evils is patience; the distancing from the defilement of stinginess is patience;
the severing of envy and jealousy is patience; the relinquishing of all enemies and thieves is patience; drawing near to Bodhi is patience.
The factors of enlightenment are patience; freedom from all unwholesome states is patience; delighting in dwelling in tranquility is patience;
and the attainment of all Buddha-dharmas is patience.

Maitreya! By practicing these thirty-two kinds of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), a bodhisattva can attain the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and swiftly achieve unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Furthermore, Maitreya!
What is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*)?
If someone reviles you with harsh words, you should contemplate that sound as being like an echo."
When being struck, one should contemplate this body as being like a reflection in a mirror.
When met with anger, one should contemplate this mind as being like a magical illusion.
When seeing wrathfulness, one should contemplate the nature of this mind as being free from agitation.
If one gains gain and offerings, one should contemplate that the self-nature of this mind is naturally subdued and not give rise to joy.
If one loses gain and offerings, one should contemplate that this mind is virtuous, wondrous, and tranquil, and not give rise to anger.
If one encounters slander, one should contemplate this body as being like empty space and should not seek retribution.
If one meets with praise, one should contemplate that the nature of one's own self is free from egoism and thus remain without arrogance.
If you receive praise, you should contemplate that the nature of the mind is originally empty and quiescent, and thus give rise to no joy or consolation.
If you are reviled or disparaged, you should contemplate that the nature of the mind is fundamentally free from fear, and thus give rise to no sorrow or distress.
When encountering suffering, one should contemplate that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally free from oppression, and thus perceive no characteristic of suffering.
When experiencing pleasure, one should contemplate that the true nature is eternally abiding and unchanging, and thus perceive no characteristic of pleasure or pain.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in patience, these eight winds cannot move or turn him.
Why is this? Because he abides in the true mark by means of the bodhicitta, being free from the notions of self and other, and because he perceives the dharmakāya.
Furthermore, one endures all matters that cause unease for the sake of subduing all demonic adversaries.
One should practice all difficult and painful austerities for the sake of disciplining the various false views of non-Buddhists.
Maitreya! You should know that I have now briefly explained the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā). Furthermore, Maitreya!
If one contemplates impermanence and attains mental forbearance by detaching from the notions of self and other, it is not true forbearance.
If one contemplates the characteristics of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena and attains mental forbearance, it is not true forbearance.

Furthermore, if one contemplates the twelve bases (*āyatana*) with patience, attaining forbearance by remaining free from the signs of anger and abuse toward the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), this is not true patience.
If one regards anger and abuse as inverted and regards patience as the authentic state, that is true patience.
To discriminate between what is heterodox and what is orthodox constitutes patience that is not true patience.
Furthermore, to see that one's own patience is justified while the anger and abuse of others are unjustified is a patience based on grasping at signs; it is not true patience.

Furthermore, abiding in the patience of the Eightfold Right Path while abandoning the patience of the Eightfold Wrong Path constitutes the patience of the path versus the non-path; it is not the true patience.

Furthermore, not contemplating all phenomena as impermanent, selfless, impure, and suffering, but instead contemplating all phenomena as permanent, blissful, self, and pure—this patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) contradicts [the former] and is not the true patience.
Furthermore, regarding the patience toward the dharma of emptiness, one does not endure various views;
regarding the patience toward the dharma of signlessness, one does not endure signs;
regarding the patience toward the dharma of wishlessness, one does not endure wishes.
Patience with phenomena that are without activity, but no patience with those that have activity;
patience with phenomena that are without affliction, but no patience with those that involve affliction;
patience with all wholesome phenomena, but no patience with what is not wholesome.
One endures the supramundane dharmas but does not endure mundane ones;
one endures faultless dharmas but does not endure those with faults;
one endures untainted dharmas but does not endure tainted ones.
"One endures the dharma of nirvana but does not endure birth-and-death.
Such forms of endurance are merely antidotal endurance, not ultimate endurance.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since such patience is not ultimate, how can it be called ‘ultimate patience’?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will analyze and explain this for us.”
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying: “Good son!

One who possesses true patience realizes through correct wisdom that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely empty. Because this emptiness and the intrinsic nature of all phenomena are non-dual, the nature of all phenomena, emptiness, and the intrinsic nature of correct wisdom are pure; they are non-dual and not two, without distinction and without interruption.”
By this one should know that worldly phenomena are themselves emptiness, and emptiness is itself worldly phenomena; for the intrinsic nature of these two dharmas is not mutually separable.
Such forbearance is called ultimate forbearance.

"Furthermore, by means of right wisdom, one realizes that the nature of all phenomena is the nature of signlessness, and that the nature of signlessness is all phenomena, because their fundamental nature is non-dual."

The nature of all phenomena is fundamentally without marks; the nature of right wisdom is inherently pure. It is non-dual and cannot be divided, for it is without distinction and without interruption.

By this one should know that all phenomena are themselves without marks, and that being without marks is itself all phenomena, because the fundamental nature of these two dharmas is not separate from one another.
Patience such as this is called ultimate patience.

Furthermore, by means of correct wisdom, one realizes that the nature of all phenomena is itself the nature of wishlessness, and the nature of wishlessness is itself the nature of all phenomena, because their fundamental nature is non-dual.
The nature of wishlessness and the nature of all phenomena are, by their very essence, pure through right knowledge; they are non-dual and not divided, being neither distinct nor severed.
Therefore, one should know that all phenomena are wishlessness, and wishlessness is all phenomena, for the essential natures of these two dharmas are inseparable.
Such forbearance is called ultimate forbearance.

Furthermore, by means of right wisdom, one realizes that the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is itself the nature of non-conditionedness; for this nature of non-conditionedness and the nature of all conditioned phenomena are, in their fundamental nature, non-dual.

The nature of all conditioned phenomena is the nature of non-conditioning; the fundamental nature of right wisdom is intrinsically pure, being non-dual, indivisible, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted.
Such patience as this is ultimate patience.

"Furthermore, through right wisdom one realizes that the nature of afflictions is itself the absence of the nature of afflictions; and the absence of the nature of afflictions is itself the nature of afflictions, because their fundamental nature is non-dual."

The nature of afflictions and the nature of the absence of afflictions are the naturally pure essence of right knowledge; they are non-dual and not divided, being without distinction and without interruption.
Thus, such patience is ultimate patience.

"Furthermore, by means of correct wisdom, one realizes that the nature of all that is wholesome is itself the nature of the unwholesome, and the nature of the unwholesome is itself the nature of all that is wholesome; for their fundamental nature is non-dual."
The nature of the wholesome and the unwholesome is the intrinsic purity of right knowledge; it is non-dual and not divided, without distinction and without interruption.
Thus, such patience is ultimate patience.

"Furthermore, by means of right wisdom, one realizes that the nature of supramundane phenomena is identical to the nature of mundane phenomena, and the nature of mundane phenomena is identical to the nature of supramundane phenomena, because their fundamental nature is non-dual."

The nature of supramundane phenomena and the nature of mundane phenomena are, by their very essence of right knowledge, pure; they are non-dual and not divided, without distinction and without interruption.
Such patience as this is ultimate patience.

"Furthermore, by means of correct wisdom, one realizes that the nature of being faultless is itself the nature of having faults, and the nature of having faults is itself the nature of being faultless, because their fundamental nature is non-dual."
The state of being faultless and the state of being faulty are, by their very nature of correct wisdom, pure; they are non-dual and not divided, without distinction and without interruption.
Such forbearance as this is ultimate forbearance.

"Furthermore, by means of right wisdom, one realizes that the nature of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) is identical to the nature of tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), and the nature of tainted phenomena is identical to the nature of untainted phenomena, because their fundamental nature is non-dual."

The nature of untainted phenomena and the nature of tainted phenomena are, by their very nature of right knowledge, pure; they are non-dual and not divided, being without distinction and without interruption.
Such forbearance as this is ultimate forbearance.

"Furthermore, by means of right wisdom, one realizes that the nature of nirvāṇa is the very nature of saṃsāra, and the nature of saṃsāra is the very nature of nirvāṇa, because their fundamental nature is non-dual."
The nature of nirvāṇa and the nature of saṃsāra are, by their very nature of right wisdom, fundamentally pure; they are non-dual and not divided, without distinction and without interruption.
Such patience as this is ultimate patience.
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"Such true and ultimate patience regarding all phenomena—neither self nor other, neither existent nor non-existent, neither arising nor non-arising, neither ceasing nor non-ceasing—one who attains this patience is said to have attained the true, ultimate patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*)."

When the Buddha had spoken this perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the Bodhisattva Maitreya, acting as the leader, together with an immeasurable assembly of great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas and this great gathering, praised the Bhagavān with one voice, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! How rare, O Sugata!"
"How truly marvelous, World-Honored One!

he exclaimed, and immediately made offerings with immeasurable, exquisite articles—namely, various wonderful incenses, *campaka* flowers, burning incense, unguents, and powdered incense; various flower garlands, robes, silken banners, streamers, and precious parasols—which he cast into the air as an offering. He provided entertainment with various kinds of music and offered praise to the Tathāgata with various songs and hymns.

When these sentient beings hear the Buddha preach this perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), they are not startled, not terrified, not frightened, and not afraid; they all attain the Tathāgata’s true dharma-patience (dharma-kṣānti).
The various kinds of incense and flowers scattered as offerings filled the entirety of the trichiliocosm in the midst of space.
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
"O son of good family!"
“You should arrange various kinds of flowers, incense, robes, and even banners and canopies.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

I have already arranged these incenses, flowers, and various garments, each placed within the very bodies of the assemblies of bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and others, serving as their dwelling places.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Maitreya had spoken these words, he immediately entered the Samādhi of All Physical Forms.

Having entered this concentration, all the various flowers, incense, garments, silken fabrics, and even banners and canopies that filled the void throughout the trichiliocosm were, by the power of his meditative concentration, entirely contained within the navel-wheel of Maitreya without any mutual obstruction; yet the offering articles did not diminish in size, nor did the body of the Bodhisattva expand.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Akṣayakośa addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son,
what is the name of this samādhi?"
"While abiding in this samādhi, one can cause all such articles of offering to enter entirely into the navel; yet your body does not increase, nor do the various objects decrease.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said: "Good son!..."
"This samādhi is named 'The Samādhi of Universally Entering All Form-Bodies.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayagarbha spoke again: "O Mahāsattva!"
"What is the nature of this samādhi’s miraculous sphere of activity?
Maitreya Bodhisattva replied,
"O virtuous one!"
All that exists within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world enters my navel-cakra; yet my body does not increase, nor do those images decrease.
Why is this? Such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
At that time, there were some among the assembly—bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, spirits, humans, non-humans, and others—who secretly thought to themselves:
"We wish to see the miraculous transformations within the sphere of this samādhi, but we do not know how."
At that time, the Bhagavān, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and the great assembly, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying: “Noble son!
“You should now manifest the supernatural transformations of this samādhi so that the assembly may all know of it.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya had long practiced such a samādhi and had mastered it with complete proficiency, free from all obstacles. He caused all the bodhisattvas, the great assemblies from other directions, the bhikṣu-saṃghas present in this gathering, and even the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to enter entirely into the body of Maitreya; yet these sentient beings felt no alarm or fear, but attained an unprecedented peace and happiness of body and mind.

For example, to the east, beyond immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, there is a world named Ratnamālāvyūha. There, all the objects enjoyed by the sentient beings are adorned with various kinds of precious jewels, and they experience every form of happiness.

Furthermore, the happiness experienced by this assembly of gods and humans within this body is equal to that of the aforementioned world, without any difference; all those in this great assembly clearly perceive it, and there is no obstruction whatsoever within the body of Maitreya.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva withdrew his supernormal powers.
Thereupon, the great assembly and the Buddha, the World-Honored One, each returned to their original seats and remained in solemn stillness.
None of those in the great assembly, nor any sentient beings, were aware of any movement of coming or going.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayakośa addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "How rare, Great Being!
This manifestation of the supernormal power of samādhi is something unprecedented, never before seen."
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"O virtuous one!

Not only do all the members of this assembly enter within my body, but even if the various Sumeru mountains, the ten kinds of jewel mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, the great oceans, rivers, the sun, moon, and stars, the palaces of the devas, the palaces of the nāgas, the palaces of the various honored spirits, and all beings of the five destinies and four modes of birth—humans, non-humans, and so forth—were all placed within my body, there would still be no obstruction."
My body does not increase, nor does theirs decrease; yet these sentient beings do not perceive any sign of coming or going.
Such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), how much more so in this assembly!

When the Bhagavān spoke these words on the perfection of patience and manifested this great supernormal transformation, seventy-six nayutas of devas and humans in the assembly all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas all attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"If there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon briefly hearing the name of this perfection of patience, are able to give rise to faith, such persons will certainly not fall into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm, and they shall never regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Principles and Sequence of the Six Pāramitās, Scroll Six.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Principles and Sequence of the Six Pāramitās, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Eight: The Perfection of Vigor. At that time, the Bhagavān, having thus spoken this perfection of patience, [continued].
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Great Sage, World-Honored One, you have already spoken of the perfection of patience; you should now extensively expound the perfection of diligence."
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide?
How should they subdue [the mind]?
How should they practice?
"How is the perfection of diligence fulfilled?
We pray that the Blessed One will explain this in detail.
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
“Good son! Listen attentively now and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it to you in detail.
That which is called the cultivation of the other five perfections is all accomplished through the power of diligence.”
The perfection of diligence refers to the body, speech, and mind; these three types of wholesome karma can only arise through diligence.
Among these three types of karma, mental karma is the most preeminent.
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the mental karma, there are two kinds of mind:
first, diligence; second, regression.
That which is called the arousal of the bodhicitta is diligence; that which is the cessation of the bodhicitta is regression.
How is it initiated? By giving rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.
How is it brought to rest?
Because it abides in the emptiness of self. How is it initiated?
Because it gathers in all sentient beings.
What is cessation? It is the relinquishing of all sentient beings. What is arousal?
Because there is no weariness within the cycle of birth and death.
How does one bring it to rest?
By seeking deliverance from the three realms.
How is it initiated?
Because of relinquishing everything entirely.
How is it brought to cessation?
Because one does not practice giving with a frivolous mind. How is it initiated?
By firmly upholding the pure precepts.
What is cessation? It is due to the violation of the prohibitive precepts.
What is initiation?
Because they are well-established in patience.
How is it that they cease?
Because they do not cultivate forbearance.
How is it initiated?
By cultivating and accumulating roots of goodness. How is it stilled?
Because of indolence and laziness,
how does one initiate [the practice]?
By abiding in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
How is it stilled? Because the mind is distracted. How is it aroused?
Because it is associated with wisdom.
How does it cease? Because it is associated with ignorance.
How is it initiated? Through extensive learning and eloquent exposition.
How is it brought to rest?
Because they have not heard the true Dharma.
How do they initiate it?
By accumulating wisdom.
How is it stilled? Because of grasping at signs and conceptual discrimination. How is it aroused?
Because one contemplates the aggregates as being like an illusion,
how does one bring them to cessation?
By generating weariness toward the aggregates.
How does it arise? Because one knows that the locus is like a dream.
How does it cease?
Because the roots and objects are eternally extinguished.
How does it arise? By contemplating that the elements (dhātus) are without arising.
What is cessation? It is the cessation of body and the cessation of wisdom. What is arousal?
Because it causes the increase of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). How does it cease?
By abandoning true wisdom (*prajñā*).
How is it initiated? Because of mastery over the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
How is it brought to rest?
Because of weariness with and detachment from that which is tainted (*sāsrava*). How is it initiated?
By correctly contemplating the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
What is meant by "stopping"?
It is because one does not cultivate the foundations of mindfulness.
What is meant by "arousing"?
Because it is associated with the right abandonments. How is it stilled?
By not practicing the right abandonments.
How does it arise? Because of mastery over the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*). How does it cease?
Because the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) are not yet perfected. How are they initiated?
By diligently practicing the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
What is quiescence?
It is because one does not increase the five faculties. What is arousal?
Because one delights in cultivating the five powers.
How does one bring them to rest?
By not cultivating the five powers.
How does it arise? Because it brings the factors of enlightenment to fulfillment. How does it cease?
Because the seven factors of enlightenment are not yet complete.
How are they brought forth?
By diligently cultivating the Noble Eightfold Path.
What is meant by "stopping"?
It is because one does not cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path.
What is meant by "arousing"?
Because one cultivates śamatha.
How is it stilled? Because one has not cultivated śamatha well.
How is it initiated? By correctly contemplating dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
How is it brought to cessation?
Because of weariness with dependent origination. How does it arise?
By hearing what has not been heard before.
What is cessation? It is because there is that which is heard.
What is initiation?
Because one disciplines the body through ethical discipline,
how does one bring it to rest?
By becoming weary of and detesting the body of the aggregates.
How is it initiated?
Because of unimpeded eloquence in discourse.
How is it brought to rest?
Because those beyond training (aśaikṣa) remain silent,
how do they initiate [practice]?
By cultivating the three gates of liberation (vimokṣamukha).
What is meant by "stopping"?
It is because one does not cultivate the three gates of liberation.
What is meant by "arousing"?
Because of subduing the enmity of Māra.
How does one bring it to rest?
By delighting in and adhering to nirvāṇa.
How is it initiated?
By skillfully cultivating expedient means.
How is it brought to rest?
Because of delighting in tranquility. How does it arise?
Because one seeks progress without ceasing.
What is cessation? It is because that which was to be done has been accomplished. What is arousal?
Because one has thoroughly understood the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). How does one bring it to rest?
Because one has realized the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya).
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"All such various practices of diligent application can be brought to fulfillment through the power of diligence; only when they are neither increased nor diminished can they benefit all sentient beings."
Why is this? Because they are able to remain far removed from all signs (*nimitta*), they are able to fulfill the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) through the power of wisdom.
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate their activities?

This refers to cultivating great loving-kindness and great compassion without abandoning the conditioned, realizing true unconditionedness without falling back or turning away, up until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Maitreya! You should know that this is the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) consisting in the purity of the mental action (manas-karma) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Maitreya!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have four kinds of diligence.
What are the four? They are:

ensuring that unwholesome states that have not yet arisen do not arise; swiftly eliminating unwholesome states that have already arisen; causing wholesome states that have not yet arisen to arise quickly; and causing wholesome states that have already arisen to increase.
Maitreya! You should know that these are the four kinds of diligence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Without these four, how could one fulfill the perfection of diligence?

The diligence initiated by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—extending to their generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and further diligence—consists of relinquishing what is difficult to relinquish and performing what is difficult to perform. Regarding such various difficult tasks, they are diligent and courageous, with minds free from weariness; the sublime practices they cultivate are such that all the devas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) are unable to perform them.

Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas extensively deliver sentient beings from the ocean of birth and death without any perception of "delivering," all of which is accomplished through the power of diligence; this is what is called the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

The power and effort exerted by indolent sentient beings in their practice of deeds are so slight that they are like drops of water that do not reach the great ocean; indolent people are just the same, unable to attain unsurpassed bodhi."

For example, suppose there is a person who lacks both hands and feet; unable to walk, stand, sit, or lie down according to their will, they cannot accomplish even the slightest task. How could such a person ever cross over a river, a stream, or the great ocean?

It is likewise for sentient beings who are indolent and lack the feet of diligence: such lazy people cannot even accomplish their domestic affairs; how much less could they possess compassion, fully cultivate ethical discipline and wisdom, deliver sentient beings from the burning house, and practice the six pāramitās—the provisions for awakening of a bodhisattva?

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva takes the perfection of diligence as a boat or raft; having been formed by the merit and wisdom accumulated over three incalculable eons, he causes all sentient beings to board this vessel together and cross beyond the great ocean of birth and death to the other shore.
Furthermore, there are generally three types of sentient beings in the world:
first, those who are indolent; second, those who are neither diligent nor indolent; and third, those who are energetic, vigorous, and resolute.
Regarding those who are indolent, they abandon even their own household duties, let alone being able to undertake projects for others.

As for those who are neither diligent nor indolent, they are entirely incapable of accomplishing great undertakings; even if they wish to strive and seek progress, they retreat as soon as they encounter obstacles.
Those who apply themselves with diligent effort constantly undergo great toil and hardship for the sake of sentient beings; they benefit others alone, without a thought for their own bodies.
As for those who are indolent, they are perpetually seized and deluded in body and mind by the demons of sloth.

It is like a person who enters the great ocean and reaches a mountain of the seven treasures; although there are immeasurable precious gems within that mountain, he is suddenly possessed by a ghost as he is about to gather them, and in an instant he returns on foot, failing to obtain a single jewel and returning home naked.

It is the same for sentient beings who are indolent: though they have been born here in this land of merit, Jambudvīpa, by the power of the ten virtuous karmas, the Bodhisattva observes that the ground is filled with immeasurable and boundless jewels of the ten virtues; yet these sentient beings, possessed and driven mad by the demon of indolence, lose their minds and, even if they were to see such wondrous jewels, have no thought of taking them, remaining as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
If a person of diligence were to take such precious objects, it would not be difficult for them, being like lifting a single hair.

Yet, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, desiring to fulfill the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) for the sake of all sentient beings, practices diligence with tireless effort throughout the long night of birth and death across immeasurable eons, not sparing even their own body or life, until they reach Bodhi.
The Bodhisattva contemplates this with a mind free from weariness for as long as it takes to eat a meal.

Furthermore, he reflects that when the Buddhas of the past practiced the bodhisattva path, they spent immeasurable kalpas fulfilling the six pāramitās, yet it felt to them as though it were only the duration of a meal.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates all the Buddhas of the present and future, who, practicing the bodhisattva path for immeasurable eons, finally achieve perfect enlightenment; such numbers of eons are difficult to calculate.

Suppose there were a city that was exceedingly high and vast, measuring one hundred *yojanas* in height and breadth on each of its four sides. Within this city, it were filled with sesame seeds. If, after the passing of a hundred thousand *kalpas*, a single seed were removed, and in this manner one seed were gradually removed at the end of each such *kalpa* until the city was empty, that duration would constitute one great *kalpa*. When such great *kalpas* are accumulated to a total of three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, [that is the time required for the bodhisattva to reach the first stage].

For kalpas such as these, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly acts with diligent vigor for the sake of each and every sentient being within the five destinies, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction until they finally reach bodhi.
“Suppose, for example, that the great earth were ground into fine dust; would such dust be very much in quantity?
Maitreya replied to the Buddha, “It would be very much, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"Suppose there were sentient beings as numerous as those atoms; for each and every one of them, a bodhisattva would practice with diligent vigor throughout the aforementioned eons, not sparing body or life and undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction, only then to achieve unsurpassed bodhi."
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should reflect in this way:

"In the past, throughout kalpas as numerous as those mentioned before, I applied myself with diligent vigor and fully perfected the six pāramitās, attaining the stage of non-retrogression before finally reaching bodhi."

He reflected thus: "If such long-lasting, courageous, and diligent effort can lead to the attainment of perfect enlightenment in what is but a mere moment compared to the years, months, and kalpas of the human world, why should I not strive even more earnestly?"

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should apply themselves with diligent vigor and fortify their resolve, so that they have no sense of stinginess regarding the head, eyes, marrow, brain, hands, feet, limbs, or joints that they may relinquish.

Having reflected thus, one practices with single-minded diligence, remaining forever free from weariness; this is precisely what is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of diligence (vīryapāramitā).
Then the Bhagavān spoke in verse:
"All fruits in the world arise from diligence;
the earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as the faculties and their objects, exist because of it."
Greed, anger, delusion, and doubt— All arise from indolence.
Within these, the Bodhisattva Is ever fearful, as if of a poisoned arrow.
Like a person with skillful arts who, Through laziness, achieves nothing at all.
A compassionate mother does not rejoice at seeing sons or daughters who are indolent;
But those with wisdom who are diligent and persevering, fulfilling the practices of a Bodhisattva,
Such people open the flower of awakening and are able to attain the stage of Buddhahood.
The wise person is always courageous and thoroughly understands the profound meaning;
the foolish and indolent person is not praised by the world.
If a person lacks diligence, they will likewise lack renown in the world.
Lacking the provisions of wholesome dharmas, one is as impure as filth and excrement.
While grass, bricks, and stones may still be of use to the world,
a person who is indolent and lazy is fit for nothing at all.
Just as a garment becomes soiled and worn out, or as a flower garland withers,
if a person lacks diligence, their physical beauty serves no purpose.
Just as a person gains renown through diligence and patience, [so too does virtue arise].
Lacking patience and diligence, she is neither female nor male.
Indolent and destitute of resources, lowly and full of arrogance, she is constantly fearful of the words of others; thus, all household affairs remain unaccomplished.
Thus, one who lacks diligence, though possessed of many arts and skills,
is constantly held in contempt by others, like a snake devoid of its venomous breath. Conversely,
though one may lack all such arts and skills, if they possess only diligent perseverance, [they are honored].
The fruit of Buddhahood and great enlightenment will certainly be fully accomplished.
All cultivation of meritorious deeds arises from the power of diligence,
just as a messenger who wishes to receive orders waits exclusively for the sovereign’s command.
Vigor is the noble foundation; one should apply oneself with diligent courage.
The Bodhisattva who delights in such practice will surely attain the unsurpassed fruit.
Constantly abiding in vigor is praised by the wise.
The ignorant cling to the heavens; wrong views are the root of saṃsāra.
The wise abide in right view; they renounce heaven and exert themselves with diligence and valor, for they are able to transcend those celestial realms.
The foolish and inferior lack diligence; abandoning effort, they serve the gods.
The wise delight in diligence and remain far removed from the teachings of the gods.
Between the destiny of fate and the power of diligence, there is a distinction between the foolish and the wise.
Belief in fate is the cause of wrong views; diligence brings forth superior fruits.
Just as there is no benefit in tilling and plowing the earth if there are no seeds, so too it is with those who lack diligence: what can be gained by relying on fate?
Just as wind fans a fire, Which grows from small to great, So too is it with diligence: Wholesome qualities increase and expand.
By practicing what is difficult to perform, One attains superior fruits.
"Without begrudging body or life, you shall succeed to the Dharma King.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya:

"When seeking bodhi, one dons the armor of diligence and takes great vows as one's weapons; day and night, through diligent effort, one increases merit and virtue, like the waxing moon gradually reaching fullness."
For example, suppose there is a person who hears that in a distant land there is a stūpa containing the relics of a Buddha, as well as people who have well-expounded the True Dharma.
Upon hearing this, the person leaps for joy; without waiting for provisions, a vehicle, or companions, they go barefoot to visit that shrine.

The path he traverses consists solely of fierce fires and sharp blades; yet, with courageous and resolute spirit, his mind does not retreat, and he advances decisively until he reaches that place to pay homage to the Buddha’s stūpa and hear the True Dharma.
Stepping with each foot upon the flames and blades, he reflected at every stride and made this vow:

"Today, while walking amidst swords and fire, I have been able to hear the True Dharma; may I, within the great suffering of birth and death, deliver sentient beings and establish them in the state of nirvāṇic peace and bliss."

Once the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has made this vow, although he treads upon blades and fire as if walking upon lotus flowers, his feet remain as soft as *sumanā* blossoms; furthermore, they seem as if sprinkled with sandalwood-scented water—cool, fragrant, and beyond compare.
Furthermore, he makes this vow:

"From this day forth until I attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, during the interval between these two points, my actions of body, speech, and mind shall constantly perform the work of a Buddha."
If I engage in other activities, may my body become like withered wood;
if I speak other words, may I be mute;
if I contemplate other dharmas with my mind, may I become deranged.
Apart from the True Dharma, one takes no pleasure in or attachment to any other sounds or teachings.
All the various virtues cultivated through these three types of action are entirely dedicated toward unsurpassed bodhi.

"Furthermore, I vow that all sentient beings shall together achieve perfect enlightenment, with merit that is inexhaustible, as vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as empty space, and continuing without rest until the end of the future."

For example, when dense clouds spread across the sky and pour down heavy rain, it dries up quickly upon reaching dry land or saline soil; yet, if even a single drop of rain enters the great ocean, that rain remains inexhaustible as long as the seawater has not been depleted.

The meritorious deeds performed by a bodhisattva are likewise: if one seeks liberation for oneself alone, it is like rain falling upon dry land, which soon dries up; but if one cultivates wholesome karma for all sentient beings within the dharma-realm and casts it into the ocean of nirvana through the power of great compassionate vows, then as long as sentient beings are inexhaustible, so too will their merit be inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

Suppose there were a Bodhisattva with an immeasurable lifespan who traveled eastward, passing through immeasurable koṭis of trichiliocosm worlds, causing all classes of sentient beings in the lands he traversed to attain the state of great parinirvāṇa and peace."

Thus, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have extensively delivered sentient beings; yet when I observe them now, those already delivered are like the soil upon a fingernail, while those not yet delivered are like the soil of the great earth.
Just as it is with the worlds of the eastern direction that have not yet been crossed over, so it is likewise for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

Although there are such immeasurable sentient beings, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not become weary or abandon them, nor does he give rise to regression; he practices with diligent vigor, never ceasing until the end.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to give rise to such a vast and great mind, there is not the slightest dharma that is difficult to practice; all the merit, wisdom, nobility, and sovereignty within the triple world are attained naturally, without the exertion of effort.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya:

“Regarding all sentient beings—whether of the past, present, or future—including those who are learners (*śaikṣa*), those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), and pratyekabuddhas—who diligently cultivate and accumulate all manner of immeasurable and boundless merits, these do not equal even one hundred-thousand-millionth part of a single hair’s worth of merit belonging to a Tathāgata.”
Thus, every single tip of a hair is born from the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata.
All the merits contained within every hair-tip of the Tathāgata’s body together constitute the merit of a single hair of the Tathāgata.

In this way, the Buddha has eighty-four thousand hairs; within each individual hair, there are all the aforementioned merits of a hair-tip. When these are combined together, they collectively constitute the merit of one of the Tathāgata’s secondary marks (anuvyañjana).

Thus, the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) consist of eighty kinds; within each individual mark, there are the aforementioned merits of the Buddha’s hair. When these are all combined together, they collectively constitute the merit of a single primary mark (lakṣaṇa) of the Tathāgata.

When these various marks are complete as the thirty-two major marks, each possessing the aforementioned merits of the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), and when these are combined and multiplied a hundred-thousandfold, they constitute the merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* (tuft of hair) between the Buddha’s eyebrows. This mark is perfectly full, curling gracefully to the right; it is as clear, bright, and pure white as *sphatika* crystal, appearing like a brilliant star in the darkness of night. When this tuft of hair is extended, it reaches upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven of the Form Realm; when retracted, it returns to its former state as the tuft of hair residing between the eyebrows.

If all the merit of this mark of the white tuft were multiplied a hundred thousandfold, it would become the mark of the fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) upon the Buddha’s crown; the merit of which is such that no one among gods or humans can see his crown.

A thousandfold the merit of such a *uṣṇīṣa* does not equal the merit possessed by the Tathāgata’s mark of the Brahma-voice; that voice penetrates downward to the Avīci Hell and extends upward to the ultimate heaven of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The immeasurable merits thus described are all manifestations of the Tathāgata’s great compassion; such emanation bodies are all formed by the accumulation of immeasurable merits, being peerless, beyond analogy, and without equal.

The merit of the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), multiplied a thousandfold, constitutes the merit of the Buddha’s reward body (saṃbhogakāya); the merit of this reward body, multiplied by hundreds of thousands of millions, constitutes the merit of the Buddha’s dharma body (dharmakāya), the measure of which cannot be known.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing the teaching of the boundless merits of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, are not startled, not terrified, and do not fear, you should know that such persons have accomplished the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). They should give rise to this vast mind: "The body of the Buddha is a measureless accumulation of merit;

I now observe it and vow to cultivate and realize it. I shall practice with diligent vigor, not begrudging my own body or life, and for the sake of all sentient beings, undergo the sufferings of the three miserable realms throughout immeasurable eons without giving rise to regret in my heart. I shall cause all to fully and perfectly accomplish the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*)."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya:
"Good son, you should contemplate the wisdom of the Buddha with close attention; listen now attentively, and I shall explain it for you."

For example, Śāriputra is the foremost in wisdom among all the śrāvakas; this Jambudvīpa is broad in the north and narrow in the south like the box of a carriage, measuring seven thousand yojanas in circumference.
The continent of Pūrvavideha is shaped like a half-moon and measures eight thousand yojanas in circumference.
The continent of Aparagoyānī is shaped like a full moon and measures nine thousand yojanas in circumference.
The terrain of Uttarakuru is square, measuring ten thousand yojanas in circumference. Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is square in shape;

it extends eighty thousand yojanas into the water and is composed of four precious substances. Its emergence above the water is equal in measure, and its four sides, each composed of four precious substances, are each eighty thousand yojanas in length.

Next outside, there are seven successive layers of golden mountains encircling the perimeter, with eight oceans of water surrounding them; beyond the outermost layer is the Great Iron Ring Mountain (*Mahācakravāḍa*).

Taking these four continents and the various kings of mountains as paper, the waters of the eight great oceans as ink, and all grasses and trees as brushes, if all humans and devas were to write for an entire kalpa, it would not equal even one-sixteenth of the wisdom attained by Śāriputra.
Furthermore, if all the sentient beings within this trichiliocosm possessed wisdom equal to that of Śāriputra and others without distinction,
the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has fully realized the perfection of generosity would surpass theirs by a hundredfold.

Furthermore, the wisdom of the perfection of generosity possessed by all sentient beings throughout this trichiliocosm does not equal the wisdom of the perfection of ethical discipline attained by a single bodhisattva mahāsattva; this remains true even up to the perfection of wisdom, which is likewise so.

Furthermore, all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm, even if they were to possess the wisdom of these six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), would not equal the wisdom attained by a single Bodhisattva Mahāsattva on the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*); and so it is for each successive stage up to the tenth stage Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with their wisdom increasing manifold at each turn.

Furthermore, the wisdom attained by a Bodhisattva of these ten stages does not equal even one-hundred-thousandth part of the wisdom attained by you, Maitreya, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in your final birth before Buddhahood.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, the Bodhisattva Maitreya thought to himself:
“Now that the Tathāgata has uttered such praise amidst this great assembly, I feel a profound sense of awe and trepidation.”
At that time, the Buddha, the Bhagavān, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son,
listen attentively now."
In this trichiliocosm, may the wisdom possessed by all sentient beings be equal to that of Maitreya and others, without any difference.

Even the wisdom of such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, when they have gone to the Bodhi tree, sat upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), subdued the hosts of Māra, and were about to achieve perfect awakening, does not approach even one hundred-thousand-millionth part of the wisdom attained by the Buddha Tathāgata.
Maitreya! You should know that the wisdom of the Tathāgata is profoundly deep, immeasurable, and inconceivable; it cannot be measured by any analogy.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing of this profound wisdom of all Buddhas, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, they should apply themselves with even greater diligence to accomplish the pāramitās.
