Furthermore, he contemplates the aggregate of sensation as being like bubbles upon water—arising and ceasing swiftly, not remaining for even a single moment.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through right wisdom, perceives the ultimate truth and realizes that the nature of sensation is empty, just like a bubble on the water.
For these reasons, it is called right knowledge and vision.

Furthermore, one contemplates the aggregate of perception as being like a mirage: just as a person suffering from heat and thirst sees a mirage in the distance and mistakes it for water, running toward it in search of it, yet finds nothing when they draw near.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, through right wisdom, perceives the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and realizes that characteristics and nature are empty.
For these reasons, this is called "right knowledge and vision" (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*).

Furthermore, he contemplates the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as being like a plantain tree (*kadalī*): it has no solidity within; though one peels it away repeatedly, in the end nothing is found.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through right wisdom, perceives the ultimate truth (paramārtha) and understands that the nature of consciousness is empty.
For these reasons, this is called right knowledge and vision.

Furthermore, he contemplates the aggregate of consciousness as being like a magical illusion, just as a worldly magician conjures gold, silver, precious jewels, pearls, and necklaces through illusion; yet, when one seeks their substantial essence, it is utterly unfindable.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through right wisdom, perceives the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), clearly understanding that the nature of consciousness is empty, like an illusion or a magical transformation.
For these reasons, this is called "right knowledge and vision" (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*).

Having performed this contemplation, one gives rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings and forms the intention to deliver them. Such observation is called skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, one contemplates that the five aggregates are like illusions and dreams, all arising from the mind of deluded conceptualization and inversion; they are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span; they are not a nourisher, not a man, not a *pudgala*, not a mind-born, not a youth, not an agent, and not an experiencer. Through skillful means, one understands that the nature of the aggregates is empty, such that like a dream, they are entirely unattainable. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s wisdom of skillfulness regarding the aggregates.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the aggregates as being like echoes, devoid of a self, devoid of a person, and even devoid of an agent or an experiencer; thus, the nature of these aggregates is like an echo in a valley, dependent upon various causes and conditions.
To understand them as they truly are, as being equal and without dual characteristics—this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful knowledge of the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya-jñāna*).

Furthermore, to contemplate the aggregates as like shadows, appearing from the conditions of karma, devoid of a self, a person, or even a feeler; and to realize that such a shadow-nature is utterly unobtainable, being equal and without dual characteristics—this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful knowledge of the aggregates.

Furthermore, one contemplates the aggregates as being like reflections in a mirror—devoid of a self, a person, and even a recipient. Just as such a reflection is neither internal nor external and is utterly unfindable, being equal and non-dual, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful knowledge regarding the aggregates.

Furthermore, observing that the aggregates arise from conditions and are like illusions or transformations—devoid of a self, a person, or even an experiencer—and knowing them as they truly are through skillful wisdom as being equal and without dual characteristics: this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the aggregates.

Furthermore, to contemplate the aggregates as having the characteristic of transformation and decay—being impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and impure—and to know them as they truly are: that their nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent, neither subject to destruction nor not subject to destruction, is called skillful knowledge regarding the aggregates.
"Furthermore, what is called skillfulness regarding the bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*)?
It refers to contemplating that the eye-base, as well as the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases—the internal phenomena—are all empty."
Next, one contemplates the sense bases of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena; these external dharmas are also empty.

Contemplating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) with right wisdom, seeing that it is neither internal nor external, is called right knowledge and vision (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*); this is what is termed skillful knowledge regarding the sense bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, there is skill regarding the bases (*āyatana*), which means realizing that the bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all entirely empty, and that they lack the characteristics of seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing; this is called the wisdom of the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-jñāna*).

Furthermore, there is the wisdom that comprehends the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). To comprehend that the intrinsic nature of the spheres of form, sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental objects is empty and quiescent, and that they do not possess the characteristics of being objects for the spheres of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind—this is called the wisdom that comprehends the sphere of mental objects.

Furthermore, there is skillfulness regarding the bases (*āyatana*), namely: the eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, and the mind-base; their dharmic nature is empty and quiescent, being without self or what belongs to a self.

The sense-base of form, and the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena—whose dharmic nature is empty, devoid of self or what belongs to a self, neither associated nor dissociated, neither wholesome nor unwholesome dharmas, neither increasing nor decreasing, without dual characteristics, and primordially empty and quiescent—this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful knowledge regarding the bases.

Furthermore, there is the wisdom of skillfulness regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*). The eye-base and the form-base are fundamentally pure, unstained, and unattached; the eye-base is firm, tranquil, and eternally abiding.

Likewise, the ear and sound, nose and odor, tongue and flavor, body and touch, and mind and mental phenomena are by nature fundamentally pure, unstained, and unattached; even the mind-faculty is firm, tranquil, eternally abiding, and immutable. This is called the bodhisattva’s wisdom of skillfulness regarding the sense bases.
Furthermore, what is called skillfulness regarding the locus (*sthāna-kauśalya*)?
It refers to the locus of the noble ones (*ārya*), which is not the locus of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), and wherein the noble path (*āryamārga*) can arise; this is called the locus.
When ordinary beings engage in unwholesome conduct and are born into the evil realms, this is called "inappropriate" (*asthāna*).

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the Eightfold Noble Path, give rise to great compassion, and cause all sentient beings to enter the assembly of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*), this is called "skillful knowledge regarding the appropriate" (*sthāna-kauśalya-jñāna*).

"Furthermore, what is called the bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of the realms (*dhātu*)? It refers to observing that the eye-realm, the form-realm, and the eye-consciousness-realm are without self and do not belong to a self;

nor do they arise conditioned by the eye-realm, the form-realm, or the eye-consciousness-realm. This extends even to the mind-realm, the phenomena-realm, which are without self and do not belong to a self, and so on up to the mind-consciousness-realm, which is without self and does not arise conditioned by the mind-consciousness-realm. Thus, with right wisdom, the bodhisattva contemplates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), knowing that the nature of the eighteen realms is itself emptiness, without self, and without person. The dharma-realm is equal, pure, and immovable. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful knowledge of the realms."

Furthermore, there is skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu-kuśala*), namely, the wisdom that thoroughly understands the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu-jñāna*). To thoroughly know that the intrinsic nature of the earth, water, fire, and wind elements is emptiness, such that solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion are all unapprehendable, being identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s wisdom that thoroughly understands the dharma-element.

Furthermore, there is the wisdom that realizes the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-jñāna*). This wisdom realizes that the nature of the eye-realm up to the mind-realm is empty; the nature of the form-realm up to the phenomena-realm is empty; and the nature of the eye-consciousness-realm up to the mind-consciousness-realm is empty. It is also devoid of the characteristics of seeing, hearing, sensing, knowing, or conceptual discrimination. This is what is called the wisdom that realizes the dharma-realm.
"Furthermore, what is meant by skillfulness regarding the truths (*satya-kauśalya*)?
It refers to the Four Truths—suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
To contemplate these five aggregates as the suffering of suffering, the suffering of conditioned existence, and the suffering of change is called the knowledge of the Noble Truth of Suffering."
To know that the increase of the five aggregates is caused by ignorance is the knowledge of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya-jñāna*).
To realize that the cessation of all suffering occurs through the non-arising of craving is the knowledge of the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya-jñāna*).
To cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path for the sake of this cessation is the knowledge of the truth of the path (*mārga-satya-jñāna*).
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the truths.
Furthermore, there is skillfulness regarding the truths, namely: knowing that suffering is non-arising is called the wisdom of the truth of suffering.
Knowing that the arising of the accumulation does not occur is called the knowledge of the truth of accumulation (*samudaya-satya-jñāna*).
Realizing that what was originally unarisen is now extinguished is called the knowledge of the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya-jñāna*).
Cultivating the contemplation of the Middle Way within the aspect of non-duality is called the knowledge of the truth of the path (*mārga-satya-jñāna*).
This is what is called skillful knowledge regarding the truths.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands that painful sensation is empty and lacks intrinsic nature, and is able to perceive that correct wisdom is likewise entirely empty, this is called the knowledge of suffering within suffering.

Contemplating that the conditioned origination of accumulation exists as a phantom arising from conditions, and that the correct wisdom capable of such contemplation is likewise entirely empty—this is called the wisdom of emptiness regarding accumulation.
Knowing that the cessation of craving is by its very nature empty, and that when correct wisdom manifests it is pure and equanimous—this is called the wisdom of emptiness regarding cessation.

Knowing that the path leading out of suffering is ultimately unattainable, and observing through right wisdom that its intrinsic nature is entirely empty, is called the middle-way wisdom within the path.
Such right wisdom, free from all conceptual discrimination, is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the truths.
Furthermore, to know that the very essence of the suffering of birth is non-arising is called true knowledge regarding suffering.
To know that the arising of birth is an accumulation that lacks any actual conjunction is called true knowledge regarding the accumulation [of suffering].
To know that birth is fundamentally non-existent and thus has no cessation is called true wisdom regarding cessation.
To know that the path for escaping suffering is free from both existence and non-existence is called true wisdom regarding the path.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands these as they truly are, it is called skillfulness regarding the truths (*satyakauśalya*).

Furthermore, there is another skillfulness regarding the truths, namely the three truths: the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and the truth of the true nature of phenomena (*lakṣaṇasatya*).
The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) refers to all worldly speech, letters, and the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing [of beings].
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) refers to that which is beyond the sphere of mental activity, devoid of further letters, and free from all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
The truth of the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) refers to the fact that all marks are non-marks; such non-marks are themselves the true nature.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is unstained by the conventional and does not dwell in the ultimate, perceiving them as equal in their single mark—this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the truths.
Furthermore, there are two truths, namely the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
As for the conventional truth, it refers to all phenomena of the world, such as form and mind; these are seen according to reality and known in accordance with reality.

"Ultimate truth" refers to the principle of the two emptinesses: pure, serene, and ultimately quiescent. Not wearying of transforming others, knowing that in truth there is nothing to grasp, and that no dharma can be attained—this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding truth.

Furthermore, there is one truth, namely suchness, the pure dharma-realm, which is without arising and without cessation, neither annihilated nor eternal, far removed from the two extremes and ultimately blissful. Regarding birth and non-birth, the mind is free from dualistic characteristics; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding truth.
"Furthermore, what is meant by skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?

A bodhisattva mahāsattva observes the continuous flow of dependent origination: conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*) are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness (*vijñāna*); conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); conditioned by the six sense bases is contact (*sparśa*); conditioned by contact is feeling (*vedanā*); conditioned by feeling is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); conditioned by craving is grasping (*upādāna*); conditioned by grasping is becoming (*bhava*); conditioned by becoming is birth (*jāti*); and conditioned by birth are old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair."

By means of correct wisdom, the bodhisattva understands, in accordance with reality, that dependent origination is without intrinsic nature, without arising, and without cessation; that the dharma-nature is manifest before them; and that it is without mind or activity, without a master and without appropriation. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding dependent origination.

Furthermore, all causes—whether wholesome causes or unwholesome causes, causes of movement or causes of non-movement, causes of birth and death or causes of nirvana—he knows these causes exactly as they are.

He knows, exactly as they are, the sharp or dull faculties of all sentient beings, as well as their suchlike natures, suchlike causes, suchlike conditions, suchlike karmic fruits, and suchlike beginnings and endings.

According to their causes and conditions, they give rise to and cultivate wholesome qualities without any loss; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Furthermore, with the cessation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), ignorance (*avidyā*) ceases; with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness (*vijñāna*) ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact (*sparśa*) ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling (*vedanā*) ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) ceases; with the cessation of craving, grasping (*upādāna*) ceases; with the cessation of grasping, becoming (*bhava*) ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth (*jāti*) ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair cease.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, through correct wisdom, thoroughly understands dependent origination as being without arising and without cessation, without a master and without appropriation, this is called skillful knowledge of dependent origination.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

All causes and conditions are merely provisional aggregations and lack intrinsic nature; they do not grow or arise from a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. To teach such a Dharma for the sake of these sentient beings—immeasurable, boundless, and inexhaustible—and to understand it as it truly is, is called the skillful wisdom of dependent origination."

Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly understands that all phenomena arising from conditions possess the characteristic of being without birth, without cessation, and inexhaustible; this characteristic of inexhaustibility is itself the characteristic of bodhi. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding dependent origination.
"Furthermore, what is skillfulness regarding the three periods of time?

It means that one mindfully practices all wholesome dharmas of the past as they truly are, and constantly remains far removed from unwholesome dharmas. Having known this as it truly is, one dedicates [the merit] entirely to all sentient beings; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s wisdom of skillfulness regarding the past."

Furthermore, to reflect upon all future roots of goodness and the provisions for enlightenment, dedicating them entirely toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the future.

Furthermore, when all wholesome dharmas associated with right mindfulness are present, and unwholesome dharmas associated with wrong mindfulness do not arise, this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the present.

Furthermore, observing that the past is entirely empty, and that the present and future are likewise entirely empty—this equality of the three periods of time, abiding in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), is true liberation.

Furthermore, observing the merit and wisdom of all Buddhas of the past, present, and future, one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the three periods of time.

Furthermore, one contemplates that the past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present does not abide; all superior practices cultivated through the wholesome dharmas of the three periods of time are wholeheartedly dedicated toward unexcelled bodhi. Although the wholesome dharmas of the present do not abide for even a single moment, one constantly gives rise to the mind of bodhi—this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the three periods of time.

Furthermore, the past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present does not abide; thus, arising and ceasing do not abide for even a single moment. To always maintain such awakening of the mind is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the three periods of time.
Furthermore, the inconceivable nature of the bodhisattva itself is called the bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the three periods of time.

Furthermore, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment, they recollect all past roots of goodness; all sentient beings, according to their respective faculties, achieve fulfillment based on those vows. Regarding all future Buddhas whom they will honor, all sentient beings, according to their respective faculties, shall achieve fulfillment. Regarding all present sentient beings, they employ supernatural powers, preach the Dharma, and provide various forms of instruction, so that they achieve fulfillment according to their faculties.

Thus, benefiting oneself and others throughout the three periods of time and perfecting the supreme and wondrous practices for awakening—this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the three periods of time.
Furthermore, what is meant by skillfulness regarding the three vehicles?
That is to say, the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and the Bodhisattva-yāna; it is by relying on these three vehicles that one seeks liberation.
What is the skillful wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva regarding the Śrāvaka-yāna?

Encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world and hearing the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, they awaken to the underlying principle through sound and give rise to right view; therefore, they are called Śrāvakas.

Because they cultivate pure precepts, they fulfill the aggregate of morality (śīla-skandha); because they attain meditative concentration (dhyāna), they fulfill the aggregate of concentration (samādhi-skandha); and because they perceive the principle of the Truths, they attain the aggregates of wisdom (prajñā), liberation (vimukti), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana).
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful knowledge regarding the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Furthermore, there is skillfulness regarding the Śrāvaka vehicle: conceiving a sense of weariness toward the three realms, deeply contemplating the impermanence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), seeing that all phenomena are entirely without self (*anātman*), and joyfully delighting in the tranquility of nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, observing the five aggregates as enemies and robbers, observing the elements as venomous snakes, and observing the six internal sense bases as an empty village, they constantly aspire for renunciation, delight in nirvana, and conceive of it as their refuge; this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
Furthermore, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas?

It refers to being weary of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), delighting in renunciation, having few desires and being content, remaining free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and finding joy in dwelling in solitude and stillness; through the conditions of dependent origination, one spontaneously awakens to the impermanence of all phenomena and thereby attains liberation. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s wisdom of skillfulness regarding the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain skillfulness regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma?

The merits of the Mahāyāna are immeasurable and boundless; they cause all sentient beings to awaken to and enter that Supreme Vehicle without obstruction, to attain great wisdom free from arising and ceasing, and to accumulate all roots of merit and virtue for the enjoyment of all sentient beings.
They accomplish the various pāramitās, thereby bringing all mental activities under thorough subjugation.
Because it increases the unsurpassed great bodhi;

because it possesses great majestic power, having gone to the Bodhi tree and sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it observes the faculties of sentient beings with great compassion and does not abandon them; because it is unobstructed and unhindered throughout all things, feeling universal pity for all as if they were its only child, and is able to transcend all terrors of the evil realms;
and because it can cause all Buddha-dharmas to manifest before one.
Because it subdues all externalists and demonic adversaries;
because it establishes the supreme banner of the Dharma of Bodhi;
and because it is able to sever and eliminate all fetters of eternalism and nihilism.
Because they have attained the unimpeded wisdom of the Buddha-Tathāgata;
because they cause the various treasures of the Buddha-dharma to flourish and increase;
and because they benefit beings according to their faculties without error.
Because the great compassion that nurtures sentient beings has been perfected;

and because it is adorned with the garland of merits consisting of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique buddha-qualities, and the primary and secondary marks, which are free from all faults.
All such skillful means as these are called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

Furthermore, because it is that which all Buddhas ride upon, the Buddha constitutes the Great Vehicle by being fully endowed with seven factors, just as a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) is endowed with the seven treasures.
What are the seven? They are:
great observation, great conformity, great wisdom, great diligence, great skillful means, great realization, and great activity.

Regarding "great observation": the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by drawing near to virtuous friends and hearing the true Dharma, realizes all phenomena in a single instant, and the true nature of reality manifests before them.
"Great conformity" refers to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s accomplishment of great wisdom, great meditative concentration, and great compassion for the sake of benefiting both self and others.
"Great wisdom" means that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives the true nature of reality: that both the self and phenomena are empty.
One of great vigor is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, is able to accomplish the myriad practices of great compassion.
One of great skillful means is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has attained the patience of equality, abiding neither in saṃsāra nor realizing nirvāṇa.
"Great realization" refers to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s immeasurable and boundless great merit consisting of the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).

"Great undertaking" refers to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attaining great enlightenment within saṃsāra and accomplishing the complete and perfect buddha-activities of tens of billions of Ganges-sands of Buddhas.
Being fully endowed with these seven kinds of supreme qualities as a Dharma King is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom of the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, what is skillfulness regarding all phenomena?
That is to say, the conditioned and the unconditioned.

When a bodhisattva possesses supreme skillful means regarding these two dharmas, and increases the purity of their physical, verbal, and mental good conduct while dedicating it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the conditioned.

When a bodhisattva possesses the three types of non-action (avijñapti) in body, speech, and mind, which are pure and equal, and dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the unconditioned.

Furthermore, there is skillful means: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva increases and cultivates the practices from generosity and ethical discipline up to meditative concentration, and dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one cultivates the various perfections while remaining free from all signs and dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, there is skillfulness in employing the wisdom of expedient means to practice the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather in sentient beings; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, there is skillfulness in abiding in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), whereby one gathers in sentient beings without grasping or attachment and dedicates [the merit] toward enlightenment; this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, there is skillful means through which one thoroughly understands that afflictions increase birth and death, while the factors of enlightenment sever birth and death; this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Moreover, knowing the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—one is able to be certain, equal, non-dual, undifferentiated, and irreversible regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, skillfulness regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) consists in acting within the three realms without being attached to them; this is called the bodhisattva’s wisdom of skillfulness regarding the conditioned.

Thoroughly understanding that the nature of the three realms is entirely empty, like an illusion or a magical transformation, and thus not grasping or becoming attached to them, is called the bodhisattva’s wisdom of skillfulness regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, to thus understand that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is pure, signless, and nameless, and to possess all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), is called "real wisdom" (*bhūta-jñāna*);
to employ provisional names as skillful means (*upāya*) for the sake of delivering sentient beings and to make such distinctions is called "expedient wisdom" (*prajñā-upāya-jñāna*).
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain mastery over these eight dharmas and the two types of knowledge, it is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, the complete and thorough understanding of the nature of all phenomena is called wisdom;
the discernment of all wholesome and unwholesome phenomena is called skillful means (upāya).
To accord with liberation and be free from all conceptual discrimination, such that noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) manifests before one, is called *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, to be able to skillfully discern various views and fetters (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*) in this way, and to extract them by means of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, is called "skillful means" (*upāya*).
To be able to fulfill the unsurpassed great vows is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
To remove that burning affliction and bring about coolness is called skillful means;
to be able to understand that the nature of afflictions is ungraspable is called wisdom.
To eliminate the suffering of body and mind and attain lightness and ease is called skillful means.
To roam within the garden of the Dharma and attain mindfulness and dhāraṇī, such that wisdom and principle manifest before one, is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
To serve as a place of reliance for all sentient beings is called skillful means (*upāya*);
to be without dwelling or attachment regarding both the supported and the support is called wisdom.
To attain the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is called skillful means;
to constantly remain free from discursive thought while being in accord with the wisdom of the true mark, thereby attaining the great joy of the Dharma, is called wisdom.
Furthermore, being able to cultivate and grow the five pāramitās is called skillful means;
according with whichever vehicle one delights in to ultimately return to the Buddha-wisdom, with self-nature illuminating, is called wisdom.
To be able to cross over the torrential flood of all birth and death is called skillful means;
that in reality there are no sentient beings who attain liberation is called wisdom.
To establish correct practice is called skillful means;
To perceive the emptiness of the fundamental nature is called wisdom.
To eliminate adventitious afflictions is called skillful means;
to be well able to awaken to the fact that the nature of wisdom is untainted is called wisdom.
To practice without anything practiced is called skillful means;
to awaken to the emptiness of phenomena is called wisdom.
To be unattached to the three realms is called skillful means.
Causing all bodhisattvas to realize the ultimate truth is called wisdom.
Gathering in all sentient beings and leading them to practice the ten thousand virtues is called skillful means;
that all worthies and sages are of one single dharma-realm is called wisdom.
To eliminate deluded discrimination according to one's faculties and nature is called skillful means;
to perceive the fundamental purity, quiescence, and non-arising is called wisdom.
To be able to give rise to skillful means and sever the darkness of ignorance is called skillful means.
To enter deeply into meditative concentration while not abiding in meditative concentration is called wisdom.
To guide and lead those of the two vehicles is called skillful means;
to sever attachment to phenomena and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is called wisdom.
To cause sentient beings to give rise to superior understanding according to their faculties is called skillful means;
to realize that the nature of the faculties is empty is called wisdom.
To transcend the realm of delusion is called skillful means;
To demonstrate the ultimate truth is called wisdom;
to provisionally teach the four truths is called skillful means;
to realize that all practices are ultimately ungraspable is called wisdom.
Diligently seeking merit with inexhaustible compassionate vows is called skillful means;
realizing that what corresponds [to phenomena] is not real, neither coming nor going, and that the dharma-realm is equal, is called wisdom.
Universally manifesting teachings in accordance with conditions to transform all beings is called skillful means;
realizing that the nature of afflictions is fundamentally liberated is called wisdom.
Thoroughly understanding that the fetters are false conceptualizations is called skillful means.
To realize that the minds of sentient beings are fundamentally quiescent is called wisdom.
To exhort them to cultivate the severance of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and habitual perfusions (*vāsanā*) is called skillful means.
That the various mental activities of all sentient beings—the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction—are themselves the gates of the Buddha’s wisdom is called wisdom.
To skillfully exhort Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to practice so that they gradually enter the Buddha-way is called *upāya* (skillful means);
for a Bodhisattva to practice such *prajñāpāramitā* and swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is called *prajñāpāramitā*.

When the Buddha spoke this Mahāprajñāpāramitā, thirty-two koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within the assembly attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and seven hundred and eight thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The great assembly in this gathering each offered various kinds of exquisite flowers, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, and other ornaments, as well as campaka flowers, as an offering to the *prajñāpāramitā*, scattering them over the Tathāgata, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, and all the other bodhisattvas.
All the devas in the void performed celestial music and offered various songs and hymns in praise of the Tathāgata, who had accomplished the boundless merit of Bodhi over immeasurable kalpas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the entire assembly:
"Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva!
You have been able to inquire about the profound Prajñāpāramitā, the inconceivable Dharma-gate of the inexhaustible merits of the Mahāyāna."
Those in the various assemblies who hear this sutra shall likewise fulfill such merits as these.

If they hear this sutra and give rise to a mind of faith and understanding, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, copying, and explaining it—such persons will bring about immeasurable and inconceivable benefit, which cannot be reached even by analogy or calculation.
At that time, the Bhagavān untied the robe from his shoulder and, handing it to Maitreya, spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
"All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions rejoice in your ability to inquire about this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, having received the robe from the Buddha, placed it upon his head with veneration and spoke these words:

"This robe is the *caitya* of the Tathāgata’s true body; all devas, nāgas, humans, non-humans, and others should pay homage to it, circumambulate it to the right, and honor it with various kinds of offerings."

At that time, the great assembly suddenly beheld immeasurable varieties of flowers, jeweled garlands, banners, and canopies coming from the ten directions; they came to rest upon the crown of the Buddha’s head and, suspended in mid-air, in an instant completely covered the great assembly and the multitude of Maitreya Bodhisattvas above them.
Furthermore, from among the banners, canopies, and articles of offering, a great sound issued forth, praising him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva!"
“Please inquire into this meaning;
we shall rejoice in our hearts and make offerings.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From where do these flower garlands, banners, and canopies come, and from whence does this sound issue forth to offer praise and sympathetic joy?
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed Śāriputra, saying:

“Good son! This Bodhisattva Maitreya, while practicing the bodhisattva path in past lives, liberated immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings. Among those who now abide on the bodhisattva stage of non-retrogression, or among those among śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, humans, and devas, there are sentient beings who, due to past causes and conditions, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, each offer various precious flower garlands and canopies to the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and the Buddha Tathāgata, praising the merits of Maitreya in this manner; such are the sounds they produce.”
Having spoken these words, the entire assembly conceived a profound sense of reverence toward the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya and all said:
“Today we have attained great and excellent benefit; we have been able to see this person, draw near to him and make offerings to him, and have heard this sutra from the Tathāgata.”
World-Honored One!

If these sentient beings merely hear the name of the Buddha and the name of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, they still attain immeasurable and boundless merit; how much more so for those who, in the very presence of the Buddha, hear this sutra and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

“If there are sons or daughters of good family who, throughout an entire eon, practice various kinds of giving—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, agate, pearls, mani-jewels, and even their own heads, eyes, marrow, and brains without any stinginess—and who maintain the prohibitive precepts, practice patience and diligence, and cultivate all meditative concentrations; yet, if they hear but a single four-line verse of this sutra, I declare that such a person accomplishes the Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā, and this merit surpasses the former merit.”
If one is separated from these dharmas, none of the pāramitās will be accomplished. Śāriputra!

For this reason, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this sutra, believes and understands it, receives and upholds it, contemplates it, and practices it, I say that such a person will swiftly be able to accomplish unsurpassed bodhi. You should know that such a person has already obtained the dharma-seal of the bodhi of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Śāriputra! If there is a bodhisattva who, when preaching this sutra, should make this vow:
"I shall now recite and chant this sutra, and explain it extensively for others."
To be able to give rise to this thought is what is called the fulfillment of the *dānapāramitā*.
Why is this? Because among all forms of giving, the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*) is the most supreme.
If one upholds this sutra and protects the Dharma-body, this is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā);
to accord with the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is likewise called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā);
to be tireless in accordance with reality is what is called the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
To abide in quiescent extinction is what is called the dhyāna-pāramitā;
to attain spontaneous wisdom without being awakened by another is what is called the prajñā-pāramitā.
Śāriputra! If there should be anyone who receives, upholds, and recites even as much as a four-line verse of this sutra, they will swiftly be able to fulfill unsurpassed bodhi.

If any bodhisattvas uphold this essential dharma, whether by reading, reciting, copying, or maintaining its scrolls, wherever they may be, that place shall be as if the Buddha were present. You should know that such persons have already attained the Tathāgata’s treasury of all dharmas.
If there are those who receive and uphold this sutra, although their physical forms differ, their bodhicitta is without dual characteristics.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
This sutra is the Dharma-seal of the true mark of non-retrogression from bodhi.
By this you should know that if any bodhisattvas accord with this sutra, it should be known that such persons shall attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed bodhi.
"If bodhisattvas accord with this sutra, you should know that they are then in accord with all Buddha-dharmas.

At that time, the Four Great Kings who protect the world, together with their retinues, all joined their palms in reverence and respect, and with single-minded right mindfulness, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"We four kings shall now serve as the protectors of the assembly that upholds the True Dharma for the Tathāgata.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who uphold this sutra, they are Dharma-preachers; we shall attend upon, make offerings to, and revere them without distinction from the Buddha."
"Why is this? Because all Buddhas and the Mahāyāna Dharma emerge from this sūtra.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Although I have heard other sūtras from the Buddha, I have never before heard such a profound and most supreme sūtra as this.

I am now able to serve as an audience for the assembly of devas wherever this sūtra may be located—in kingdoms, cities, towns, villages, mountain forests, beneath trees, or in secluded places—where there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, and explain it.”

By means of this sutra, we shall cause the king, his queen, and their retinue to increase in physical vigor and beauty, remaining forever free from sorrow and affliction. We shall constantly provide protection for the ministers, high officials, all the people, and the Dharma-preacher, ensuring they suffer no decline or distress. We shall ensure that within the various kingdoms, the yin and yang are in harmony and free from calamity; that no enemies can inflict harm; that the crops ripen and the people live in peace and happiness; and that the physical vigor, eloquence, and mastery of the Dharma-preacher increase, becoming free and unimpeded. Furthermore, we shall enable the Dharma-preacher to attain great fearlessness when amidst the great assembly, so that he may expound the teaching extensively for others, like a lion king.
At that time, the Blessed One said to Śakra,
Lord of the Devas: “Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!”
"You shall thus protect this sutra and the Dharma-preacher, ensuring they suffer no decline or affliction.
You should now know that to protect the Dharma-preacher is to protect the Dharma; and to protect the Dharma is to protect the land and all sentient beings."
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I, together with the gods of the Brahma-pāriṣadya realm, shall relinquish the bliss of meditative concentration and go to wherever this sutra and the Dharma-preacher may be. There, I shall manifest four signs so that the Dharma-preacher may know that we have come.”

What are the four? First, seeing a great radiance; second, smelling a rare fragrance; third, causing that Dharma master to possess unimpeded eloquence; and fourth, causing all listeners to focus their minds with single-minded concentration.
"By these four signs, know that I am present in this assembly, listening to the True Dharma, and acting as its protector.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
When the Buddha spoke this sutra, my palaces were all deprived of their radiance, trembling with unease, and their power and majesty diminished. Why is this?

It is because the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas listen to this sutra. Wherever this scripture may be, if there are sons or daughters of good family who receive and uphold even a single verse or a single phrase of it, or who hear it once and believe, understand, and uphold it, you should know that such persons have already received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and shall succeed to the rank of a Buddha.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Because those sons and daughters of good family uphold this sutra, they cause the majesty, virtue, and power of my retinue to be utterly destroyed.”

If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, or explain this sutra, wherever they may be, we vow to constantly provide protection and never give rise to even a single thought of obstruction.
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed Śāriputra:
"In a future age, you should receive, uphold, read, recite, and disseminate this sutra, so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time."
Śāriputra said: "So be it, World-Honored One!
I shall receive and uphold it."
He further addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should receive, uphold, read, recite, and disseminate this sutra. Ānandā replied:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
We shall receive and uphold it.
Although we are able to practice and carry it out, we cannot propagate and disseminate it as extensively as the bodhisattvas do.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Do not worry that this sutra will not be widely disseminated; there are immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas present in this assembly, all of whom vow to transmit and propagate it.”
In the assembly, there were sixty koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, desiring to protect and uphold this sutra, rose from their seats and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Great Sage, World-Honored One!
"We vow that we shall circulate this sutra throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

In this Sahā world, Maitreya himself shall proclaim this sutra so that it is never interrupted. If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, there are sentient beings who even briefly hear this scripture but once, you should know that such persons have been prophesied by the Buddha."
"Know that upholding even a single verse or a single line of this sutra is entirely established through the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya.
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“O sons of good family!
You who now uphold this sutra in my presence shall likewise uphold this sutra in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya knelt with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Great Sage, World-Honored One!
In asking about this sutra, I have offended the Tathāgata; I now sincerely repent before the Buddha and pray only that you will compassionately pity and forgive my transgression."
"And may all the bodhisattvas likewise accept my confession of these transgressions.
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"Regarding this sutra, you have attained the profound principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*; you have no doubts concerning the Mahāyāna teachings; and you are free from error in body, speech, and mind. All Buddhas together certify you, and I do so as well."
"The Dharma you have preached is no different from my own.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What shall this sutra be named?
How should we receive and uphold it?
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed Ānanda, saying:

“This sutra is the Mahāyāna principle of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, present, and future; it serves as the eye for all sentient beings and the fundamental mother of all Buddhas. Therefore, this sutra is titled ‘The Sutra on the Immeasurable, Boundless, and Inexhaustible Meaning of the Six Pāramitās of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva Principle.’”
"By this title, you should uphold it.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda and the other great śrāvakas, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas such as Maitreya, and the entire assembly—including gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas such as Akṣayamati from the world-system of Animiṣā—all who heard what the Buddha had spoken were filled with great joy, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Principles and Practices of the Six Pāramitās, Scroll Ten.
